ideas_up_hard.coling::1a16d27a-89fc-4df9-8b4f-cf2532a8: We study a two-dimensional tight-binding model of a topological crystalline insulator protected by rotation symmetry. The model is constructed by stacking two Chern insulators with opposite Chern numbers. These insulators transform under conjugate representations of the rotation group, exemplified by $p_\pm$ orbitals. Despite its apparent similarity to the Kane-Mele model, it does not host stable gapless surface states. Nevertheless the model exhibits topological responses including the appearance of quantized fractional charge bound to rotational defects called disclinations. The model also demonstrates the pumping of angular momentum in response to threading an elementary magnetic flux. These phenomena are described by a mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field corresponding to the rotation symmetry. In addition, we show that the filled bands of the model do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation. This obstruction is removed upon the addition of appropriate atomic orbitals. The removal of this obstruction implies fragile topology. As a result, the response of the model can be derived by representing it as a superposition of atomic orbitals. These orbitals carry positive and negative integer coefficients. Following the analysis of the model, which serves as a prototypical example of two-dimensional TCIs protected by rotation, we examine all TCIs protected by point group symmetries. Those TCIs which do not have protected surface states are either atomic insulators or fragile phases. Remarkably, this implies that gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only if there is a stable Wannier obstruction. We then use dimensional reduction to map the problem of classifying two-dimensional TCIs protected by rotation to a zero-dimensional problem. This zero-dimensional problem is then used to obtain the complete non-interacting classification of such TCIs. We also determine the reduction of this classification in the presence of interactions.
ideas_up_hard.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: The reliable prediction of temporal behavior in complex systems proves essential across numerous scientific disciplines. Strong interest in this capability encounters significant modeling obstacles. Governing equations that describe underlying physics are frequently inaccessible to researchers. When these equations are known, solving them may demand computational resources exceeding available time budgets for real-time prediction. Approximating complex systems using generic functional formats has become standard practice during the machine learning era. Training these approximations directly from observational data without prior assumptions represents a widespread approach. Deep neural networks have demonstrated numerous successes in this domain across varied applications. Model generalizability receives insufficient attention in many implementations. Guarantee margins remain poorly characterized in current methodologies. Data's influence on model performance is often examined superficially, with analyses depending heavily on pre-existing physical knowledge rather than systematic investigation. We address these challenges by implementing a curriculum learning framework. Curriculum learning organizes datasets so training progresses from simple examples toward increasingly difficult ones. This progression enhances both convergence speed and the model's ability to generalize beyond training conditions. The concept originated in robotics research where it proved highly effective. Control systems have also benefited substantially from curriculum learning applications. We apply this methodology to dynamical systems in a comprehensive and systematic manner. Ergodic theory provides mathematical foundations for assessing data requirements. We determine the minimum data volume needed to guarantee faithful representation of physical systems before training begins. Training set structure's influence on long-term prediction accuracy receives thorough investigation. Entropy serves as our quantitative measure of dataset complexity. Informed training set design based on entropy analysis yields substantial improvements in model generalizability. We demonstrate how entropy-guided data selection enhances performance metrics. Our findings provide concrete guidance on data volume requirements for effective modeling. We establish principles for selecting optimal data subsets that maximize learning efficiency. These insights advance data-driven modeling methodology for complex dynamical systems.
ideas_up_hard.coling::7876816d-0ac2-4404-b2bf-deeaa0b7: The CII 158 microns line serves as the primary coolant of interstellar medium in galaxies. Substantial variations appear when comparing different astronomical objects. The emission's main source at galactic scales remains poorly understood by researchers. Earlier investigations of CII emission achieved resolutions of several kiloparsecs or coarser. These observations averaged emission from multiple distinct ISM components within their fields. This study examines CII emission at spiral arm scales for the first time in astronomical research. We investigate this spectral line's physical origin in spiral structures. The line's utility as a star formation tracer is evaluated through observational analysis. CII and OI observations were obtained for one segment of M31's spiral arms. The Infrared Space Observatory provided the spectroscopic data for this investigation. We compared CII emission against neutral gas tracers including CO molecular clouds and HI atomic hydrogen. Star formation indicators H-alpha and Spitzer 24 micron emission were also examined. The CII emission morphology closely resembles Ha when both datasets are smoothed to identical angular resolution. The 24 micron dust continuum shows similarly striking morphological agreement with CII distribution. Neutral gas tracers exhibit significantly weaker correlation with the CII spatial distribution. The CII cooling rate per hydrogen atom shows dramatic spatial variation across the mapped region. Border areas display cooling rates of approximately 2.7×10^-26 ergs per second per atom. Star-forming regions reach approximately 1.4×10^-25 ergs per second per atom. The CII to FIR(42-122) ratio maintains near-constant values at 2 percent. This exceeds typically cited values by a factor of three in the literature. M31 does not represent an anomalous galaxy in our interpretation. Whole-galaxy flux measurements incorporate central regions where CII/FIR ratios drop significantly. Previous resolved observations failed to isolate individual spiral arms from surrounding emission. Earlier studies did not extend to the outer galactic disk radii sampled here. Published PDR models were fitted to our observational data. The best-fit solution yields G_0 approximately 100 for the radiation field. The density parameter n reaches approximately 3000 cm^-3 for PDR emission in M31's star-forming arm regions.
ideas_up_hard.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a novel artificial intelligence methodology termed the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS), which extracts selected attributes from objects spanning multiple domains including chess problems, classical music compositions, and renowned artworks. The system recombines these extracted features to generate new attributes, which can subsequently be employed to create novel objects possessing creative value for human audiences. These novel objects may relate to any single source domain from which attributes were originally harvested. The methodology permits transferring substantial portions of creative content generation responsibility from human creators to computational machines. We validated this approach specifically within chess problem composition as our experimental testbed. The system automatically composed numerous distinct sets of chess problems by processing attributes drawn from human-authored chess problems, competitive tournament games, renowned paintings by master artists, computer-evolved abstract artworks, photographic portraits of human subjects, and classical music recordings. Generated chess problems underwent quality assessment using a pre-existing computational chess aesthetics model that had received prior experimental validation. Human domain experts provided additional independent quality assessments of the generated problems. Experimental findings indicate that attributes gathered from both chess-related and non-chess domains, when recombined via DSNS methodology, successfully generate chess problems exhibiting reasonably elevated aesthetic quality. Notably, low-quality chess source material consisting of tournament game sequences played between inexperienced players, when combined with actual photographic images of people, produced three-move chess problems matching or exceeding the quality of problems generated from high-quality chess sources. These high-quality sources comprised published compositions created by acknowledged human experts in problem composition. The photograph-enhanced low-quality source also demonstrated superior generation efficiency compared to expert-sourced material. The underlying mechanism enabling information from unrelated domains to integrate successfully and function effectively in chess problem generation remains unexplained at present. The DSNS methodology exhibits scalability in principle and maintains applicability to any problem domain where objects possess attributes representable through real number encoding systems.
ideas_up_hard.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad: The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) peak appears in cosmic matter distribution at redshifts reaching ~3.5. This feature represents continuing expansion of the sonic horizon. Temperature anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background first revealed this sonic horizon. Galaxy surveys now measure the BAO peak position to better than ~1% accuracy. Ly-alpha forests achieve ~1.4-1.6% precision in these measurements. Quasar clustering provides an independent method for detecting the BAO signal. The Alcock-Paczyński (AP) effect emerges from changing ratios of angular to spatial/redshift dimensions. Source distributions are presumed spherically-symmetric in this analysis. Distance variations alter these geometric ratios systematically. Combined with the BAO measurement, this effect becomes a powerful cosmological tool. Universe geometry can be assessed through this combined approach. Our paper employs five BAO peak measurements exclusively. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV final release provided this data. Average redshifts span <z>=0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33 across these measurements. We conduct a direct head-to-head comparison between two cosmological models. The standard model Lambda-CDM serves as one candidate. The R_h=ct universe represents its principal competitor in this test. We complement the AP diagnostic with an additional probe for completeness. This volume-averaged distance probe assumes constant comoving distance scale r_d. The Hubble constant introduces uncertainty into many cosmological tests. Both probes avoid this uncertain parameter entirely. Model selection benefits from these parameter-free diagnostics. The AP effect alone favors R_h=ct over the standard model. This preference shows likelihood ~75% versus ~25% for Lambda-CDM. Planck-Lambda-CDM receives stronger support from the volume-averaged distance probe exclusively. That probe yields likelihood ~80% versus ~20% against R_h=ct. Joint analysis combining both probes produces inconclusive results. Comparable likelihoods emerge for both cosmological models under combined testing. BAO data alone cannot confirm accelerating Universe expansion based on this work.

Context. Filaments are ubiquitous in the Galaxy, and they host star formation. Detecting them in a reliable way is therefore key towards our understanding of the star formation process.

Aims. We explore whether supervised machine learning can identify filamentary structures on the whole Galactic plane.

Methods. We used two versions of UNet-based networks for image segmentation. We used H2 column density images of the Galactic plane obtained with Herschel Hi-GAL data as input data. We trained the UNet-based networks with skeletons (spine plus branches) of filaments that were extracted from these images. Background masks were produced to exclude non-filamentary regions. Missing data masks were created to handle observational gaps. We tested eight training scenarios to determine the best scenario for our astrophysical purpose of classifying pixels as filaments.

Results. The training of the UNets allows us to create a new image of the Galactic plane by segmentation in which pixels belonging to filamentary structures are identified. With this new method, we classify more pixels as belonging to filaments than the spine plus branches structures we used as input. The increase ranges from a factor of 2 to 7. The specific factor depends on the classification threshold used. New structures are revealed by our neural network approach. These structures are mainly low-contrast filaments. Previous detection methods had missed these features. We use standard metrics to evaluate the performances of the different training scenarios. This allows us to demonstrate the robustness of the method. We determine an optimal threshold value through systematic comparison. This threshold maximizes the recovery of the input labelled pixel classification.

Conclusions. This proof-of-concept study shows that supervised machine learning can reveal filamentary structures. These structures are present throughout the Galactic plane. The detection includes low-density structures never seen before. Low-contrast structures have also been newly identified. This offers important perspectives for future filament studies.

ideas_up_hard.coling::f4961832-eeb4-41fc-8a64-82c30107: Let me preface this by saying that I really do like Cowboy Bebop. The animation quality surpasses most series from its era. The character designs demonstrate exceptional artistic vision. The soundtrack blends jazz with various genres seamlessly. The action sequences choreograph combat with cinematic precision. When these elements unite, the show occasionally becomes a jaw dropping audiovisual masterpiece. The finale delivers breathtaking emotional catharsis. Spike demonstrates compelling complexity as a protagonist. Jet serves as an effective counterbalance to Spike's recklessness. Together they comprise only two-fifths of the entire Bebop Crew. Ein's introduction labels him a "data dog" with hyperintelligence. This premise vanishes immediately after his debut. He subsequently functions merely as the crew's pet. Faye exhibits the worst characteristics that writers assign female characters. She displays constant bossiness toward her teammates. Her greed motivates most of her individual decisions. She obsesses over her own physical beauty. The narrative requires her rescue more frequently than she provides assistance. She creates hindrances for the group during critical missions. Her clothing reveals excessive skin purely for fanservice purposes. Ed vacillates between endearing and annoying viewers. She walks this precarious line throughout her appearances. Her character receives minimal development beyond her introductory episode. The main villain Vicious proves especially problematic. He possesses minimal discernible character traits. His motivation extends barely beyond craving additional power. The show explores fragments of his backstory. It never establishes coherent motivation for his actions. By the finale, Vicious remains little more than an evil figure. He wears a black coat as his defining visual characteristic. His fighting skill forces Spike to struggle landing bullets. He becomes a representation of the syndicate Spike abandoned. Five episodes center on him directly: Sympathy for the Devil, Jupiter Jazz parts one and two, and Real Folk Blues parts one and two. ideas_up_hard.coling::3bec38ad-9c98-4004-95a3-5b24858e: I live in New Zealand, which is located in the southwestern Pacific Ocean. We are currently in the middle of "one of the most important elections in our country's history" (apparently), though similar claims are made during every electoral cycle. I am not planning to vote in this election, which marks my first time abstaining. I think that the campaigns that the electoral commission are running to encourage everyone to vote are stupid, particularly given their condescending tone. A lot of the political-minded people around me don't seem to understand that some people simply don't have a view, despite this being a legitimate position. When Helen Clark's government ended after nine years in power, John Key came in representing the National Party. Did it really affect me in any measurable way? I mean, not really in terms of daily routine. Actually, not at all in terms of personal circumstances. If Labour win this year under their current leadership, will it affect me personally? I don't really think so given my economic position. I'll continue doing what I do in my current job, and people will continue to hate the government regardless of who leads it. Until a couple of terms later National come back in, which follows historical patterns. And it still has no real effect on my daily life given my stable situation. So, therefore, I am of the opinion that I really don't give a shit about electoral outcomes. It's not worth my time researching to try and give a shit, given my limited free hours. Therefore I should leave the voting to people who know somewhat what they're talking about, including policy experts. And that's fine with most reasonable observers. It's a generally accepted attitude here among younger demographics. But recently there has been a whole lot of guilting people into voting through aggressive advertising. With campaigns with slogans like "It's only democracy if you vote, idiot," which insults non-voters. I've even seen some extreme ones with a picture of the earth decaying from pollution. Something about climate change being the urgent issue. Just a huge block letter "VOTE" next to it without further explanation. If I were to mention I wasn't planning on voting to half of my friends, they'd be fine with it based on past reactions. But the other half would fucking grill me alive with moral arguments. Saying that I'm "not contributing to my country's future," as if my single vote determines outcomes. And this guilt makes people feel that they need to vote out of social pressure. They obviously don't know who for since they haven't researched. So they are easily vulnerable to manipulation by partisan actors. Just yesterday I saw a flyer in one of my lectures with a run-down on each parties' policies, distributed anonymously. Except it wasn't a run-down presenting objective information. In fact it had colour-coded which policies were good according to someone's subjective opinion. It basically stacked up left to right that right is evil and left is good, using inflammatory language. The green party also came in last week offering material incentives. Offered free bus passes outside of peak hours for uni students exclusively. Which is the most moronic policy in the universe from a transport planning perspective. Because it achieves nothing in the real world regarding congestion reduction. But it gets a bunch of voters converted through self-interest alone. I'm sure the right wing is doing it too with their own demographic targets. But the left is more apparent to me as a uni student attending a progressive campus. So in conclusion - people should not be encouraged to vote without understanding issues. They should be encouraged not to vote if they do not know what they're talking about regarding policy implications. People will vote for all the wrong reasons including peer pressure and minor bribes. Politics becomes open to extreme manipulation of voters through emotional appeals. The only reason the electoral commission is guilting people into voting is because they are all interested in politics professionally. They don't realise that a lot of people just quite simply don't care about governmental composition. It's like forcing the entire country to watch the rugby when they prefer other sports.
ideas_up_hard.coling::bd4df89c-701f-407b-9fc6-2c51aa5b: I'm talking about the type of condemnation voiced consistently by certain users of rpolitics, certain members of OWS, and Gawker's Hamilton Nolan. It is a viewpoint I will paraphrase roughly as follows: The mere fact that we live in a system where some people can amass vastly more money than others is, itself, immoral. If you do amass wealth under this system, you are quite arguably a bad person. Hedge fund managers are sitting around spending tens of millions on embalmed sharks. Don't they know that a tiny fraction of their daily earnings would make a huge difference in others' lives? Would be enough to pay off the average redditor's student loans, for example? Every time I've heard this shitty argument, I've heard it from activists who hail from the middle-class tier of an advanced Western economy. I've also encountered this reasoning from internet commenters who belong to the working-class demographic. Here's the thing, though: you, too, have vastly more resources than most people worldwide. If you could save 100 by not upgrading your smartphone, you would retain a functional device. By walking home in the rain instead of taking a cab, you would get moderate exercise. By eating lentils for a few weeks you would consume adequate protein. By eating beans as an alternative you would maintain proper nutrition. By foregoing that new item of clothing you wanted, your current wardrobe would remain sufficient. You could donate that 100 to save the lives of dozens of kids who would otherwise die of Malaria. Is your comfort more important than other peoples' lives? Is your convenience worth more than children's survival? Is your entertainment a higher priority than preventing deaths? And, btw, I will not tolerate deflections to the effect of: "but charities might not use the money responsibly." I reject arguments claiming charitable donations could have negative effects on local industry in the long run. As a premise of this CMV, we must stipulate that if wealth could be redistributed, that redistribution would, indeed, benefit the recipients. We must further stipulate that if the average American wanted to donate in a genuinely-beneficial manner towards a worthy cause, he'd be able to do so. I don't think these are crazy assumptions to make. So, my view is that people who rail against "the rich," purely on the ground that they're rich, are hypocrites for overlooking their own relative economic standing in the world. If they believe others' wealth should be redistributed to curb inequality, they are hypocrites for not redistributing their own wealth to curb inequality. Now, I don't donate much to charity. But nor do I regard people richer than me as innately evil human beings. I can acknowledge the preference revealed by my decision-making. That preference is: I'd rather upgrade to business class than save 500 lives in a developing country. For this reason, if some billionaire would rather upgrade his yacht than dissolve all his assets to promote communism, I don't really blame him. It seems quite a few people disagree with me. The rebels ousted President Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi from power during their takeover. Hadi still claims he's Yemen's legitimate leader. He is working with the Saudis to return to his country. Other regional allies have joined this effort. Since mid-March, more than 700 people have been killed in violence. The World Health Organization provided these casualty figures. The conflict shows no sign of slowing down. The Houthis say they have the support of the country's people behind them. "It's the right of the Yemeni people to stand against the attacks in all possible means as long as the attacks continue," Al-Houthi said Sunday. "After our people move and react against the attacks and killing of children and women, we do not want to hear any voices and cries." There are signs of some fracturing among forces loyal to former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh. Many of these troops have fought alongside the rebels in recent battles. Gen. AbdulRahman AlHalili leads more than 10,000 troops. He has now allied himself with Hadi, military sources said Sunday. Saudi Brig. Gen. Ahmed Asiri said Sunday that airstrikes had decimated the Houthis' central command. The coalition achieved this by targeting their communications infrastructure. The rebels are now holding a defensive stance in besieged areas, he claimed. The Saudi-led coalition began the campaign known as Operation Decisive Storm on March 26. Since that date, the coalition has launched 2,300 airstrikes, Asiri said. After hours at sea, chaos and desperation gripped a Yemeni city. CNN's Don Melvin contributed to this report. Christine Theodorou also provided reporting assistance.

The cake's exterior frosting remained neutral in color to maintain the surprise element. Lair expressed nervousness about raising a daughter in their testosterone-dominated household. Another viewer noted that having six protective older brothers represents a unique advantage. The little girl will benefit from their watchful care throughout her childhood years. Lair is set to have her seventh child in August. Currently there is no word on possible names being considered by the parents. The couple has not revealed whether they plan to have additional children after this pregnancy.
ideas_up_hard.coling::17ad7e76-2fa1-4c9b-a42b-44a53287: I remain genuinely uncertain about this debate's resolution, though I'll begin by defending opposition to same-sex marriage for specific tactical reasons: 1. My sympathies actually tilt toward the opposing viewpoint, making the conservative position appear more vulnerable and less socially accepted, which means championing arguments I find personally unconvincing will sharpen my rhetorical abilities through difficult advocacy. 2. The responsibility for justifying institutional change falls upon those seeking marriage expansion (my reasoning follows below), which determined my initial argumentative stance. Before proceeding further, please view [this linked video] (its runtime spans exactly two minutes). That presentation convinced me that justification obligations rest with those proposing to alter marriage's defining characteristics (while I harbor no inherent objection to definitional evolution, substantive rationales must precede any institutional transformation). Responses like "Why not?" to inquiries about same-sex marriage acceptance actually exemplify the teapot fallacy, which involves improperly transferring justification responsibilities to one's opponent. Equality arguments strike me as fundamentally unpersuasive in this context. Constitutional guarantees of life, liberty, freedom, and happiness-pursuit certainly apply regardless of sexual orientation. Yet equality invocations here constitute a red herring distraction. Marriage functions not as a universal privilege requiring identical availability across all relationship configurations. The institution emerged around reproductive capacity, whereas same-sex partnerships, however loving or committed they may be, cannot by biological definition produce offspring. Certain heterosexual unions also lack procreative potential, including elderly spouses and infertile partners, but the video clarifies why this comparison fails; exceptional cases don't justify extending definitions to encompass what lies outside the norm, since norms derive their meaning from typical instances rather than outliers. This equality claim differs fundamentally from women's suffrage or slavery's abolition. The criteria often gets framed through this question: "If mutual love exists between two individuals, what justification exists for marriage prohibition?" Love bears no relation to marriage's actual criteria, including romantic affection specifically. Accepting romantic or sexual attraction as sufficient criteria would logically permit incestuous marriages. Objections arise that incest differs due to familial power imbalances and genetic abnormality risks. Power disparities can emerge in heterosexual relationships, homosexual partnerships, or any other configuration. Marriage law shouldn't incorporate such concerns as foundational principles. Furthermore, incestuous partners might choose childlessness, pursue adoption instead, face infertility naturally, or themselves be homosexual. One could consistently advocate for incestuous marriage alongside homosexual unions. You're welcome to defend this position, though remember that justification burdens fall upon you as the change advocate. The "why would you care?" objection lacks logical force; an institution shouldn't undergo transformation merely because proposed changes produce no obvious harm. Utilitarian frameworks also fail to validate this reasoning. Same-sex couples can maintain fulfilling long-term romantic and sexual partnerships without requiring the marriage label. Altering marriage definitions to satisfy one demographic group resembles (in logical structure, not emotional weight) acquiescing to lobbyist pressure for their satisfaction. Most pro-gay-marriage arguments rely on emotional manipulation or popularity appeals. The phrase "gay rights" was strategically crafted to evoke images of internment camps. Similarly, "homophobe" entered vocabulary specifically to delegitimize opposing perspectives. This issue's current cultural prominence, combined with the fact that many opponents are religious fundamentalists deploying straw man tactics, doesn't automatically validate the "more reasonable side." If incestuous marriage legalization became a popular movement, complete with online videos and websites celebrating such couples' struggles, public opinion would likely shift in that direction too. Programs fail for numerous distinct reasons. The following examples illustrate typical failure modes: Division by zero: Elementary mathematics teaches that dividing by zero yields no meaningful result. When software instructs a processor to perform this impossible operation, the processor signals an error condition. Programs lacking proper error-handling routines will terminate abnormally when receiving such signals.

Access violation: Operating systems allocate specific memory regions to each running application. Attempting to read or write outside these designated boundaries triggers a protection fault. The operating system immediately notifies the offending application of the boundary transgression. Applications without defensive code to handle such notifications will cease functioning.

Deadlock: Imagine two children engaged in a toy exchange scenario. Child A possesses a red toy while Child B holds a blue toy. Child A refuses to release the red toy until receiving the blue one. Meanwhile, Child B maintains the same conditional stance regarding the blue toy. This mutual waiting creates an endless stalemate where no progress occurs. When software components exhibit this circular dependency pattern, the entire application becomes unresponsive. The only remedy involves forcibly terminating the frozen process and launching a fresh instance.

Unhandled exception: Modern software architectures incorporate structured error detection mechanisms. One code segment identifies an anomalous condition and signals this discovery by raising an exception. A different code segment should intercept this signal and execute corrective measures. When no component successfully intercepts a raised exception, a diagnostic message typically appears on screen. The application then shuts down after displaying this notification.

Software defects cause all these malfunction scenarios. Defects represent portions of code that contain logical errors or fail to anticipate certain runtime conditions. Different applications exhibit varying defect densities. Several factors explain this variation: developers working under tight deadlines may skip thorough validation procedures, insufficient quality assurance testing leaves problems undetected, or the sheer complexity of certain systems makes comprehensive scenario coverage impractical.

Consider programs as procedural instructions for accomplishing tasks. A frequently cited illustration involves assembling a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. An initial instruction set might specify: obtain bread slices, acquire peanut butter jar, locate jelly container, retrieve spreading utensil, apply peanut butter to first slice, spread jelly on second slice, press slices together, present finished sandwich. Should the peanut butter supply become exhausted mid-process, the instruction sequence provides no continuation path, resulting in a crash scenario.

A more elaborate program would model pizza restaurant operations. Such a system involves numerous ingredient varieties. The combination possibilities multiply exponentially. Multiple employees perform simultaneous tasks. Coordination challenges increase proportionally. Potential failure points proliferate throughout the workflow.

Certain problems admit straightforward solutions. Other issues resist easy remediation. Developers sometimes postpone addressing difficult bugs indefinitely. These unresolved defects manifest as crashes during actual usage. Time constraints often force teams to prioritize features over stability. Budget limitations prevent exhaustive testing across all possible usage patterns. Legacy codebases accumulate technical debt over years of modifications. Documentation gaps leave current maintainers guessing about original design intentions. Integration with third-party components introduces unpredictable behaviors. Hardware variations create environment-specific failures that testing environments never reproduce. User actions follow unexpected sequences that developers never imagined. Edge cases emerge only after deployment to production environments. The complexity inherent in modern software makes completely crash-free applications virtually impossible to achieve.

They now converge on a larger portion of the view area. The camera on DSCOVR used to take these pictures has a FOV of just 0.61deg. There's a certain distance where your hand and the monitor get smaller together. At this distance they shrink at the same rate. This is because the distance between you and those two things becomes a lot greater. The distance between those two things themselves remains constant. I believe the amount sits somewhere around five million dollars per individual. This replacement could occur without creating a strict increased tax burden on their people overall. For instance: if you owe ten thousand dollars in income tax this year under current law, but a two thousand dollar capital tax is instituted next year as new policy, then you are still in the same position as long as your income tax is reduced to eight thousand dollars correspondingly. Whether these taxes are effective or preferable remains debated. That question belongs to economics rather than personal finance. I will not belabour that point further here. Note: if the money you have saved earns money through returns (interest, or dividends, or maybe rent from a condo you own as property), then those earnings are typically taxed alongside your wage income under existing rules. The first thing you need to do is look at your terms and conditions of your credit card. Alternatively, you can ask your bank directly about their payment application policies. Different financial institutions follow varying protocols for allocating customer payments. As Dilip notes in his answer, US regulations govern how banks must distribute funds. They will likely apply the minimum payment to the lower rate balance first. Any amount exceeding the minimum must go toward the higher rate balance. Other countries have different legal frameworks governing payment allocation. Local customs also influence how banks handle these transactions. Never assume the bank will prioritize the higher balance without verification. Some institutions use proportional distribution across all outstanding amounts.

Let's take the following example to illustrate these concepts. You owe $6000 total across different transaction types. $5000 accrues interest at 13.5% representing normal purchase rate. $1000 carries a 22% rate from a cash advance. Your bank applies payments to both balances proportionally in this scenario. A payment of $600 will reduce your purchase balance by $500. The remaining $100 decreases your cash advance balance.

The average APR calculation requires summing products of rates times balances. In this case, (.135*5000 + .225*1000)/6000 equals 15%. This mathematical approach is called a weighted average. It reflects the actual cost of borrowing across multiple rate categories.

If the bank applies the payment differently, complications arise in your calculations. Some banks direct funds to the lower rate first exclusively. Others apply a specified portion to lower rates before addressing higher ones. Entering a simple average into a calculator will be misleading under these circumstances. Your average APR will rise over time as purchase balances decrease. The cash advance balance remains untouched during this period. The opposite scenario may decrease your effective rate if higher balances get paid first.

The weighted average is probably reasonably close for rough estimates. This holds true even with rules applying balances differently. The exception occurs when banks pay 100% toward lower rates exclusively. It may be the simplest option for preliminary financial planning. Use it when approximations suffice rather than precise figures.

One approach using online calculators treats these like two separate loans. Many calculators exist specifically for multiple balances simultaneously. You can allocate funds differently to the two 'cards' in these tools. This would allow you to see payoff timelines for higher balances. It probably won't perfectly match your actual statements from the bank. You'll have to either live with small calculation errors. The alternative is doing the math by hand using spreadsheet formulas.

I cannot stress this enough, so I'll just repeat it: Don't plan your finances around your credit score. Don't even think about your credit score at all. Plan a budget and stick to it religiously. Make sure you include short and long term savings in your budget, allocating percentages wisely. Pay your bills on time without exception. Use credit responsibly by keeping balances low. Do all of these things consistently, and your credit rating will take care of itself without intervention. Don't try to plan your finances around raising it artificially.

On the subject of 0% financing specifically, my rule of thumb is to only ever use it when I have enough money saved up to buy the thing outright in cash. Even then only proceed if your budget will still balance with the added cost of repaying the loan monthly. Other people have other rules they follow, including not taking such loans at all under any circumstances. You should develop a rule that works for you based on your income, but you should have a rule written down somewhere. One rule you shouldn't have is "do whatever will optimize your credit score" because you shouldn't plan your finances around your credit score ever.

All things considered, I think the most important thing in your situation is to make sure that you don't let the teaser rate tempt you into making purchases you wouldn't otherwise make with regular financing. You're not really getting free money from the lender; you're just shifting around the time frame for payment to a later date, and only within a limited window at that which eventually closes. Also, be sure to read the fine print in the credit agreement carefully; they can be filled with gotchas and pitfalls designed to catch unwary borrowers. In particular, if you don't clear the balance by the end of the introductory rate period completely, you can sometimes incur interest charges retroactively to the date of purchase at high rates. Make sure you know your terms and conditions cold before signing anything.

It sounds like you're just getting started on your financial journey, so best of luck with building wealth, and remember that Rome wasn't built in a day by ancient workers. Patience can be the most effective tool in your personal finance arsenal for long-term success.

p.s. Don't plan your finances around your credit score under any circumstances.

What do you think I should wear tomorrow?"
"What do you think of this outfit?"
"Would this necklace look good with these shoes?"
Many people ask these types of questions everyday. You may even be one of them. Research from Stanford University indicates that individuals who seek multiple perspectives tend to make purchasing decisions they regret less frequently. Why? Studies have shown that more than 50 percent of Americans ask for a second opinion before doing it. For example, have you ever been shopping and asked your friend if you should get fancy expensive shoes? And if they said no, you would ask someone else? Well you are not alone. This is very common according to a recent study conducted by Harvard University. Fashion is changing whether it be fast fashion, or street wear. The global apparel market now generates over 1.5 trillion dollars annually. Consumers spend an average of four hours per week browsing clothing options online. People often ask for second opinions because they feel the need to. Imagine yourself trying on an ugly over sized t-shirt. You may like it, and maybe your friend does too. But if you were to ask someone else like your dad to see if they would like it do you think they would? No! Absolutely not. Dads hate over sized ugly t-shirts. Asking for a second opinion is always a good idea. Whether it be positive feedback, or negative feedback. It shapes your mind to make the correct choice. This will not always be the case though. Some people refuse to listen, even if it is constructive negative feedback. A study found by George Mason University reports that after asking for a second opinion and the response is negative feedback, they will still continue to choose the opposite of the feedback they were given. Why are our mentalities like this? Humans have evolved over time to become the dominant species. Our brains in away think we are always right, and everyone is wrong. This is why some people have so much trouble respecting other people's opinions. They refuse to believe they are wrong. The FBI reported that even serial killers asked for multiple opinions to see if they should kill their first victim. Although everyone said no, the serial killer continues to make the bad choice anyway. Although many people do ask for more opinions for feedback, what about the people that don't? Research found by the Virginia Department of Health has found out that those with depression, anxiety, and insomnia were 10 times less likely to ask for multiple opinions and advice. Due to over thinking, shyness, and embarrassment, they think they will only get negative feedback, which leads to them not even asking. This is another reason why depression is on the rise. Mental health disorders now affect approximately one in five adults in the United States each year. People feel like they are trapped, that there is no one to help them, not even their close friends can help them. They are scared of getting judged and humiliated for asking for advice because they are scared of being wrong or appearing stupid. This is a common issue today that is still growing. Another study found by Virginia Tech discovered that people who typically do ask for advice almost everyday, almost always asks someone older due to them being wiser and having more knowledge in life than they do. Looking for feedback and asking for multiple opinions is always the best if you are trying to look for good advice, or wanting to make improvements to something in your life. Whether it be a school project, important office work, or trying on different clothes, there will always be room for improvement. So don't be afraid to ask multiple people for advice and feedback.

Summer is a time for students to take the stress off of school and to have fun with their friends. Some schools think kids should still have projects throughout the summer to continue their learning. Each school is different, some schools have the teachers come up with the project, while others lets the students make it. Schools should have teacher-designed projects for the summer because it would get students ready for what they will learn that year, teachers could count it as a grade once school starts, and it would be an easy project that would not take too long to do.

Teachers know what they will be teaching in the upcoming semester, so they would make the projects on specific units to prepare students for the class. Doing this is great because it will get the students ready and interested into the subject early on. This will help the students for when they start school because they will already know a little about the topic. The more students know to start with, the better they might do in the class throughout the entire year.

Another great thing is if the teacher designed the project, then they could count the project as a grade to get the school year started with a solid foundation. This is good because right off the bat the student could have a good grade if they do the project correctly and follow all instructions. Knowing this, more people, for sure, would do the project to secure that initial grade boost. Starting the year off with a good grade can help benefit you later on, if you start to struggle a little bit in more challenging units. The project would be easy, so it would be easy to get a good grade, which is a great way to start a school year with confidence. The more students doing the project, the more students you will have thinking and getting involved in school during the summer months when learning typically stops.

Summer is the teachers' vacations as well, and they know as much as the kids do that they want to relax and recharge. Lots of kids travel and hangout with friends during summer, and teachers know that reality, so they would make it a pretty fair and easy project that respects students' free time. This paper extends Lenc&Vedaldi15 by examining CNN representations at the FC7 layer for equivariance properties. The original work focused on different network depths. Training with specific transformation groups enhances representational equivalence according to the findings.

Authors trained over 30 networks using varied jitter configurations, demonstrating substantial experimental effort. The central thesis remains elusive despite this comprehensive approach. Measurements on FC7 differ from Lenc&Vedaldi15's chosen layer, yet novel theoretical contributions are scarce. Jitter's role in achieving invariance was already established in prior literature. The evaluation methodology appears sound in most respects. The title promises solutions that the content fails to deliver adequately.

Representation distance experiments contain several critical flaws that undermine the conclusions:
* FC7's position immediately before the output layer raises methodological concerns. FC8 serves as the sole classification layer separating FC7 from final predictions. Class likelihoods emerge directly after this linear projection step. The equivalence map merely re-projects FC8 weights from the attached network back to original network parameters. Multi-layer analysis would strengthen the investigation since all networks have completed training. Deeper architectural analysis could reveal patterns invisible at single-layer examination.
* Classification error rates on test data are conspicuously absent from the representation distance experiment. Linear transformation compatibility between representations cannot be verified without these metrics. Performance benchmarks would confirm whether the learned representations maintain functional equivalence. Accuracy measurements serve as ground truth for representation quality.
* K-NN experiment methodology lacks essential procedural details about measurement granularity. Per-example test set evaluation remains unspecified in the documentation. Timing relative to equivalence map training is ambiguous throughout. Networks trained on similar jitter transformation groups should demonstrate superior compatibility on target tasks as a clearer demonstration.
* Equivariance improvements fail to materialise consistently across all experimental tasks. Lambda_1 and lambda_2 parameters assume extremely small values in the formulation. The composite loss function effectively reduces to standard data jitter under these conditions. Original and transformed image losses simply accumulate without meaningful interaction. FC7 layer selection may introduce fundamental limitations not present at other depths.

This manuscript presents FC7 equivariance findings that possess some intrinsic interest. Novel observations drawn from the experimental data remain disappointingly sparse. Equivalence experiment design flaws compromise the interpretability of results. Equivariance finetuning methodology exhibits significant weaknesses requiring revision. Acceptance cannot be recommended given these substantial deficiencies. Refining experiments on pre-trained networks would address several concerns. Restructuring the manuscript as an investigative study could enhance its contribution. The field would benefit from a more thorough analytical treatment.

Additional minor problems warrant attention before publication:
* The new equivariance mapping criterion lacks experimental validation for performance gains. Comparative benchmarks against baseline methods are missing entirely.
* Angular measurements on pages 1 and 5 omit necessary unit specifications. Degrees versus radians remains ambiguous to readers.
* Page three states "In practice, it is difficult..." but incorrectly identifies M_g as the optimisation target. The loss function computed over M_g undergoes maximisation/minimisation instead.
* Footnote 2 on page 4 describes activation halving as dropout incorrectly. Constant scaling factors transfer readily to adjacent weight layers. True dropout involves stochastic neuron deactivation during training.
* RVL-CDIP network architecture correspondence to Alexnet requires explicit confirmation. Architectural details determine result interpretability across datasets.
* Figure 3a and 3b on page 7 employ white diagonal elements creating visual confusion. Identical representations should display zero distance mathematically. This visualisation choice obscures experimental correctness verification.
ideas_up_hard.coling::07106895-c293-4117-be28-f7598533:
Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see its application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies IB to train deep networks, though the original papers only presented the concept without implementation. Please see below for my note regarding the independent work claim that requires verification.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound is very clear and accessible. Even researchers who are not very familiar with variational inference can follow the mathematical steps presented. The explanation of the IB principle demonstrates strong pedagogical clarity that benefits newcomers to this area. Experimental results seem to be very promising and suggest practical utility. The empirical validation appears thorough across multiple benchmark datasets.

I found the presentation for the model a bit confusing in several respects. In variational inference and information maximisation frameworks, p usually denotes the generative model being learned. Meanwhile q represents the "inference engine" that approximates intractable posteriors. This convention means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure itself. However the presented VIB framework assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** from which samples are drawn. This distribution is approximated by the empirical distribution over training examples. Thus here the actual model is q(y|z)p(z|x) rather than following standard notation. Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, specifically in paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense needs clarification here? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this particular case. But this interpretation makes the two definitions contradict to each other in problematic ways!

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder architectures. They also discuss the warm-up training strategy that involves tuning beta gradually. However, even when the loss function formula is mathematically identical to the variational lowerbound used in VAE literature (in this case beta = 1 exactly), the underlying probabilistic model is fundamentally different in structure! For example, r(z) in VIB serves as the variational approximation to p(z). This means r(z) is not a component in the generative model itself. While in VAE frameworks it represents the prior distribution over latent variables. That prior is actually defined in the modelling procedure as a design choice. Similarly p(z|x) in VIB is included in the model as an encoder. While in VAE literature that term represents the approximate posterior distribution. It can be independently chosen without affecting other model components (e.g. you can use p(x|z) as a deep NN architecture but p(z|x) as a deep NN or alternatively a Gaussian process).

In summary, I think the presentation for the modelling procedure is unclear and needs revision. I hope these points would be made clearer in the camera-ready version. The current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a Bayesian person trained in probabilistic modeling conventions. In the VAE comparison section, it's better to clearly mention the structural differences between VIB and VAE frameworks. Provide some intuitions explaining why the VIB interpretation is preferred for this application.

Typos:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 caption states "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

**claim for independent work**
The authors claimed that the manuscript presented an independent work to Chalk et al. 2016. That preprint has been online since May 2016 on arxiv. It seems to me that nowadays deep learning research is very competitive globally. Many research groups publish the same idea at nearly the same time independently. So I would trust this claim provisionally and commend the authors' honesty in disclosure. But in case this claim is not true upon investigation, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance at this venue.
ideas_up_hard.coling::745b25d5-34c6-4c43-a690-6414f205:
The paper describes an MT training data selection approach that scores and ranks general-domain sentences using a CNN classifier. Comparison to prior work using continuous or n-gram based language models is well done, even though it is not clear if the paper also compared against bilingual data selection (e.g. sum of difference of cross-entropies).

The motivation to use a CNN instead of an RNN/LSTM was first unclear to me, but it is a strength of the paper to argue that certain sections of a text/sentence are more important than others. This selective emphasis is achieved by a CNN architecture. However, the paper does not experimentally show whether a BOW representation is more important. The paper also omits testing whether a SEQ representation yields better results. No analysis compares the combination of both representations against using them individually.

The textual description of the CNN using one-hot encoding is clear and detailed. The alternative approach employing semi-supervised learning with pre-trained embeddings receives equally thorough explanation. The description points out the important aspects of the architecture. However, a picture of the layers showing how inputs are combined would be worth a thousand words.

The paper is overall well written, but some parentheses for citations are not necessary since \citet differs from \citep in formatting requirements (e.g. line 385 demonstrates this error).

Experiments and evaluation support the claims of the paper comprehensively. I am a little bit concerned about the method of determining the number of selected in-domain sentences described at line 443. This determination relies on a separate validation set whose composition remains unspecified.

What validation data is used here remains an open question. It is also not clear on what data hyperparameters of the CNN models are chosen during the tuning process. How sensitive are the models to different hyperparameter configurations has not been investigated. Whether small changes in validation data composition would alter the selected sentence count significantly deserves exploration.

Table 2 should really compare scores of different approaches with the same number of sentences selected to ensure fair evaluation. As Figure 1 shows, the approach of the paper still seems to outperform the baselines even under this constraint.

Other comments worth considering include the following points. I would be interested in an experiment that compares the technique of the paper against baselines when more in-domain data is available beyond just the development set. The results section could feature some example sentences selected by the different methods. The discussion section would benefit from concrete illustrations supporting the claims made in section 5.4 about abstraction benefits.

In regards to the argument of abstracting away from surface forms in 5.4, another baseline deserves mention. Axelrod's 2015 work replaced some words with POS tags to reduce LM data sparsity. Comparing against this method would reveal whether the word2vec embeddings provide an additional advantage over grammatical abstraction alone.

Using the sum of source and target classification scores is very similar to source & target Lewis-Moore LM data selection employing sum of difference of cross-entropies. A reference to this work around line 435 would be reasonable for completeness. Finally, I wonder if you could learn weights for the sum of both source & target classification scores through optimization. Extending the CNN model to the bilingual setting would enable joint parallel sentence representation. Such an architecture might discover optimal weighting automatically during training.
ideas_up_hard.coling::4e7728dc-010d-47cb-95f2-16525a71:
This submission presents character-based language modeling that preserves word-level representations in context vectors. The approach additionally offers optional word-level outputs. Kim et al. 2015, cited within this paper, already documented this methodology. Jozefowicz et al. 2016 also implemented comparable techniques. Both previous studies surpassed the current work by deploying RNNs and LSTMs in their implementations. Jozefowicz's research includes comparative analysis of character-level modeling variants. The present submission lacks discussion of these prior contributions. The novel aspect reduces to applying this framework within machine translation systems. The paper leaves unclear how N-best list reranking addresses out-of-vocabulary challenges. The translation-specific dimension of OOV problems deserves deeper examination. Certain claims appear overstated, particularly the assertion in Section 2.3 about eliminating vocabulary concepts entirely. The authors simultaneously express uncertainty about perplexity interpretation without explicit output vocabularies. Frequent word forms likely still benefit from dedicated modeling, as arXiv:1609.08144 demonstrates.

Section 2.3 states the objective function necessitates finite vocabularies. This claim holds true only when restricting units to complete word forms. Subword representations enable coverage of larger lexical spaces. Individual characters permit implicitly infinite vocabulary handling through log-likelihood criteria. Alternative models beyond the one proposed here can achieve this coverage. The corresponding statement requires qualification to acknowledge these possibilities.

The output mechanism's use of character embeddings needs clearer explanation. Section 2.4's description lacks sufficient explicitness for full comprehension.

The NCE configuration deserves more detailed justification. Section 3.4 describes specific parameterization choices without explaining the selection process.

Section 4.1 should acknowledge Kim et al. 2015's parallel findings regarding character embedding performance at outputs. Their suggested improvements warrant discussion in this context.

Section 4.2 overlooks established methods for calculating perplexity with unknown words, as Shaik et al. documented at IWSLT 2013.

Section 4.4 and Table 4 omit the complete training vocabulary's size.

Page 2's bottom contains a grammatical error: "three different input layer" should use plural "layers."

Figure 1 employs excessively small fonts that impair readability.

Page 3's first item beneath Figure 1 contains a verb error: "note" should read "denote."

Section 2.3 includes an article error: "the parameters estimation" requires either "parameter" (singular) or "parameters'" (possessive).

Page 5's opening paragraph omits an article: "in factored way" needs "a" inserted.

Page 5's second paragraph incorrectly uses "a" before vowel sounds: both "a n-best list" and "a nk-best list" should begin with "an."

Section 4.2's concluding sentence begins "Despite adaptive gradient" but lacks both a main verb and necessary article, rendering it grammatically incomplete and requiring revision for proper sentence structure.

The paper introduces Edward, a probabilistic programming language
built over TensorFlow and Python, while supporting inference algorithms
popular in contemporary probabilistic machine learning research.

Quality:
The Edward library provides an impressive collection of
modern probabilistic inference methods that users can access easily.
The paper reviews important techniques
from a representation learning perspective, then presents
two experiments implementing various modern variational inference
methods alongside GPU-accelerated HMC.
The first experiment (variational inference) would gain value if
complete code for reproducing the results
was clearly linked. The HMC experiment appears satisfactory, though
characterising Stan
as hand-optimised seems unfair since the codebase is
not optimised for this specific model, nor was it tuned for this hardware configuration.
Nobody doubts the implementation quality you achieved, so
avoid ruining credibility with unsubstantiated sensationalist
claims that lack supporting evidence. Instead of creating drama unnecessarily, compare
head-to-head against Stan using single core execution, then separately report
extra speedups gained from parallelisation, and document improvements from GPU acceleration. These performance numbers
would help readers estimate the method's performance
across other hardware configurations they might encounter.

Clarity:
The paper maintains clear writing throughout while remaining easy to read for most audiences. The numerous
code examples prove helpful to practitioners, yet also present difficulties since readers sometimes cannot determine what is missing from snippets. Authors could greatly assist readers by
providing a machine-readable companion that is clearly linked, where a Jupyter
notebook would prove ideal, though even text format or HTML pages would enable easier
copy-pasting than extracting code from a pdf document like the submitted paper, and such materials should contain complete runnable code
for all examples shown.

Originality:
The Edward library represents a unique collection of probabilistic
inference methods not found elsewhere. Regarding the paper itself, the main threat to novelty
stems from previous publications by the same research group. The main paper
cites Tran et al. (2016a), a work covering similar material extensively,
though approaching topics from a different analytical perspective. Whether the other
paper has been published remains unclear, and its submission status is unknown, as is the venue where it might appear.

Significance:
Edward will very likely have profound impact on Bayesian machine learning research
and advance deep learning methodologies.

Other comments:
Section 2 draws a clear distinction between specialised languages
(including Stan) versus Turing-complete languages such as Edward. This

no formal proof appears in the paper to support Edward's claimed Turing-completeness property.
ideas_up_hard.coling::d8e4451f-f606-413a-a2c5-5f2b5e9c:
Initially, I must emphasize that this submission exceeds reasonable length expectations. The manuscript spans 17 pages, which excludes appendices or supplementary files. Although ICLR imposes no strict page maximum, authors should consider the burden placed on volunteer reviewers. Exceeding the traditional 8-page standard by one or two pages remains acceptable, whereas tripling this convention demonstrates inconsideration. 

Proceeding to substantive evaluation: The authors introduce a synthetic sequential learning benchmark. I term it synthetic because the data derives from transforming MNIST, which contains 60,000 training images of handwritten numerical characters. Beyond creating this benchmark, the researchers implement a training curriculum that gradually increases sequence length, terminology they describe as "incremental learning". Their experimental results demonstrate superiority over baseline training without any curriculum on their proposed benchmark. Additionally, comparisons reveal advantages over several alternative curriculum strategies that might seem intuitive. The authors support these claims through ablation experiments that isolate individual model components on their newly introduced benchmark.

My concerns regarding this submission include the following points:

-- The work lacks genuine novelty in my assessment. The incremental curriculum they advocate represents an obvious strategy when training on sequential data. Bengio's 2015 work on curriculum learning already explored these principles extensively. Ranzato's 2015 paper on sequence-level training also investigated similar scheduling approaches. The sole contribution appears to be ablation analyses that confirm the curriculum causes the observed performance improvements.

-- The evaluation restricts itself to one artificially constructed benchmark that the authors themselves designed. Real sequential tasks like language modeling receive no experimental attention whatsoever. Perhaps the method fails when applied to naturalistic data distributions. I strongly suspect that language modeling scenarios, where vocabularies contain tens of thousands of tokens, would yield improvements nowhere near the 74% gain they report.

-- The utility of introducing this synthetic benchmark remains unclear to me. Text corpora provide abundant sequential learning challenges already. Speech recognition datasets offer another rich source of temporal dependencies. Financial time series present yet another domain with real-world sequential structure. The specific advantages this benchmark offers over existing alternatives lack clear articulation. While additional benchmarks might provide some value in principle, this one appears designed specifically to showcase the proposed curriculum strategy. Demonstrations on established benchmarks would have strengthened the submission considerably.

-- The manuscript suffers from excessive length, as previously mentioned. Much of the page count stems from experiments that bear no connection to the central thesis. Section 6.2 presents an experiment whose relationship to the main narrative remains obscure. Section 6.4 explores transfer learning scenarios that similarly diverge from the core message. These tangential investigations should have been removed or relegated to supplementary materials. The authors needed to exercise greater editorial discipline in focusing their presentation.
ideas_up_hard.coling::60e5cc06-240c-4ed3-80bd-353d0ba8:
Solar power represents a breakthrough in harnessing renewable energy from the sun. A significant obstacle remains in its implementation. The technology requires higher upfront investment than conventional electricity generation methods. Without this financial barrier, adoption rates would increase dramatically across residential and commercial sectors.

Advocates frequently argue that utility-scale solar installations match the construction costs of traditional generating facilities. This comparison holds validity when examining multi-megawatt projects developed by energy companies. Individual homeowners lack the capital to construct coal-fired or nuclear facilities on their property. Therefore, the relevant comparison for consumers involves retail pricing rather than industrial-scale infrastructure investment.

Calculate the purchase price of photovoltaic modules against their typical energy output over time. The mathematics reveal the economic reality.

Some suggest federal funding could replace one or two atomic energy facilities with solar arrays. This proposal rests on several misconceptions about energy policy and market structure. California already provides substantial rebates and tax incentives for residential solar adoption. Private utility companies own and operate the nuclear reactors throughout the United States. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission oversees safety and compliance at these facilities. Building a reactor requires enormous capital expenditure that must be amortized over decades. Decommissioning involves complex procedures for handling radioactive waste that cost billions. Operational expenses for active plants remain relatively modest compared to these other factors. Closing a functional reactor forfeits the investment already made in its construction.

Despite economic challenges, photovoltaic technology offers numerous compelling advantages that justify continued development. Generating electricity at the consumption location eliminates transmission losses that plague centralized power systems. The generation process produces virtually no greenhouse gases during operation. Panels operate without any mechanical noise or vibration. Peak production coincides with maximum demand periods on hot summer afternoons when air conditioning loads strain the grid.

Climate control applications may represent the optimal deployment strategy for rooftop solar systems. Scorching weather that drives up cooling requirements also maximizes panel efficiency and output. Direct conversion of sunlight into refrigeration power creates elegant synergy. Modules installed overhead block solar heat gain through the roof membrane. This dual benefit reduces the building's thermal load while simultaneously powering its cooling equipment.

Nevertheless, when evaluated strictly on levelized cost of energy, fossil fuel combustion still delivers cheaper kilowatt-hours than photovoltaic generation in most markets today.

Depends on if your business is a sole proprietorship, single member LLC, multi member LLC, an LLC with the "S" tax election, an S Corporation, or a C Corporation.

Sole Proprietorship: All profits and losses pass to you individually. You're also personally liable for anything that goes wrong. Pro Tip: form an LLC or go get a free consultation with a business attorney.

Single Member LLC: Profits and losses pass through to you personally, but your liability is limited to the Company's assets. You also have to pay self employment tax on net earnings.

Multi-Member LLC: Profits and losses are split in proportion to each members ownership interest in the company. You also pay self employment tax on your distributive share. Each member reports their portion on Schedule K-1 forms.

LLC with "S" election: You pay yourself a reasonable salary determined by industry standards, and that salary is not subject to the self employment tax. Remaining profits and losses are passed through to you and any other shareholders in proportion to each shareholders percentage interest in the corporation. Whether or not you get taxed on any distributions depends on your basis, but this is where is gets complicated and I can't ELI5 (just let the CPA worry about this).

S Corporation: see above

C Corporation: The corporations profits are taxed at the corporate tax level under federal rates, and then any dividends made to shareholders are taxed as well at individual income rates. This is called double taxation, which occurs because corporations are separate legal entities, and it's why C Corporations are not ideal for small business owners seeking pass-through treatment.

Say you're a merchant living in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a bunch of super-rich ladies who really, really love cumin (as in, the spice). Unfortunately, cumin doesn't grow anywhere near Amsterdam. The spice must be imported from the middle east or India where it thrives naturally. In those distant lands, cumin grows like a weed. Local prices there remain extremely low due to abundant supply. If only you could transport that cheap cumin over to Amsterdam, you could make a fortune selling it at premium prices.

Unfortunately, the only way to accomplish this is to send out a big-ass ship for like nine months. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you have to get a ship, and a captain and crew who all want nine months worth of pay), but it is also really risky. The boat could sink during the treacherous ocean voyage, after all. Alternatively, all the cumin could spoil in the ship's hold before reaching port.

So how do you accomplish this ambitious trading venture? Assuming you're not stupendously rich yourself (and very few people or groups, aside from maybe whole nations, are that rich), how do you finance this expensive expedition? You could go to a bank or money-lender and take out a loan. Such a loan would have a very steep interest rate that could almost eat up all of your profits. And what if the boat sank during its journey? You'd be completely bankrupt with no way to repay your debts. You'd be thrown into prison for defaulting on the loan. The money-lender might even waste your broke ass first before legal authorities intervene.

So, you come up with an innovative idea to solve this financial problem. You can't finance this trip alone with your limited personal wealth. But you could rather easily finance, say, one tenth of the total cost of the trip. And look at that, you have nine friends who are also merchants in Amsterdam. All of them could also afford one tenth of the cost of the trip. So you all come to an agreement that spreads both investment and risk. You decide to each finance part of the cost for the trip (i.e. you "buy stock" in the enterprise). Each investor gets shares worth one tenth of the total enterprise value. With this pooled money, you pay for the boat and crew. The ship departs Amsterdam harbor on its long voyage. Then nine months later, it comes back with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive cumin that Amsterdam's wealthy women crave. The profits far and away compensate for the initial cost of the expedition. Each of you and your friends gets one tenth of the enormous profits generated by selling the imported spice.

But what happens if your boat sinks in a storm? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the crew who may drown!), but you only paid for one tenth of the cost. This was a cost you could afford to eat without facing financial ruin. You're not gonna get killed over it by angry creditors. Since the risk was spread around to 10 people, no one landed in debtors prison. Everyone took a small hit that they could absorb, instead of one person taking an enormous hit that would destroy them.

Think about this example, and all the people involved in it. The fancy ladies got their cumin (and for cheaper than they would have otherwise paid through other channels). The shipwrights got work building a new ship, earning wages for their families. The captain and crew all got work and a salary for nine months of labor. The trader in India got a new customer for his cumin, expanding his business. And obviously, you and your friends got really rich in the process of this successful venture. In short, every single person is better off than before this trade occurred, and it wouldn't have happened if this notion of "buying and selling stocks" didn't exist to pool capital.

This is the advantage of a stock market in facilitating commerce. It moves capital around from where it just lies around doing absolutely nothing productive to where it can be put to use creating value. In the meantime, everybody gets richer through mutually beneficial exchange. It also distributes risk between lots of people, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke all the time from a single failed venture.

Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day American version of the stock market functions. But the critique is that it stopped doing what it is supposed to be doing (i.e. allocating capital so that it can be put into productive use). It stopped being a means to an end and became an end unto itself, with speculation replacing investment. The basic concept of a stock market is a fantastic idea that enables economic growth. You'd have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose it entirely. It is why we have railroads, cars, computers, telephones, cheap and plentiful food, medicine, and all the other modern things we value so highly today.
