It's about anonymity and vulnerability.

On the internet, you're anonymous and well outside the reach of the person you're talking to, so when people disagree, they tend to be a lot more confrontational and aggressive... because it's easy to be aggressive and confrontational when there's no chance of being punched in the face.

In the real world if you're 5" tall and weigh 90lbs soaking wet, you're probably not going to tell a 6"5 250lb guy that he's full of shit, even if that's what you think. Online, who cares? What's he going to do?

The flip side is it's also much easier to be abusive or aggressive (or honest) when the person you're communicating with is just words on a screen. The internet dehumanizes the person you're speaking to by removing visual cues like facial expressions. Studies show that text-based communication lacks the emotional feedback present in face-to-face conversation. This absence of immediate human reaction lowers our psychological barriers against cruelty.

Basically, it's really easy to watch a bad youtube video and tell xXUsernameXx that they're a talentless piece of shit. It's a different thing to watch that same video and then walk up to Jenny, the 14 year old girl who makes Minecraft videos to take her mind off her parent's divorce...and look her in the eye and say "You're a talentless piece of shit."

As for cars? Well, the same applies. You're in a big, locked metal box that's basically half suit of armor, half escape pod. Road rage incidents have increased by 30% over the past decade according to traffic safety organizations. Lean on your horn, give the middle finger, because you're at your turning and will never see whoever's driving that car again. Fuck that fucking stupid fucking Ford that cut you off in traffic, because it's a stupid fucking Ford...not Jenny's Mom who's had a really bad day and distracted because she doesn't know how she's going to make rent that week.

The energy of the clap remains unchanged so we look at where that energy is going. In a regular clap on earth, the energy of the collision goes into a variety of things; 

1) sound 

2) deformation of your hands

3) heat

4) some others that are probably constant in both scenarios and I won't address

Let's model (horribly roughly) a clap. Each hand weighs approximately 500 grams. The hands move toward each other at 2 meters per second. Using the formula E=mv2 gives us roughly 4 joules of total energy. 

Claps are generally considered elastic collisions. Nevertheless, some small energy loss occurs due to deformation. Under microscopic examination, cellular damage would be visible. However, this damage remains minimal in extent. The largest portion of energy converts to heat. According to one source, a typical clap lasts about 20 milliseconds. Another reference provides sound power measurements for various everyday objects. An alarm clock serves as a reasonable comparison for our purposes. Even a hundredfold error in our estimates wouldn't significantly affect the final conclusion. Performing a crude integration of the sound wave's amplitude over time yields specific results. Multiplying by the power output from the comparison table gives us the acoustic energy. This calculation produces approximately 2×10^-6 joules released as sound. The input energy from the collision totals 4 joules. Therefore, sound accounts for only 0.00005% of the total energy released. Heat and deformation absorb the remaining energy. The precise ratio between these two sinks is difficult to determine.

So, to answer your question: 

On earth, only 0.00005% of the energy goes into the sound of a clap. The rest goes into heat and deformation of your hands. In space, 0% of the energy goes into sound. That tiny bit that would have created sound on earth converts to additional heat instead. The acoustic energy represents an infinitesimal fraction compared to thermal output. The collision's fundamental nature remains essentially identical. The only perceptible difference is the absence of audible sound. Your hands still warm up from the impact. Tissue deformation still occurs at the cellular level.

ideas_up_hard.coling::8e0f7cff-07ca-48c6-b381-34b577d1: Before babies start to use language they form speech through babble. These utterances require minimal motor control for developmental babies who are exploring their vocal capabilities. The open and closed mouth positions function analogously to binary code in computing systems. Zero represents the open vowel sound, exemplified by 'aaaaaa'. One corresponds to the closed mouth position that produces consonant sounds like 'm' or 'p'. Readers can test this by closing their lips as if beginning a word starting with 'm' or 'p'. ideas_up_hard.coling::97ce3bac-5618-4fcb-8600-bcf08ed8: To be blunt, unless you're very experienced with wines, you probably won't be able to look at 2 similar wine bottles and immediately figure out which one you'll like better. ideas_up_hard.coling::f249dac3-f3a2-4db9-9758-e18c9f8f: There are a bunch of people in a town. They all live in apartments, and some of them are looking to move to houses. The house-builders in this town see this demand and start building houses. When they look for people to buy these houses, there is a lot of demand. This competition among buyers can push prices higher. This represents the opposite of competition on the supply-side, where it brings prices down. A bunch of people buy houses at these high-demand prices. Prices continue to climb as demand remains high. Once the price gets too high, demand begins to weaken. Most of the demand subsides from everyone wanting a house having one. There suddenly becomes much lower demand. This drops the cost of purchasing a house. Those that have already purchased at peak prices now see themselves as losing money. They want to move back into an apartment. They also want to get rid of the house they bought. This cranks up supply in the market. The increased supply causes a precipitous drop in prices for these houses. The decline continues until the prices reach a level where demand begins to stabilize at a new equilibrium point. When we talk about a bubble, it really comes down to a market of low-supply and high-demand quickly changing to a high-supply and low-demand market. The major problem is that both versions are self-reinforcing through feedback loops. High-demand brings people in to invest in the asset class. These investors take advantage of the price increases by buying more. Low-demand gets people to try to push away from the market entirely. Their exit from the market makes supply even higher than before. This selling pressure accelerates the downward spiral of prices. The cycle completes when new buyers eventually see value at lower price points. Market psychology plays a crucial role in amplifying both phases of the bubble cycle.

ideas_up_hard.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) monitors network traffic to identify security threats. Machine learning has transformed IDS capabilities by enabling automated pattern recognition in data streams. Deep learning architectures process network packets with unprecedented speed and accuracy. Internet of Things devices present expanding attack surfaces due to their minimal security implementations. Generative adversarial models create synthetic data by pitting two neural networks against each other. Our research introduces SIGMA, which produces hardened classifiers through systematic adversarial training. The framework combines Generative Adversarial Networks with evolutionary optimization techniques to synthesize novel attack vectors. Adversarial examples are crafted samples designed to fool machine learning classifiers into misclassification. SIGMA operates through iterative cycles that progressively strengthen detection capabilities. Training continues until performance metrics plateau, indicating the model has reached maximum robustness. The generative phase employs GANs alongside metaheuristic algorithms to create synthetic attack instances. ideas_up_hard.coling::f4f3b137-0da5-4cc5-a8e0-08f5a284: High-speed transmission requires viewing signals as analog rather than digital phenomena. ideas_up_hard.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs that model evolutionary scenarios where horizontal gene transfer occurs. These structures extend phylogenetic trees by accommodating reticulation events in evolutionary history. The hybridization number equals the sum of all vertex indegrees minus the total vertex count plus one. This metric quantifies the minimum reticulation events needed to explain observed evolutionary patterns. The Hybridization Number problem requires finding a network that displays all input trees while minimizing this numerical measure. Our contribution is an algorithm solving this problem for exactly three binary phylogenetic trees containing n taxa. The algorithm achieves O(c^k poly(n)) time complexity, where k denotes the optimal network's hybridization number and c represents a fixed positive constant independent of input size. Previous work addressed the two-tree case with O(3.18^k n) running time. No prior research achieved O(c^k poly(n)) complexity when the input contained more than two phylogenetic trees. Algorithms for two trees exploit acyclic agreement forests to obtain linear factors in their complexity bounds. Earlier approaches for three or more trees conducted exhaustive searches over all conceivable network topologies. Such brute-force enumeration prevented achieving O(c^k poly(n)) running time for any fixed constant c. Acyclic agreement forests provide weaker structural constraints when three or more trees are considered. Even possessing the correct agreement forest leaves the network reconstruction problem computationally challenging. We establish new structural theorems enabling network reconstruction without enumerating possible topological configurations. These theoretical advances apply to inputs containing four or more phylogenetic trees with one critical exception. A specific lemma creates a correspondence between network vertices and nodes appearing in the input trees. This mapping result drastically reduces the search space that must be explored during network construction. Unfortunately, our proof technique for this correspondence lemma fails when applied to four or more input trees. The primary unresolved question is whether analogous mapping results can be proven for larger tree collections. Resolving this question would extend our algorithmic approach to arbitrary numbers of input phylogenies.
ideas_up_hard.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their spectral embeddings play an important role in multiple areas of machine learning. This paper focuses on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for spectral clustering of data as a primary application. The methodology can also be applied in data mining contexts. Data manifold learning represents another application domain. Spectral embedding provides a low-dimensional parametrization of the data manifold. This parametrization makes subsequent tasks much easier to execute. Clustering with k-means represents one such subsequent task. Various approximations of k-means can also benefit from this parametrization. Despite reducing the dimensionality of data, the overall computational cost may still be prohibitive for large data sets. Two factors contribute to this computational burden. First, computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large Krylov subspace. Second, after the spectral embedding is complete, one still has to operate with the same number of data points. This large number of points may ruin the efficiency of the approach. For example, clustering of the embedded data is typically performed with various relaxations of k-means. The computational cost of these relaxations scales poorly with respect to the size of data set. These algorithms become prone to getting stuck in local minima. Their robustness depends on the choice of initial guess. In this work, we switch the focus from the entire data set to a subset of graph vertices. This subset is called the target subset. We develop two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional representation of the original graph. These algorithms preserve important global distances between the nodes of the target subset. In particular, our approach allows ensuring that target subset clustering is consistent with the spectral clustering of the full data set. Consistency is achieved by a properly parametrized reduced-order model (ROM) of the graph-Laplacian. The ROM approximates accurately the diffusion transfer function of the original graph. Inputs and outputs are restricted to the target subset in this approximation. Working with a small target subset reduces greatly the required dimension of Krylov subspace. It also allows exploiting the conventional algorithms in the regimes when they are most robust. These regimes also correspond to when conventional algorithms are most efficient. This was verified in numerical clustering experiments with both synthetic and real data. We also note that our ROM approach can be applied in a purely transfer-function-data-driven way. This makes it the only feasible option for extremely large graphs that are not directly accessible. There are several uses for our algorithms. First, they can be employed on their own for representative subset clustering. Such employment is valuable when handling the full graph is either infeasible or simply not required. Second, they may be used for quality control purposes. Third, they drastically reduce the problem size. This reduction enables the application of more sophisticated algorithms for the task under consideration. More powerful approximations of k-means based on semi-definite programming (SDP) represent such sophisticated algorithms. These SDP-based methods offer advantages over the conventional Lloyd's algorithm. Finally, our algorithms can be used as building blocks of a multi-level divide-and-conquer type algorithm. Such multi-level algorithms can handle the full graph. The latter will be reported in a separate article.
ideas_up_hard.coling::d9b96a87-ee9b-46e9-995f-edfccd85: We investigate the challenge of constructing [ n , k ] linear codes for distributed storage systems (DSS) that fulfill the (r , t) - Local Repair Property , where any t ( t) simultaneously failed nodes can be locally repaired, each with locality r . The parameters n , k , r , t are positive integers such that r k n and t - n k . Our work focuses on the functional repair model, which permits newcomer packets to differ from original lost data provided they maintain the (r , t) -local repair property. We employ the sequential approach for repairing multiple failed nodes, wherein the t newcomers are ordered in a proper sequence such that each newcomer can be repaired from the live nodes and the newcomers that are ordered before it. These codes are designated as (n , k , r , t) -functional locally repairable codes (FLRC) in our terminology. FLRCs represent the most general class of LRCs currently known. This broad category encompasses several subclasses of LRCs reported in the literature as special cases. The primary objective of this paper is to optimize the storage overhead of FLRCs, which equivalently means maximizing the code rate. We establish a lower bound on the code length n given t {2 , 3 } and any possible k , r . When t 2 , our bound generalizes the rate bound proved in earlier work on doubly-failed systems. When t 3 , our bound improves the rate bound proved in previous research on triply-failed configurations. We provide explicit constructions of exact LRCs for t {2 , 3 } whose length n achieves the bound of (n , k , r , t) -FLRC. These constructions prove the tightness of our bounds by demonstrating achievability. The constructions also imply that there is no gap between the optimal code length of functional LRCs and exact LRCs for certain sets of parameters, settling an open question. Our constructions are over the binary field, making them computationally efficient for implementation. The binary nature ensures practical relevance in real-world distributed storage applications. The codes require minimal finite field arithmetic operations during encoding and decoding procedures.
ideas_up_hard.coling::60c879b9-6ebb-4551-8f22-52c6a144: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) addresses the challenge of building environmental maps while tracking a mobile agent's position. Dense SLAM methods reconstruct scenes and determine locations at individual pixel resolution. The computational demands of these approaches have prevented deployment on battery-powered embedded systems. Approximate computing techniques can accelerate SLAM when inaccuracies remain within navigation tolerance thresholds. Earlier research on SLAM approximation presumed complete knowledge of movement paths prior to execution. Those investigations examined static controllers that fixed approximation parameters before motion commenced. Real-world scenarios typically involve unknown routes determined during operation. Dynamic parameter adjustment creates additional possibilities for conserving processing cycles and electrical power. This paper presents SLAMBooster, which incorporates application-specific knowledge into its online control architecture. Our system modifies approximation settings throughout agent movement in real time. The foundation uses proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control theory from classical feedback systems. Initial experiments revealed that generic PID implementation caused excessive positioning errors. SLAMBooster addresses accuracy degradation through two domain-informed techniques. The first technique identifies planar regions where approximation can safely increase. The second technique applies corrective adjustments to estimated poses when drift accumulates. We integrated our approach into SLAMBench, which provides open-source infrastructure for SLAM research. Evaluation covered more than twelve distinct movement sequences from published datasets. Additional test trajectories came from experiments we conducted specifically for this study. Results demonstrate average computation time reduction of seventy-two percent across all tested scenarios. Energy consumption decreased by thirty-five percent when measured on ARM-based embedded hardware. Localization accuracy remained within acceptable margins throughout these experiments. The combined improvements enable SLAM deployment on resource-limited platforms previously unsuitable for such algorithms. Mobile robots with constrained power budgets can now perform dense reconstruction tasks. Augmented reality headsets represent another device category that benefits from these optimizations. Autonomous drones operating on battery power gain extended flight duration while maintaining mapping capabilities.
ideas_up_hard.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb: We introduce the binary value principle which is a simple subset-sum instance expressing that a natural number written in binary cannot be negative, relating it to central problems in proof and algebraic complexity. We prove conditional superpolynomial lower bounds on the Ideal Proof System (IPS) refutation size of this instance, based on a well-known hypothesis by Shub and Smale about the hardness of computing factorials, where IPS is the strong algebraic proof system introduced by Grochow and Pitassi in their foundational work. Conversely, we show that short IPS refutations of this instance bridge the gap between sufficiently strong algebraic and semi-algebraic proof systems, establishing a precise characterization of their relative power. Our results extend to full-fledged IPS the paradigm introduced in Forbes et al., whereby lower bounds against subsystems of IPS were obtained using restricted algebraic circuit lower bounds, demonstrating a novel connection between circuit complexity and proof complexity. We demonstrate that the binary value principle captures the advantage of semi-algebraic over algebraic reasoning for sufficiently strong systems, providing the first such characterization in this framework. Specifically, we show the following: Conditional IPS lower bounds: The Shub-Smale hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of the binary value principle over the rationals, which is defined as the unsatisfiable linear equation summing from i equals 1 to n of 2 to the power negative i plus 1 times x sub i minus 1, where the variables x sub i are constrained to be boolean. Further, the related tau-conjecture from algebraic complexity theory implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of a variant of the binary value principle over the ring of rational functions in several variables. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for IPS, which is the strongest algebraic proof system studied in the literature. No conditional lower bounds were previously established for apparently much weaker propositional proof systems such as Frege systems or their extensions. Though simple in its formulation, the binary value principle is not a direct translation of a boolean formula into algebraic form, hence similar to work by Grigoriev and other results on algebraic proofs such as those by Razborov, IPS lower bounds on this principle do not necessarily entail lower bounds for Frege or its subsystems operating on boolean formulas. Algebraic vs. semi-algebraic proofs: Admitting short refutations of the binary value principle is necessary for any algebraic proof system to fully simulate any known semi-algebraic proof system that reasons about polynomial inequalities. For strong enough algebraic proof systems this condition is also sufficient to achieve such simulation. In particular, we introduce a very strong proof system that simulates all known semi-algebraic proof systems including Positivstellensatz calculus, under the name Cone Proof System (CPS). CPS also simulates most other known concrete propositional proof systems beyond semi-algebraic ones. CPS serves as a semi-algebraic analogue of the ideal proof system in the algebraic setting. CPS establishes the unsatisfiability of collections of polynomial equalities and inequalities over the reals by representing sum-of-squares proofs as algebraic circuits with specific structural properties. CPS also handles extensions of sum-of-squares methodology through the same circuit representation framework. We prove that IPS is polynomially equivalent to CPS if and only if IPS admits polynomial-size refutations of the binary value principle, where this equivalence applies to the language of systems of equations that have no solutions with coordinates in the set containing only zero and one, and this result holds over both the integers Z and the rationals Q as base rings.

Speech recognition is an interdisciplinary subfield of computer science and computational linguistics that develops methodologies and technologies that enable the recognition and translation of spoken language into text by computers with the main benefit of searchability. It is also known as automatic speech recognition (ASR), computer speech recognition or speech to text (STT). It incorporates knowledge and research in the computer science, linguistics and computer engineering fields. The reverse process is speech synthesis.

Some speech recognition systems require "training" (also called "enrollment") where an individual speaker reads text or isolated vocabulary into the system. The system analyzes the person's specific voice and uses it to fine-tune the recognition of that person's speech, resulting in increased accuracy. Systems that do not use training are called "speaker-independent" systems. Systems that use training are called "speaker dependent".

Speech recognition applications include voice user interfaces such as voice dialing (e.g. "call home"), call routing (e.g. "I would like to make a collect call"), domotic appliance control, search key words (e.g. find a podcast where particular words were spoken), simple data entry (e.g., entering a credit card number), preparation of structured documents (e.g. a radiology report), determining speaker characteristics, speech-to-text processing (e.g., word processors or emails), and aircraft (usually termed direct voice input).

The term voice recognition or speaker identification refers to identifying the speaker, rather than what they are saying. Recognizing the speaker can simplify the task of translating speech in systems that have been trained on a specific person's voice or it can be used to authenticate or verify the identity of a speaker as part of a security process.

From the technology perspective, speech recognition has a long history with several waves of major innovations. Most recently, the field has benefited from advances in deep learning and big data. These technological improvements emerged during the early twenty-first century. Commercial applications now serve millions of users daily across multiple platforms. Research laboratories in universities continue exploring novel algorithmic approaches. The advances are evidenced not only by the surge of academic papers published in the field, but more importantly by the worldwide industry adoption of a variety of deep learning methods in designing and deploying speech recognition systems.

Control theory is a field of mathematics that deals with the control of dynamical systems in engineered processes and machines. The objective is to develop a model or algorithm governing the application of system inputs to drive the system to a desired state, while minimizing any delay, overshoot, or steady-state error and ensuring a level of control stability; often with the aim to achieve a degree of optimality.

To do this, a controller with the requisite corrective behavior is required. This controller monitors the controlled process variable (PV), and compares it with the reference or set point (SP). The difference between actual and desired value of the process variable, called the error signal, or SP-PV error, is applied as feedback to generate a control action to bring the controlled process variable to the same value as the set point. Other aspects which are also studied are controllability and observability. Control theory is used in control system engineering to design automation that have revolutionized manufacturing, aircraft, communications and other industries, and created new fields such as robotics.

Extensive use is usually made of a diagrammatic style known as the block diagram. In it the transfer function, also known as the system function or network function, is a mathematical model of the relation between the input and output based on the differential equations describing the system.

Control theory dates from the 19th century, when the theoretical basis for the operation of governors was first described by James Clerk Maxwell. Control theory was further advanced by Edward Routh in 1874, Charles Sturm and in 1895, Adolf Hurwitz, who all contributed to the establishment of control stability criteria; and from 1922 onwards, the development of PID control theory by Nicolas Minorsky.

Although a major application of mathematical control theory is in control systems engineering, which deals with the design of process control systems for industry, other applications range far beyond this. As the general theory of feedback systems, control theory is useful wherever feedback occurs. Modern implementations often employ digital computers running specialized software algorithms. Adaptive control systems can modify their behavior in response to changing environmental conditions. Optimal control seeks to minimize cost functionals over time horizons. Robust control addresses uncertainty in system models and external disturbances.

A digital signature is a mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of digital messages or documents. A valid digital signature, where the prerequisites are satisfied, gives a recipient very high confidence that the message was created by a known sender (authenticity), and that the message was not altered in transit (integrity).

Digital signatures are a standard element of most cryptographic protocol suites. They are commonly used for software distribution. Financial transactions employ them regularly. Contract management software incorporates digital signatures. Detection of forgery motivates their implementation. Detecting tampering is another crucial application.

Digital signatures are often used to implement electronic signatures. Electronic signatures include any electronic data that carries the intent of a signature. Not all electronic signatures use digital signatures. Electronic signatures have legal significance in Canada. South Africa recognizes them legally. The United States grants them legal status. Algeria has legal provisions for electronic signatures. Turkey includes them in its legal framework. India recognizes their validity. Brazil has enacted supporting legislation. Indonesia provides legal recognition. Mexico has established their legal standing. Saudi Arabia acknowledges them legally. Uruguay has legal provisions for them. Switzerland recognizes electronic signatures. Chile has incorporated them into law. The countries of the European Union provide legal recognition.

Digital signatures employ asymmetric cryptography. In many instances, they provide a layer of validation to messages sent through a non-secure channel. They also add security to such communications. Properly implemented digital signatures give the receiver reason to believe the message was sent by the claimed sender. Digital signatures are equivalent to traditional handwritten signatures in many respects. Properly implemented digital signatures are more difficult to forge than the handwritten type. Digital signature schemes are cryptographically based. They must be implemented properly to be effective. They can provide non-repudiation. Non-repudiation means the signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a message while also claiming their private key remains secret. Some non-repudiation schemes offer a timestamp for the digital signature. Even if the private key is exposed, the signature with timestamp remains valid. Digitally signed messages may be anything representable as a bitstring. Electronic mail can be digitally signed. Contracts are suitable for digital signatures. Messages sent via other cryptographic protocols can carry digital signatures.

Data dredging (also known as data snooping or p-hacking)[a] is the misuse of data analysis to find patterns in data that can be presented as statistically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives. This is done by performing many statistical tests on the data and only reporting those that come back with significant results.

The process of data dredging involves testing multiple hypotheses using a single data set by exhaustively searching—perhaps for combinations of variables that might show a correlation, and perhaps for groups of cases or observations that show differences in their mean or in their breakdown by some other variable.

Conventional tests of statistical significance are based on the probability that a particular result would arise if chance alone were at work, and necessarily accept some risk of mistaken conclusions of a certain type (mistaken rejections of the null hypothesis). This level of risk is called the significance. When large numbers of tests are performed, some produce false results of this type; hence 5% of randomly chosen hypotheses might be (erroneously) reported to be statistically significant at the 5% significance level, while 1% might be (erroneously) reported to be statistically significant at the 1% significance level, and so on, by chance alone. When enough hypotheses are tested, it is virtually certain that some will be reported to be statistically significant (even though this is misleading), since almost every data set with any degree of randomness is likely to contain (for example) some spurious correlations. If they are not cautious, researchers using data mining techniques can be easily misled by these results.

Data dredging is an example of disregarding the multiple comparisons problem. One form is when subgroups are compared without alerting the reader to the total number of subgroup comparisons examined. Another manifestation occurs when investigators selectively report outcome measures. The practice undermines the scientific method's reliance on reproducibility. It violates principles established for proper experimental design since the nineteenth century.

Black bears and grizzly bears require different deterrents. Stay alert and avoid coming between a bear and her cub.

A black bear can actually be black, brown or cinnamon colored. They are usually smaller than grizzlies, have pointier ears than their cousins, and don't have a shoulder hump. Their claws are shorter and more curved for climbing trees.

A grizzly bear is brown, blonde or even slightly silver in coloration. They have a distinctive hump on their back made of muscle, have a dish shaped face profile, and rounder ears than black bears. Full-grown grizzlies weigh between 400 and 800 pounds. Male grizzlies are significantly larger than females of the species.

Their sense of smell is extremely acute—seven times better than a bloodhound's. They are constantly foraging in the summer months to build fat reserves. In fall they enter a state called hyperphagia when eating becomes their sole focus.

Bear spray is a type of pepper spray derived from capsaicin compounds. It creates a 30-foot (9 m) cone of irritating mist. The spray is only to be used when a bear is charging directly at you. Its purpose is to change the bear's direction and halt its advance.

Keep your bear spray within arms reach at all times while hiking. Learn where the trigger is located in advance of any encounter. Remove the safety clip before entering areas with fresh bear sign.

Pull the trigger when the bear is within 40 feet (12 m) of your position.

Never use bear spray as a preventative measure around your campsite. It is extremely potent and can attract bears once it settles. The spray should not be applied to equipment or clothing as a repellent.

Grizzly and black bears try to avoid loud human voices and conversation. Bear bells are usually too quiet because wind and terrain muffle their sound. Human conversation will alert bears to your presence from greater distances.

Don't hike alone in bear country since solo hikers face higher risk. If you don't want to talk constantly, carry a satellite radio and set it to a talk show with continuous dialogue.

Bears are more likely to approach an individual than a group of three or more people.

Bears run up to 35 mph (56 km/h) on flat terrain. They can also follow you up trees using their powerful claws. Grizzlies are surprisingly capable swimmers despite their bulk.

The bear will smell you from miles away and typically keep its distance. If you haven't hidden your food in an airtight container, the scent could work to your disadvantage by attracting curious bears. Hanging food from trees is insufficient protection in areas with experienced bears.

Stand your ground and make noise by yelling firmly. Avoid direct eye contact which bears interpret as aggression. Wave your arms slowly to appear larger without making sudden movements.

They may stand on their hind legs to catch your scent better, but this behavior is investigative rather than threatening. It's best to remain confident and hold your position without retreating.

If a small black bear attacks you physically, you may be able to fight back by targeting its nose and eyes with any available objects.

If a grizzly bear attacks you, curl up in the fetal position to protect vital organs. Keep your hands laced behind your neck to prevent the bear from flipping you. If the bear realizes you are not a threat, it may walk away after a brief investigation.

Remember that bear attacks are rare compared to other wilderness dangers like dehydration or hypothermia.

Wipe your knee with a damp washcloth and, if necessary, a mild soap. Wash away grease, sweat, and any soap residue, then dry your knee thoroughly. Making sure your knee is clean will help prevent irritation, while dryness ensures proper tape adhesion. You can also shave the area 12 hours prior to taping if it will be taped repeatedly. This advance timing allows any minor skin irritation from shaving to subside. Hair removal reduces pain when the tape is removed. Shaving also improves the tape's ability to stick to skin.

Lie with your back propped up or supported and legs outstretched in front of you. Your knees should be completely relaxed and slightly bent. To help keep your knee bent and relaxed, place a rolled towel under it. This positioning prevents muscle tension during the taping process. The elevation also makes the kneecap easier to access.

You'll use rigid sports tape to perform the actual McConnell technique. However, sports tape can be irritating and uncomfortable, so you should first cover your entire knee with a strip of low irritant, hypoallergenic tape. A permeable, breathable white cotton tape is a good underwrap option. The underwrap creates a protective barrier between your skin and the rigid tape. Cotton material allows moisture to escape during activity.

Use a marker or pen to gently trace all four sides of your kneecap. This will define your work surface on the underwrap layer. It'll be easier to apply the sports tape properly if you can actually see the kneecap's boundaries. The markings serve as guides for precise tape placement. Accurate positioning is essential for the McConnell technique to work effectively.

Use non-stretch adhesive sports tape for the McConnell technique. Cut a two to three inch (five to eight cm) strip, or enough tape to cover your knee from outer to inner edges. Sports tape with a width of 38 mm (1.5 inches) is the best size for knee taping. Narrower tape may not provide adequate support. Wider tape becomes difficult to apply smoothly around the knee's contours.

Apply one end of the tape to the outer edge of your kneecap so the tape is vertically centered with the knee. Adhere the tape to your skin in a downward direction toward the lower inside corner of your knee, and use your thumb to gently push the kneecap toward the inside of the leg. This medial glide corrects patellar tracking problems. The diagonal angle maximizes the corrective force on the kneecap.

While moving the kneecap and applying the tape, use your fingers to carefully pull the skin on the inside of your leg toward the kneecap. Your goal is to push the kneecap toward the inside of your leg, wrinkle the skin there so it meets the kneecap, and use the tape to hold them tightly together. The skin wrinkles indicate proper tension has been achieved. This technique maintains the corrected kneecap position throughout movement.

Place one edge of the second strip of tape on the outer edge of your knee and, again, make sure it's vertically centered with your kneecap. Secure the tape to your skin in a straight, horizontal motion. The tape should make a straight line from the outside of your knee to the inside. Apply one to three more layers of tape until you feel your desired level of tightness and support. Additional layers increase the corrective force gradually. Individual comfort levels vary based on injury severity.

Make sure you've created skin wrinkles on the inside part of your knee. These wrinkles should run vertically, or up and down, and you should be able to see them through the underlay. Wrinkling of the skin results when you pull the kneecap inward and secure it to the skin on the inside of the leg. Visible wrinkles confirm successful tape application.

Wear the tape during physical activity as directed by your physical therapist or another medical professional. In general, you should remove the tape within 48 hours of application. Prolonged wear can cause skin breakdown or maceration. As strength, range of motion, and balance improve, keep the knee taped for shorter periods of time during general activities. Progressive reduction helps muscles learn to support the knee independently.

Hold your kneecap as you slowly peel off the tape to prevent worsening an injury. Place your fingers as close as you can to the tape's line of attachment, or where it meets your skin. Pulling too fast can cause skin irritation or abruptly force the kneecap out of position.

Remove the tape immediately if it worsens your pain. Take the tape off if you experience discoloration, pins and needles, or swelling after applying the tape. Consult a medical professional before taping, especially if you have circulatory problems or a knee fracture.

Select a moment when your parents display positive emotions and appear receptive. Skip any conversation immediately following their return from a stressful workday. Gauge their emotional state by inquiring, "How was your day?" Identify a window when interruptions are unlikely and their focus won't be divided among siblings or household crises. The period following the evening meal often provides tranquility, while the hour before sleep offers maximum privacy.

When home opportunities prove elusive, consider unconventional settings such as accompanying them on a neighborhood stroll. During a car journey, you might benefit from the enclosed space where eye contact is less intense. Propose the outing by saying, "Dad, do you want to go on a quick walk? I have some things I'd like to talk with you about." Speaking with a single parent initially remains an option, particularly if you can request their assistance in persuading the other. This strategy proves most effective when your mother demonstrates greater flexibility in her attitudes. Alternatively, you might choose whichever parent you share deeper emotional bonds with, as that connection can facilitate difficult conversations.

Maintaining honesty and directness demonstrates your emotional maturity to skeptical parents. Therefore, reject all forms of deception, including seemingly harmless fabrications that might appear insignificant. Should they inquire about prior dates with this person, acknowledge any that have already occurred rather than concealing the truth. Discovery of any dishonesty will immediately destroy whatever credibility you have established through your approach.

Genuine honesty also requires your willingness to hear their worries without becoming defensive or dismissive. When they express distrust of your boyfriend stemming from limited personal interaction, suggest arranging family dinners or group activities. Facilitating these encounters allows them to evaluate his character firsthand rather than relying on assumptions.

Refrain from citing peer examples if doing so requires stretching or distorting reality. Claiming that your closest friend has maintained a relationship for twenty-four months will backfire unless this statement is completely accurate. Parents possess strong instincts for detecting exaggeration and can verify such claims through conversations with other families. False comparisons will undermine your entire argument rather than strengthening your position.

Achieving your goal may require accepting certain restrictions or modifications to your initial vision. Your parents' consent will almost certainly come attached to specific requirements and boundaries they consider non-negotiable. When these conditions are realistic and achievable, agreeing to them demonstrates good faith and cooperation. Proposing your own compromises can also revive negotiations after an initial rejection has occurred.

Fulfilling agreed-upon terms establishes a foundation for expanded privileges as time passes and confidence builds. Numerous conditions will center on maintaining academic standards, such as preserving a minimum grade point average throughout the relationship. They might mandate dedicated study time each evening, perhaps requiring you to complete homework before making phone calls. These expectations align with your own long-term interests, making acceptance a logical choice regardless of the boyfriend situation.

Expect them to impose limitations on how frequently you can meet your boyfriend, reflecting their desire to prevent emotional overwhelm. They may restrict outings to once weekly or establish a non-negotiable curfew for all dates. Some parents might require that early dates occur in group settings rather than one-on-one encounters.

They could insist you consult with a counselor or healthcare provider about relationship readiness and sexual health information. Whether you accept this particular compromise depends on your personal comfort level and your assessment of their underlying motivations.

Regulate your emotional responses throughout this challenging discussion to maintain credibility. Eliminate yelling, crying, whining, or pleading from your communication style entirely. Any emotional outburst will cause them to dismiss your arguments as childish and unworthy of serious consideration. To maintain composure, silently repeat calming words like "control" or "breathe" inside your mind. Pause for five full seconds before responding to provocative questions or making statements you might later wish you could retract.

Monitor your vocal tone with equal vigilance, since pleasant words can convey hostility through sarcastic delivery. The phrase "That's great" communicates vastly different meanings depending on inflection and emphasis patterns. When frustration threatens to overwhelm your self-control, mentally rehearse a post-conversation activity that will release accumulated tension. Imagine yourself running several miles, completing laps in a swimming pool, or browsing stores with supportive friends who will listen to your venting.

Your parents will undoubtedly articulate numerous perspectives and concerns, making attentive listening absolutely essential to productive dialogue. Maintain direct eye contact while they speak to signal confidence rather than embarrassment about relationship topics. Nod affirmatively when they raise valid points, and smile genuinely when you find yourself agreeing with their observations.

Effective listening includes asking clarifying questions that demonstrate intellectual engagement rather than passive reception. Following a rejection, inquire "Why not?" to show genuine interest in understanding their reasoning process. Explain that you sincerely want to comprehend their viewpoint, which helps identify specific anxieties you can potentially address through behavioral changes.

Unless previously addressed, your parents may schedule a separate conversation specifically about sexual activity and its consequences. This potentially awkward 'sex talk' actually offers valuable opportunities to gather information in a judgment-free environment. Use this dedicated time to pose questions or voice concerns you've been hesitant to raise elsewhere.

When face-to-face conversation feels impossible due to anxiety or family dynamics, composing a written letter provides an alternative communication channel. This approach also proves advantageous if you anticipate an explosive or disproportionate reaction to your request.

Ensure your letter maintains professional quality and emotional restraint throughout, avoiding inflammatory language you'll subsequently regret. Rather than writing "I'm going to have a boyfriend whether you like it or not," choose phrasing like "I really want you to understand where I'm coming from." Before delivery, ask a trusted friend, older sibling, or sympathetic relative to review your draft and suggest improvements. Their outside perspective can identify passages that might trigger defensive reactions you failed to anticipate.

Matt Wozniak (born January 6, 1983) is a Canadian curler from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He currently plays second on Team Jason Gunnlaugson. Wozniak is the former second for the Mike McEwen team which curled out of the Assiniboine Memorial Curling Club in Winnipeg.

Career

2005–2010
In 2005, Wozniak joined the new Mike McEwen rink that included Justin Richter and Andrew Melnuk. For the 2006-07 season, Richter and Melnuk left the team and were replaced with Geordie Hargreaves and Adam Guenther. The team disbanded after just one season together.

Wozniak and McEwen joined with brothers Denni and B. J. Neufeld in 2007. In their first season together, they were a semi-finalist at the 2008 Safeway Championship, Manitoba's provincial championship. Their first Grand Slam event as a team was at the end season, at the 2008 Players' Championships. The team won two games, before being eliminated.

At the conclusion of the 2008-09 season the McEwen team was ranked 7th on the CCA rankings. They had made it to three Grand Slam playoffs that year. The team finished 4th at the 2009 Safeway Championship.

During the 'Road to the Roar' 2009 Olympic Qualifier, the McEwen team just lost out to fellow Manitobans the Jason Gunnlaugson team in the semi-finals. Team McEwen thus missed out on the 2009 Canadian Olympic Curling Trials final. McEwen had been the favourite in that particular matchup vs Gunnlaugson.

McEwen's rink made it to his first provincial final in 2010, when he lost to Jeff Stoughton in the 2010 Manitoba provincial final. The game was being played in Steinbach, Manitoba. The Neufeld brothers and their father have roots in Steinbach. The crowd treated them very much as the home team and favourites.

2010-2015: Grand Slam success and perennial provincial runner-up
Team McEwen started the 2010-11 season off well by defeating provincial rival Jeff Stoughton to win the World Cup of Curling. This was his first ever Grand Slam title in November, 2010. The team's runner-up result in the provincial finals of 2010 contributed to their recognition. The team had 4 victories on the World Curling Tour season as of November 2010. They were leading the overall money winnings at that time. The McEwen team was named as a nominee for the provincial team of the year by the Manitoba Sportswriters and Sportscasters Association.

The team continued their strong season that year by defeating provincial rival Stoughton in the semi-final of the 2011 Canadian Open. They would then go on to beat the Glenn Howard team in the extra end of the final. This victory marked their second career Grand Slam. It was their second Grand Slam of that season.

Wozniak's rink once again made it to the Manitoba provincial final, this time being the top seed. They were also ranked 1st in Canada at the time. However, once again lost to Stoughton in the final of the 2011 Safeway Championship. They lost by one point in the final end. The McEwen team then lost their third straight provincial final game at the 2012 Safeway Championship. This time they were losing to Rob Fowler. This tied a provincial record for consecutive final losses. The record had been previously set by Kerry Burtnyk from 97-99. This dubious record was avoided in 2013, when the McEwen rink failed to reach the final. They lost to the rival Stoughton rink in the 2013 Safeway Championship semi-final. Once again, at the 2014 Safeway Championship, the team lost the final to Stoughton.

Despite being ranked first in the world on both the World Curling Tour Order of Merit rankings and on the WCT money list, Wozniak lost his fifth provincial final in six years in 2015. He was losing to Reid Carruthers.

Three Briers and team breakup 
Wozniak's rink won their first provincial title in 2016. This sent them to their first Brier. The Matt Dunstone rink had committed themselves to the 2016 World Junior Curling Championships. These championships occurred at the same time as the 2016 Tim Hortons Brier. The Dunstone rink beat Reid Carruthers in the semi-final. McEwen's team would go to the Brier, even if they had lost to Dunstone.

In 2017, Wozniak defended his Manitoba Championship by beating Reid Carruthers in the final. He would then better his 2016 Brier showing. The team went 9–2 in the round robin to enter the playoffs in first place. They had hammer and choice of rocks. Brad Gushue was also 9–2 but lost first place due to losing his round robin meeting with Manitoba. McEwen then lost 7–5 to Brad Gushue in the 1 vs. 2 game. In the semi finals against reigning Brier and World Champion Kevin Koe, they were in control for most of the game. They were up 5–3 with hammer in the eighth end. Koe made a comeback with a steal in the eighth end. He scored two points in the tenth end. He made another steal in the extra end. This dropped Manitoba to the bronze medal game. They recovered to win their first Brier medal. They defeated Brad Jacobs in their rematch of the 2016 bronze medal game, 7–6 in an extra end.

While competing at the 2018 Viterra Championship, skip McEwen came down with chickenpox. He was unable to play after the first game. B. J. Neufeld skipped the team in his absence. McEwen made a surprise appearance in the final. They lost to Carruthers. Despite the setback, they still had a chance to qualify for the 2018 Tim Hortons Brier through the wildcard game. They won the wildcard over Jason Gunnlaugson. Team McEwen had a difficult Brier. Alongside Carruthers they were unable to qualify for the playoffs. Following the Brier, the McEwen team announced they would be breaking up at the end of the 2017–18 season. Just days after the announcement, the McEwen team won the 2018 Elite 10 Grand Slam of Curling event. They won the top $28,000 prize money. They were the first team to go through the entire event undefeated. The Grand Slam victory was the team's seventh overall.

Wozniak took a few years off from men's play after Team McEwen broke up. However, he played mixed doubles with his current girlfriend Marlene Albrecht. He spared for McEwen's new team. After Alex Forrest stepped away from competitive curling after the 2019–20 season, Wozniak joined the Jason Gunnlaugson rink. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic in Manitoba, the 2021 provincial championship was cancelled. As Team Gunnlaugson were the reigning provincial champions, they were chosen to represent Manitoba at the 2021 Tim Hortons Brier. At the Brier, they finished with a 6–6 record.

Personal life
Wozniak is employed as a mortgage broker for Vertuity Mortgage. He is currently in a relationship with Swiss curler Marlene Albrecht. He has two children.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. The short was released on February 17, 1934.

Earl Duvall supervised the film's production. Jack King animated characters and received credit for his work. Frank Tipper also animated characters and was credited. Bob Clampett contributed animation without receiving credit. Paul Fennell worked as an uncredited animator on the project. Chuck Jones participated in animation duties without credit. Frank Tashlin completed the animation team as an uncredited contributor. Bernard Brown composed the music score and received sole credit for this work. Norman Spencer also composed music but went uncredited. Bernard Brown recorded the sound without receiving credit for this technical role. The production was assigned number 6125.

Plot
The cartoon follows a male bug who checks into a hotel. A female insect accompanies him to the establishment. The hotel subsequently catches on fire during their stay.

Music
Al Dubin wrote lyrics for the song "Honeymoon Hotel." Harry Warren composed the music for this song. The 1933 Warner Bros. film Footlight Parade originally introduced this musical number. This animated short appears on the DVD release of Footlight Parade.

Color process
The film marked the first Warner Bros. cartoon produced in color. Cinecolor was the color system employed for this production. Walt Disney held exclusive rights to the Technicolor process at that time. Beauty and the Beast was the only other Merrie Melodies cartoon produced in Cinecolor. The series temporarily reverted to black-and-white after these two films. Merrie Melodies later adopted Technicolor for its productions. Looney Tunes continued using black-and-white until 1943. Several late 1940s Looney Tunes employed Cinecolor again. Multiple late 1940s Merrie Melodies shorts also returned to using Cinecolor.

Operation Claw () was a joint Swedish–American operation, with Norwegian support, that was carried out at Lillehammer shortly after the German capitulation by the end of World War II. Thirty-five German intelligence specialists were transferred along with various equipment first to Sweden and then to U.S. camps in occupied Germany through an agreement between the Americans and the German High Command of the Wehrmacht in Norway. The intelligence material from Operation Claw, among it a Soviet codebook, became very useful for the Americans during the Cold War. Operation Claw was controversial both when it happened and afterwards. In 1945, it was controversial that the Americans operated in what was seen as a British controlled country, and that they secured information about its ally the Soviet Union, in cooperation with neutral Sweden. In later years, a hypothesis that the Norwegian resistance fighter Kai Holst's sudden death in June 1945 was related to his involvement in the Operation Claw has been put forward by among others the historian Tore Pryser.

Even before the war in Europe ended the various allied states had begun the search for German scientists and other German expertise. Signals intelligence had been vital during World War II. The British work with breaking the German codes from the Enigma had been of huge importance. The Yalta Conference in February 1945 had revealed conflicts of interest between the western allied nations on one side and the Soviet Union. Relations between these powers were severely strained after the conference. American intelligence organisations were very interested in German intelligence experts knowledge of the Soviet Union. Immediately after the war in Europe ended they began to cooperate with the German Major General Reinhard Gehlen. His organisation Fremde Heere Ost (FHO) had led German intelligence on the Eastern Front. The cooperation was part of an organized effort to obtain as much German intelligence information and personnel as possible. The operation had the name Target Intelligence Committee (TICOM). The war was however still fought in East-Asia at this time. The US and the Soviet Union were still allies in mid-1945. The Americans were counting on Soviet assistance in the war against Japan. The allies had designated Norway as part of the British sphere of influence. Both for the US and the neutral Sweden the operation was thus very sensitive. The operation was conducted in great secrecy to avoid diplomatic incidents.

In the Wehrmacht camp at Lillehammer a group of 35 German experts on signals intelligence were gathered. They had been working on the Eastern Front against Soviet forces. They possessed an archive of intercepted communications. They had extensive knowledge about Soviet military procedures and communication protocols. This was knowledge the Western Allies, and especially the Americans, wanted. The knowledge probably proved of use during the Cold War. In cooperation with the American intelligence organisation Office of Strategic Services (OSS) the operation proceeded. Swedish intelligence had knowledge and support from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm. Agents for the Swedish intelligence organisation C-byrån traveled together with two Norwegian intelligence specialists to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. The German group of experts were taken out of the camp. They were transported to Sweden by truck convoy. After a few weeks in Sweden they were on June 12 flown from Torslanda Airport close to Gothenburg to US occupied Germany. They were interned in an American military camp at Wiesbaden.

The transfer to Sweden of the German experts at Lillehammer, that OSS called Operation Claw, was directed from the highest level. From the U.S. side the leader of OSS, Major General William J. Donovan was involved. From the Swedish side the chief of the Defense Staff, Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd coordinated the effort. The famous Swedish police director Harry Söderman was also involved from the Swedish side in planning logistics.

More than a month after the German capitulation, a British led search supported by Norwegian personnel was executed. The search aimed to find people from Gestapo hiding among ordinary soldiers. Other German key personnel were also sought in German military camps. The search force that Kai Holst and other Norwegians were assisting discovered missing personnel. They were soon aware of that a number of German key personnel had been removed in the Swedish–American operation a month earlier. Kai Holst had been working at the military office number 4 (Mi4) at the Norwegian legation in Stockholm. After the search he unexpectedly traveled right back to Stockholm without filing a complete report. The next day he was found shot at the top of the staircase in an apartment building at Rindögatan 42 on Gärdet. The official cause of death was stated as suicide by investigating authorities. Neither Holst's family nor many of his colleagues from the resistance movement have accepted this verdict. They are of the opinion that he was liquidated by intelligence operatives.

The historian Tore Pryser has put forward the hypothesis that Holst brought with him information from Lillehammer that could damage Operation Claw. According to this theory he was thus killed to prevent disclosure. To be able to damage the operation Kai Holst can not have been trusted as others were with the same knowledge. He must have been considered a threat due to his contact with Alexandra Kollontaj. She was ambassador in Stockholm representing Soviet Union during the final war years. A possible reason for a murder of Kai Holst was thus not his knowledge as such but his connections to Soviet diplomatic circles.

Operation Claw was the beginning of the postwar era cooperation between Swedish and US intelligence services. This cooperation violated Sweden's officially stated neutrality policy. From the American side the operation was viewed as a great success in intelligence gathering. The responsible officers within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, were both honored with decorations. The operation specifically were mentioned in their citation documents. For the Swedish C-byrån Operation Claw quickly became toxic to their reputation. Even though the operation was to be kept confidential, information leaked to the Swedish press in late 1945. C-byrån were dissolved in February 1946 as a consequence of the scandal. Information regarding Operation Claw continued to be classified as confidential in the post-war years. Some of it still remains classified today under national security provisions. A report about the operation in the British National Archives is restricted until 2020 under official secrets regulations.

Corfe Castle railway station is a railway station located in the village of Corfe Castle, in the English county of Dorset. Originally an intermediate station on the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch line from Wareham to Swanage, the line and station were closed by British Rail in 1972. It has since reopened as a station on the Swanage Railway, a heritage railway that runs from Norden station just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage station.

Corfe Castle is on a railway line connecting Wareham and Norden.

History
Corfe Castle lies in the centre of the Isle of Purbeck, which is actually a peninsula rather than a true island. The English Channel borders this peninsula to the south. The marshy lands of the River Frome form part of the northern boundary. Poole Harbour provides the eastern limit of this geographical area. At the beginning of the 19th century, the area around Corfe Castle was known for its supply of Purbeck Ball Clay. This clay was transported by the Middlebere Plateway, one of two horse-drawn tramways serving the region. The Furzebrook Railway formed the second tramway system in operation. These tramways delivered their cargo to wharves on Poole Harbour. The port of Swanage occupied the tip of the Isle. Purbeck Marble was mined in the local quarries near Swanage. This marble was shipped out by sea from the port facilities.

The presence of these industries attracted railway promoters. The L&SWR main line reached Wareham in 1847, creating new opportunities for branch connections. Several schemes were promoted during the following decades. These early proposals all failed to secure financing or parliamentary approval. Eventually the Swanage Railway received its Act in 1881, granting legal permission to construct the line. The railway opened on 20 May 1885 for passenger and freight services. The position of Corfe Castle commanded the only relatively low level route across the hilly spine of the Isle of Purbeck. The line passed close to the centre of the village due to this geographical constraint. Corfe Castle station was built for the opening of the line in 1885. From its opening, the line was operated by the L&SWR under a working agreement. The line was absorbed into that railway in 1886 through formal merger. Corfe Castle station was the only intermediate station on the Swanage branch throughout its operational history under British Rail ownership. The station possessed the only passing loop between the junction with the main line at Worgret Junction and Swanage, making it operationally significant for train scheduling. At least one camping coach was positioned here by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1967 for holiday accommodation. The camping coach service probably extended from 1948 to 1953 based on company records. From 1960, the allocated coach was a camping coach converted from a Pullman car, representing upgraded tourist facilities. This converted coach was fitted with a full kitchen for self-catering guests. Two sleeping compartments provided accommodation for families. A room with two single beds offered additional sleeping space. From 1962 until 1967 there were two of these coaches here, doubling the available holiday capacity.

The development of Swanage as a tourist resort brought additional passenger traffic to the line during summer months. The collapse of the clay industry removed a major source of freight revenue. The marble industries also declined, eliminating another traditional traffic source. The increase in private car ownership in the second half of the 20th century made the line unprofitable as passengers switched to road transport. Closure was first proposed in 1967 by British Railways management. Despite local opposition the line finally closed on 3 January 1972 under the Beeching axe policies. During the final few years of the line's operation under British Rail, passenger train services were operated by two-car Class 205 diesel electric multiple units. These units were also known as type 2H in British Rail's classification system.

From the time of the first proposal of closure, a campaign to reopen the railway as a steam locomotive operated heritage railway developed among local enthusiasts. Most of the track bed was bought by Dorset County Council to preserve the route from development. Corfe Castle station was included in this purchase by the county authority. Proposals to use the railway route through the Corfe Castle gap as a road bypass for the village were considered during the 1970s and early 1980s. These bypass proposals were eventually rejected by the county council in 1986 after environmental studies. In the meantime the Swanage Railway had started operating a steam service at the Swanage end of the line in 1982, beginning the heritage railway operation.

There were concerns that reopening Corfe Castle station as a northern terminus for the Swanage Railway would cause parking problems in the village centre. It was therefore decided to extend the line a further half a mile north to avoid congestion issues. A new Park and Ride site was built on the former location of the exchange sidings between the Swanage branch and the clay tramways. Here the new Norden station was built to serve as the primary northern terminus. Most trains terminate at Norden rather than Corfe Castle to utilize the parking facilities. Corfe Castle station reopened on 12 August 1995 for heritage railway services. The official opening ceremony was not until February of the following year with dignitaries present.

A 5-year project by Swanage Railway volunteers to install a footbridge across the running lines between the platforms at Corfe Castle was completed in April, 2007. David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official opening of this restored structure. The footbridge was originally built in 1893 by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway for use on their network. Cast-iron columns support the structure's weight. A wrought iron span forms the bridge deck. The footbridge spent its life at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon station. The structure served the West Croydon line until removed by Swanage Railway volunteers for relocation. The footbridge can accommodate the people who now use Corfe Castle station safely. The new bridge is safer than the previous arrangement. It is more convenient for the public than crossing over the track via the gated and locked foot crossing that previously existed. The project won the National Railway Heritage Awards in December 2007 for engineering excellence. A plaque was presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones of the Swanage Railway recognizing his leadership. His team of volunteers received recognition for their contribution. The late Gwyneth Dunwoody, Chairman of the House of Commons' Transport Select Committee, made the presentation.

In summer 2018 South Western Railway operated two trains per day to Wareham from Corfe Castle. In summer 2019 this service continued with the same frequency. One of these trains continued to Poole beyond Wareham. The other train ran to London Waterloo via Weymouth on the main line. There were also National Rail services on Saturdays between Wareham and Swanage in summer 2018. Sunday services also operated during this period. Summer 2019 saw continuation of these weekend services. West Coast Railway Company operated these additional services under contract. Three trains per day ran in each direction on these weekend services. However, in July 2019 these services were stopped due to operational difficulties. There are currently no National Rail services to Corfe Castle as of the text's writing.

Services
Services run every day from the beginning of April to late October under the summer timetable. Weekend only operation occurs in March during the spring shoulder season. November sees weekend-only trains continuing. December maintains this reduced winter pattern. The level of service varies from 6 to 17 trains a day in each direction across the operating year. Service frequency depends on the season with summer seeing maximum trains. The day of the week affects service levels with weekends busier. Southbound, trains operate to stations at Harman's Cross, reached in 10 minutes. Herston is served by trains that stop only on request from passengers. Swanage is reached in 21 minutes as the southern terminus. Northbound, trains operate to Norden station, taking 3 minutes.

Museum
Corfe Castle station is also the home of the Swanage Railway's Railway Museum, housed in dedicated exhibition space. The old goods shed provides the main display area. An adjacent rail van offers supplementary exhibition room. The museum is open on most operating days when trains run.

The museum includes Secundus, a narrow gauge steam locomotive of historical significance. Bellis and Seeking built this locomotive in 1874 for industrial use. The nearby Furzebrook Railway was its original operator. This locomotive was in use until 1955 when it was retired. It was then displayed in the now defunct Birmingham Museum of Science and Industry until 2000 when that institution closed. It is planned that the locomotive will eventually be transferred to a new home for better interpretation. The Purbeck Mineral and Mining Museum will receive this exhibit. This new museum is currently being developed adjacent to Norden railway station on heritage railway property.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" is a short story by British author P. G. Wodehouse, which first appeared in the United States in the October 1923 issue of Cosmopolitan, and in the United Kingdom in the November 1923 Strand. It features the irrepressible Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, and was included in the collection Ukridge, published in 1924.

Plot

Ukridge and Corky run into a friend of Ukridge's, a chauffeur driving a shiny new Daimler, and he offers to take them for a ride. Along the way they are seen by a creditor of Ukridge's, who they shake off, and almost hit a young girl, who Ukridge insists they drive to her home near Clapham Common. He befriends her family, who are impressed by the car and Ukridge's famous Aunt Julia.

When Corky meets Ukridge a week later in the British Museum, he is accompanied by two children. He reveals he has been visiting the house, mainly for the free food, and promising to take the family out on trips in his friend's car, which they believe to be his, and to introduce them to his aunt, who, he reveals, has disowned him, in a letter which states "from now on, I have no nephew".

Returning from short holiday, Corky hears from George Tupper that Ukridge is engaged. Visiting his friend, he finds him with a black eye, and hears the tale of how Ukridge found himself inadvertently engaged to the girl from Clapham Common, and got punched by a rival suitor named Finch. As they talk on Ukridge's doorstep, the creditor from the car ride arrives, and Ukridge hides. A friendly passer-by soothes the enraged creditor, arguing that he knows where Ukridge lives; Ukridge moves out of his house, remarking on the good fortune that led him to use the pseudonym "Mr. Smallweed" when dealing with the man.

Ukridge and Corky form a plot to get Ukridge out of the engagement by feigning ill-health, but as Corky is delivering his speech to the family, the passer-by arrives. He is George Finch, Ukridge's rival for the girl; he reveals that Ukridge is an impoverished imposter, in fact called Smallweed, and produces the creditor to prove it. He also bears a letter from Ukridge's aunt, claiming that she has no nephew. Once Corky has paid off the debt to the creditor, the two are chased from the house.

Main characters

Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, the irrepressible entrepreneur
Julia Ukridge, his haughty writer aunt
Jimmy Corcoran, Ukridge's writer friend
George Tupper, an old schoolfriend of Ukridge and Corcoran
Frederick, a chauffeur, a friend of Ukridge
Mabel Price, a girl Ukridge meets on the road
Mr Price, her doting father
Ernie Finch, her admirer, a resourceful man
Mr Grindlay, a man Ukridge owes money to, who knows him only as "Mr Smallweed"

Publication history

The story was illustrated by T. D. Skidmore in Cosmopolitan. It was illustrated by Reginald Cleaver in the Strand. The story was included in the 1932 collection Nothing But Wodehouse, which was edited by Ogden Nash. That collection was published by Doubleday, Doran & Company. The story was included in Week-End Wodehouse (UK edition), a volume first published by Herbert Jenkins Limited in 1939. The story was also collected in The World of Ukridge, a book published in October 1975. That later collection was issued by Barrie & Jenkins.

Adaptations

The story was adapted for radio in 1956, with Michael Shepley as Ukridge. Hubert Gregg portrayed Corcoran in that radio version. Olaf Pooley played Frederick in the 1956 adaptation. Jeffrey Segal took the role of Mr Grindley. Mairhi Russell appeared as Mabel Price. Brewster Mason performed as Tupper in the broadcast.

The story was adapted for the television series The World of Wodehouse. The episode, titled "The Wedding Bells", aired in 1968. That television version included the character Looney Coote, a figure drawn from "The Long Arm of Looney Coote", another Wodehouse story.

After mentally reviewing each possibility, Kevin concluded that these footsteps belonged to an unfamiliar intruder. A stranger was currently prowling through his apartment uninvited. His mouth flooded with saliva while his tongue detected the metallic taste of salt. His entire body seemed to be marshaling resources for another round of vomiting. Unfortunately, his stomach had been completely emptied hours earlier. Whatever remained of the Demon Food Item had already departed his digestive system.
