ideas_up_hard.coling::32e519e5-5c7c-4bcb-a0ea-bfeb2b47:
Modern Greek art encompasses creative output from the emergence of an independent Greek state through the end of the 19th century. Because Mainland Greece endured Ottoman domination for four full centuries, it remained isolated from the Renaissance that transformed Western European culture. Greek islands including Crete experienced extended periods under Venetian administration, while the Ionian islands came under various European powers' control, enabling these regions to absorb the revolutionary artistic transformations sweeping through Europe from the 14th through the 18th centuries.

The Cretan School emerged as one significant artistic movement, while the Heptanese School developed as another important tradition, both following developmental trajectories that mirrored those of Western European art. Modern Greek artistic expression was predominantly molded by Greece's unique socioeconomic circumstances, the extensive Greek diaspora communities scattered throughout Europe, and the newly formed Greek social elite that emerged after independence. External artistic influences came predominantly from Germany, which provided academic training, and from France, which offered exposure to avant-garde movements.

Sculpture and painting

19th century

The School of Munich

Modern Greek art commenced its development during the Romanticism era. Greek artists absorbed numerous elements from their European counterparts, which resulted in a distinctive style of Greek Romantic art inspired by revolutionary ideals. The country's unique geography provided additional inspiration, while Greece's historical legacy shaped artistic themes. Following centuries of Ottoman domination, educational opportunities in the arts were virtually nonexistent in newly independent Greece. Studying abroad became imperative for aspiring artists seeking professional training. Munich served as an important international center for artistic education during that period. The majority of 19th-century Greek artists selected Munich as their destination for advanced study. Karl von Piloty led the Munich school, where true fresco techniques were taught specifically for mural paintings executed on fresh wet lime plaster. Much of the artwork produced during this period exhibited emotional intensity, while theatrical elements characterized the overall tone. Urban life emerged as one prominent theme explored by Munich school artists. Rural life provided another major subject area, while still life compositions attracted significant attention, and landscape painting completed the primary thematic categories.

These trained artists would eventually return to Greece to transmit their acquired knowledge. Some artists remained permanently in Munich, which contemporaries called Athens on the Isar due to its Greek population. Academic relationships developed between early Greek painters and Munich artistry, while personal bonds strengthened these connections, giving birth to the Greek "Munich School" of painting as a distinct movement. Nikolaos Gysis became an important teacher at the Munich Academy, and he soon emerged as a leading figure commanding respect among Greek artists. Academism dominated early approaches, while realism gained prominence in subject treatment. Genre painting flourished as artists depicted everyday scenes, while upper middle class portraiture satisfied wealthy patrons' demands. Still life compositions demonstrated technical mastery, and landscape painting often incorporated impressionist features that would later become more pronounced. By the end of the 19th century, Symbolism replaced earlier approaches, while Jugendstil introduced new aesthetic principles. Art Nouveau appeared in various works, which are mainly traced in creations by Nikolaos Gysis. Aristeas explored these new directions, while others experimented with emerging styles. Early-20th-century modernism found representation through significant Greek artists working in Munich. Many Munich School artists selected subjects depicting everyday Greek life, while local customs provided rich material for artistic exploration, and living conditions offered commentary on social realities.

Several important painters emerged during this formative period. Theodoros Vryzakis specialized in historical painting, drawing particular inspiration from the 1821 Greek War of Independence that established national sovereignty. Nikiphoros Lytras concentrated on realistic depictions capturing authentic Greek life in all its dimensions. Georgios Jakobides devoted his artistic attention to infants and children as primary subjects, and he would later assume the position of first Director leading the new National Gallery of Athens. Georgios Roilos was another leading painter whose career closely associated him with Munich School principles, especially during his early career when academic training most influenced his work. Konstantinos Volanakis drew inspiration mostly from the Greek sea, which became his signature subject matter.

Other artists associated with the School of Munich included Symeon Sabbides, who contributed to the movement's diversity. Yannoulis Chalepas worked primarily as a sculptor, while Leonidas Drosis created both sculptural and architectural works. Quite a few modernist artists studied in Munich during later periods, which included Theofrastos Triantafyllidis who explored contemporary styles. Jorgos Busianis developed his own distinctive approach, and also Giorgio de Chirico began his artistic education in this environment before achieving international fame.

Notable sculptors of the new Greek Kingdom included Leonidas Drosis, whose major work comprised extensive neo-classical architectural ornament decorating the Academy of Athens building. Lazaros Sochos produced important sculptural works, while Georgios Vitalis contributed to the period's sculptural output. Dimitrios Filippotis created significant pieces, and Ioannis Kossos added to the sculptural tradition. Yannoulis Chalepas achieved recognition for innovative approaches, while Georgios Bonanos worked in classical modes, and Lazaros Fytalis completed the roster of major sculptural figures.

The School of Paris

A few Greek painters pursued their studies in Paris rather than Munich. Despite residing in the French capital and following guidelines established by the French Art Academy, they invariably developed their own distinctive interpretations reflecting Greek sensibilities. Jacob Rizos was involved with rendering female grace in his compositions. Theodoros Rallis focused on scenes from the Orthodox East that captured religious and cultural traditions. Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos specialized in portraiture that captured individual character, while also producing still life works and genre paintings that depicted everyday scenes. During this period in Paris the avant-garde Impressionist movement developed revolutionary approaches to light and color. Most Greek painters remained faithful to academic precepts taught by their teachers, with only some nebulous thrusts in the direction of this radical movement that challenged traditional representation. The first Greek impressionist was Périclès Pantazis, who initially trained in Paris before settling in Belgium. He became a part of the avant-garde group Circle de la pâte that promoted innovative artistic techniques.

Themes-artistic depictions

Many Greek artists of this period drew upon El Greco's style for inspiration, particularly when creating art based on religious themes that required spiritual depth. This tied in with the idea of modern secular Greek art referencing more classical styles from ancient Greece. Religious art referenced Byzantine traditions, or Byzantine inspired art that maintained Orthodox visual theology. Moreover, an important and often pioneering role was played by artists from Ionian islands during the 18th century. The beginning of the 19th century saw these artists exploiting conquests of the Italian Renaissance that had transformed European art. Baroque ateliers provided additional technical training and stylistic influences. As efforts persisted with new directions being explored and objectives being refined, Greek artists emerging in the world during the first decades of the 19th century reconnected Greek art with its ancient tradition spanning millennia. The quests of European ateliers provided contemporary technical frameworks, especially those of the Munich School that dominated Greek artistic education. Defining examples of Greek contemporary art from the period include works by Theodoros Vryzakis depicting historical scenes, and Nikiphoros Lytras capturing everyday Greek life with unprecedented realism.

20th century

At the beginning of the 20th century landscape painting held sway over other genres. The interest of painters turned toward the study of light as a primary compositional element. Color became an obsession for artists seeking to capture Greece's unique luminosity. The dependence on Munich slackened as French artistic movements gained prominence. Paris became the pole of attraction for artists of the period seeking exposure to avant-garde developments. In the early 20th century Demetrios Galanis emerged as a contemporary and friend of Picasso. He achieved wide recognition in France for his innovative printmaking techniques. Lifelong membership of the Académie française followed his critical acclaim. The critic Andre Malreaux praised him as an artist capable "of stirring emotions as powerful as those of Giotto," comparing him to the Italian master. Later in the century Nikos Engonopoulos achieved international recognition with surrealist conceptions that merged painting and poetry in unprecedented ways. In the late 1960s Dimitris Mytaras became associated with European critical realism that addressed social issues. Yiannis Psychopedis developed a parallel practice within critical realism that examined contemporary Greek society. Impressionism was the original influence on leading figures dominating the art of the first half of the 20th century. Konstantinos Parthenis absorbed impressionist techniques while developing a uniquely Greek visual language. Konstantinos Maleas created landscapes infused with Mediterranean light that transcended mere impressionist imitation. Nikiphoros Lytras associated himself with avant-garde groups of Munich during his later career, constituting the last known link with the series of painters in the great tradition of Munich's influence on Greek art. The further development of these painters led to other roads beyond impressionism. They always worked within the framework of the avantgarde movement despite maintaining a distinctly Greek dimension that reflected national identity.

Gradually the impressionists and other modern schools increased their influence on Greek artistic production. In the early 20th century Greek artists turned from Munich to Paris as their primary destination for advanced training. The interest of Greek painters shifted from historical representations to Greek landscapes emphasizing the country's unique visual qualities. Light became a primary concern, while colors so abundant in Greece received unprecedented attention in compositions. Representatives of this artistic change included Konstantinos Parthenis, who pioneered new approaches to color and composition. Konstantinos Maleas developed landscape painting to new heights of expressive power. Nikiphoros Lytras continued evolving his style toward more modern approaches. Georgios Bouzianis introduced expressionist elements that challenged academic traditions. Konstantinos Parthenis, in particular, introduced historical elements alongside religious and mythological subjects. These thematic expansions allowed the classification of Greek painting into modern art categories recognized internationally. The same holds true with the landscapes of Konstantinos Maleas, which demonstrated sophisticated understanding of modern pictorial space. The expressionism of Georgios Bouzianis brought emotional intensity that paralleled northern European developments. The period of the 1930s was a landmark for Greek painters seeking to establish national modernism. Yiannis Tsarouchis emerged with a distinctive style combining folk elements and modernist techniques. Yiannis Moralis developed geometric abstraction rooted in Greek light and form. Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas created cubist-influenced landscapes that captured Greek architecture and topography. Spyros Vassiliou worked across multiple media, while Alekos Kontopoulos introduced pure abstraction into Greek painting for the first time. Spyros Papaloukas came into the limelight of Greek Art with expressionist works. These painters tried mainly to link leading European trends with Greek tradition, creating synthesis rather than imitation.

Notable 20th- and 21st-century artists

The second half of the 20th century has seen a range of acclaimed Greek artists achieving international recognition. Constantine Andreou received the French Légion d'honneur for his sculptural contributions. Thodoros Papadimitriou became an internationally acclaimed sculptor working in monumental forms. Giorgio de Chirico was an influential pre-Surrealist Greek-Italian painter who founded Metaphysical art as a distinct movement. Jannis Kounellis ranks among the pioneers of the Arte Povera artistic movement that challenged consumerist culture. Electros Vekris emerged as a Kinetic artist and Sculptor working with innovative materials. He is the most well-known artist working in the field of light as a medium. Sound became another element in his installations, while Motion completed his exploration of temporal art forms. Theodoros Stamos was a renowned abstract expressionist painter associated with the New York School. Takis created electromagnetic sculptures that moved in response to invisible forces. Chryssa developed neon light sculptures that transformed urban signage into high art. Constantin Xenakis produced internationally acclaimed works of Kinetic sculpture exploring mathematical principles. Other notable Greek artists include Hermon di Giovanno, who worked in figurative modes. Varotsos creates monumental glass sculptures for public spaces. Dimitris Mytaras continued his critical realist practice into the 21st century. Spyros Vassiliou maintained a prolific output across decades. Alekos Fassianos developed a distinctive figurative style combining Greek mythology with contemporary life. Theocharis Mores explored abstract forms. Dimitris Koukos (1948-) works in mixed media. Nikos Stratakis creates minimalist compositions. Steven Antonakos produced geometric neon installations. Kostas Tsoklis experiments with multimedia approaches. Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas influenced generations of younger artists. Thanassis Stephopoulos works in contemporary painting. Aggelika Korovessi creates installations addressing social themes. Yiannis Melanitis rounds out this impressive roster of modern Greek artistic achievement.
ideas_up_hard.coling::bb048a1e-39f8-4c80-9db0-70176b1c: Grace Files The Department Break-Room is always a fun place. Its employees, like me, all share one little gift from the Chief Executive: Immortality. So long as we continue to do our jobs, we're given all the time we could ever want or need. A large chunk, usually a bit less than three quarters of it, is spent working. Mostly because there are so many people running around the world dying at any given moment. Even with the advantage of existing outside of Time and Space, we Reapers still have a bit of trouble processing all the people who are dying. Of course, we can all still take off a quarter of our infinity to chill out on Earth or around the Department's Campus. That leads to another fun thing that being immortal causes: you get people from everywhere and everywhen you can think of. One of the older reapers was around when the Aztec Empire was basically a handful of guys with an insane idea involving a cactus. The symbol also required a snake coiled around the plant's base. An eagle perched on top completed the prophetic vision they sought. Another of us was on the Senate Floor when Gaius Julius Caesar was killed. That particular Reaper claims she heard Caesar's final words clearly. The dagger wounds numbered twenty-three according to her count. You get a lot of weird interactions when you mix in so many people. For example, you get Roman sitting in front of a big screen TV watching a Chariot Race. The race he selected occurred during the reign of Trajan. The Blue faction won that particular competition by half a length. The Aztec is chatting with a Norseman about the merits of hanging as opposed to cutting the heart out. The Norseman argues that Odin's preferred method shows greater respect. Blood sacrifice to Huitzilopochtli required the heart be removed while still beating. Some of the Americans, such as myself, are chatting about college sports around a water cooler. My alma mater lost its bowl game last season. The quarterback threw three interceptions in the fourth quarter alone. The younger members of our staff are setup in the region we call "The Arcade." They prefer virtual reality games that didn't exist during their mortal lives. The newest gaming consoles get installed within days of their Earth release. After all those people... there's the guy at the bar. He's the oldest of the Reapers. We don't even know the guy's name, since he hasn't bothered telling anyone. His records are covered up by some administrative seal we can't access. He doesn't get out much to social functions or Department gatherings. We've all seen him milling around the Department hallways late at night. Never seen him in the Break Room though, much less at the bar. We've got every drink imagined, at least up until the present day out on Earth. I took a seat next to him on a worn leather stool. "Evening," I said without thinking too much about the guy understanding me. Language barriers don't exist for Reapers since we hear everything in our native language. Everyone hears us in their native language as well. This leads to all kinds of insanity in the modern world with its multilingual populations. Ancient Greece presented fewer complications due to linguistic uniformity in most regions. Rome had Latin as the administrative tongue throughout its territories. "Evening," the Eldest said in response to my greeting. His voice sounded deep like ocean trenches. An ancient quality permeated every syllable he uttered. "What are you drinking to," I asked him directly. "Death," the Eldest said without hesitation or elaboration. I didn't laugh at his answer. Neither did he crack even the smallest smile. "Whose?" I asked to clarify his meaning. "Millions," he said flatly while staring into his glass. I nodded in reply to acknowledge his burden. Reapers may be immortal with our supernatural longevity. We may have a lot of not-quite-natural abilities beyond mortal ken. We're all still human at our core despite our powers. Our minds are just like the minds of the people we reap in structure. Doing our job is rough on our psychological well-being. I'd honestly call it the hardest job in the world without exaggeration. Having to be there when someone's dying never becomes routine. Seeing the grieving families of those who slip away to cancer breaks you. Other diseases claim victims with equal tragedy and suffering. Having to deliver a bitter mercy to spare someone the pain weighs heavily. That's not even thinking about the horrors you witness in combat zones. Retrieving the deceased from battlefields exposes you to humanity's worst violence. Having to retrieve someone who succumbed to despair by their own hand haunts you. Anyway, there isn't a Reaper on staff who hasn't gotten depressed over that reality. Not being able to help the dying beyond giving them the bitter mercy frustrates us. We're all human underneath our supernatural duties. We all still have our empathy intact despite centuries of service. I figured that the Eldest had managed to experience that emotional toll. "You talked to the Councilors about it?" I asked with genuine concern. The Councilors aren't Reapers for the most part as a rule. They're among the Dead who completed their mortal existence. The people who live in whatever comes next volunteer for this duty. They're also volunteers who come into the Department specifically to help us. Our mental hang-ups require professional intervention from those who understand death. I know I spend a lot of time talking to them weekly. "No..." the guy said after a long pause. "At least... not this century," he added with bitter emphasis. "Which deaths have you down?" I asked to identify the problem. "Fratricide..." the Reaper said with visible pain in his expression. "It... it reminds me of myself a bit too much," he confessed quietly. I nodded to show I understood his implication. Reapers come in all forms across human history. Some of us are like me who took the job offer voluntarily. We did it to get someone else a better afterlife than default. Some are here serving sentences to get themselves into something halfway decent. The Eldest was apparently among the latter category of condemned servants. "So," I said carefully, "You thought about requesting that those assignments be diverted?" "Can't..." he said with resignation in his tone. "It's part of my... my sentence," he explained with difficulty. "Ouch," I said with genuine sympathy for his predicament. When it comes to Reapers like the Eldest, they have something called a Sentence. This Sentence is designed to reform them to a state of worthiness. They would be acceptable in the Afterlife they're due eventually. It's a set of obligations they must fulfil without exception. Failure means being sent on ahead of schedule to punishment. If they're lucky, they just get reincarnated as newborns without memory. If they're unlucky, they're supposed to get thrown into Torment eternally. "It's just..." He said while gripping his glass tighter. "I've seen so many of them over the millennia. Every time I go out on assignment I experience this. I don't see the person I'm sent for initially. I see someone... someone I knew back before I was a Reaper in life. I see myself standing over them with the weapon that killed them." I saw a tear roll down the Eldest's cheek. Those words carried centuries of guilt and remorse. I remained silent to let him process his emotions. "Damn it..." the Eldest said while wiping his face. "I need to get back to work immediately. Need to get out of here before I lose composure completely," he added urgently. "Luck," I said as my parting wish. "And consider scheduling an appointment with the Councilors soon. We don't need you going renegade on us now. That generally results in a lot of paperwork for the rest of us to process. Emergency interventions require forms in triplicate minimum," I added practically. The Eldest scoffed at that bureaucratic reality. He nodded in my direction as he got up to leave the bar area. It was only once he'd left the room completely that I realized something. I still didn't have his name after our entire conversation.
ideas_up_hard.coling::76136b55-6fc5-43fa-b998-384c79a1: We are about a third of the way down the road," she says. Having been one the major players behind Manchester's recent cultural renaissance, she takes on the leadership of the Tate with palpable energy and ambition. Her intention, she says, is to change the Tate in the next 20 years as much as her predecessor - Sir Nicholas Serota - changed it in the last two decades. Given that he oversaw the transformation of the museum from a respected gallery in Pimlico (with a regional outlet in Liverpool) into a global mega art brand, it is a bold claim. Sir Nicholas built his Tate empire with bricks and mortar, refurbishing existing galleries and creating new venues such as Tate Modern. Balshaw will take a different approach with her expansionist agenda, focussing more on people rather than real estate. Roughly speaking, according to statistics collected by the newly-renamed Department of Digital, Culture, Media Sport, around 50 of the British population visit a museum or gallery at least once a year, meaning - of course - 50 do not. These absentees are her target audience. She says: "We should absolutely reasonably expect 75 of the population to love the fact we have a national collection and feel happy to be visiting Tate." Every young person should be given the opportunity to think and play and experiment in the spaces Tate holds, she adds. That represents a big, big shift from current practice, she acknowledges. Her clarity of vision is impressive, though her ability to explain how it will be realised is less exact. She wants to usher in "an easier language to talk about the joy of art" yet couldn't be specific beyond saying that arcane words should be either avoided or explained. She talks of a radical transformation in audience profile, noting a lack of representation of people from BAME background among the staff. The sector more generally suffers from similar diversity problems, she observes. But when it comes to the organisation she is now leading, which is to be the agent for the change she desires, she says, "it's not that we need to change anything particularly." There is no doubt she is sincere in her ambitions, being probably more capable than most in the museum and gallery world when it comes to broadening the audience. But if she is to be successful in her aims she will need to take a leaf out of Sir Nicholas's job application for the Tate director's job back in the 1980s - in which he wrote that for the institution to change he would need to grasp the nettle. Digital engagement will form a cornerstone of her strategy moving forward. Partnerships with schools across disadvantaged regions will expand access significantly. Community consultation will shape programming decisions in ways previously unexplored. Follow us on Facebook, on Twitter BBCNewsEnts, or on Instagram at bbcnewsents. Usually the low advertised rates are for term life insurance. This type of life insurance has an expiration date that marks when coverage ceases. The product is typically used to protect during periods of higher expenses such as child-rearing years. For example, one might buy a term policy that expires when the kids graduate college, ensuring education costs can be covered. Another common endpoint is when a house mortgage is paid off completely. The goal is making sure than an untimely death doesn't prevent the kids from attending university. It also prevents forcing a surviving spouse to sell the house to meet financial obligations. But if you live until that point in time specified in the contract, the policy expires without payout to any beneficiary. So say the average buyer is in their 30's when purchasing coverage. Most policies cover into their 50's as a typical endpoint. Some extend into their 60's depending on the specific financial obligations being protected. Most will live past the term period, so only a small fraction pay out to estates. The ones that don't claim help cover the ones that do through pooled premiums.

The chances of a payout are so small that insurers profit easily. The number of people paying is so large it creates massive revenue pools. For example let's say 100 people buy a policy. Each 100 dollar life insurance plan costs 10 dollars in premiums. Only 1 person dies during the coverage period. The insurance company gets 100 times 10 equaling 1000 dollars total. The insurance company pays 100 to the dead person's estate as the death benefit. This transaction leaves them with 900 dollars in profit from this cohort. The insurance company can also invest the 900 in financial markets. They earn money from the investment returns on these funds. Now raise the numbers of people buying insurance to thousands. Lower the percentage of people making claims to fractions of a percent. The potential profits for the insurance company are huge under these conditions. The insurance company is also very careful to screen out people who are more likely to make an insurance claim through medical underwriting. Life insurance is difficult to get if you have a life threatening condition like cancer. Vehicle insurance gets harder the worse your driving record is with accidents.
ideas_up_hard.coling::4622a5f2-c96d-4ea1-9629-b734e976: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey covers sufficient area that low-density environment galaxies are now detectable. Rojas et al. developed a method extracting over 1000 void galaxies meeting delta rho/rho < -0.6 on scales r>7 h^{-1} Mpc. We present these galaxies' luminosity function while comparing it to populations in denser cosmic regions. Our measurement spans -21.5<M_r*<-14.5 in SDSS r-band photometry. A Schechter function fits the void galaxy luminosity function with Phi*=(0.19 +- 0.04)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}. The characteristic magnitude equals M_r* - 5logh=-19.74 +- 0.11. The faint-end slope yields alpha=-1.18 +- 0.13. Wall galaxy populations show Phi*=(1.42 +- 0.03)*0.01 h^3 Mpc^{-3}. Their characteristic magnitude reaches M_r* - 5logh=-20.62 +- 0.08. Their faint-end slope measures alpha=-1.19 +- 0.07. The fainter M_r* value agrees with Rojas et al.'s earlier findings about void galaxy dimness. The alpha parameter shows remarkable similarity across different density environments. We examined luminosity functions as density varies for both populations. Wall galaxies inhabiting the densest regions alone exhibit shallower faint-end slopes. We compared void galaxy luminosity functions to wall galaxies sharing similar physical characteristics. Wall galaxies with the bluest colors show nearly identical shape. Those with Sersic index n<2 match the void distribution closely. Galaxies having EW(Halpha)>5A produce similar luminosity function shapes. These wall subsamples display only marginally brighter M_r* values. Their alpha parameters remain consistent with void galaxy measurements. The alpha ~ -1.2 value from void galaxies contradicts predictions from CDM models. Cold dark matter simulations predict steeper faint-end slopes. This discrepancy suggests voids lack large dwarf galaxy populations. The shallow slope indicates fewer faint galaxies than theoretical expectations. Void environments thus appear relatively empty of low-luminosity objects. This finding challenges standard hierarchical structure formation scenarios. The deficit of dwarf galaxies requires explanation within cosmological frameworks.
ideas_up_hard.coling::a31907c5-c035-4dca-ba29-cb4c6fe3: The mass brawl which broke out at a bar opening inside a Queens casino Friday night was allegedly caused by an argument in an enormous line for drinks. ideas_up_hard.coling::f05692cf-092b-40e0-9f4a-d3f7ccd6: I know I'm going to get crap for this but, oh well here goes... Starving, I ventured into the oppressive humidity that characterizes Scottsdale during Arizona's dramatic monsoon season, desperately hunting for sustenance on a lazy Sunday afternoon when many establishments close early. After encountering several businesses that observe strict Sunday closures as their policy, I reluctantly decided to lower my standards at Schlotskys Deli, which had consistently failed to impress me during previous visits to their Scottsdale location. Lo and behold, the gleaming new Capriottis had recently replaced the former tenant, while Everything Bagel had also opened nearby to enhance the area's dining options. Initially I felt relieved by these welcome additions to the neighborhood's culinary landscape.... No wait, suspend all interruptions because my story contains additional developments worth sharing. Upon entering I immediately noticed the oppressive indoor temperature hovered around 85 degrees, making the dining room uncomfortably warm for customers. Approaching the counter I encountered a visibly pregnant employee whose face glistened with perspiration, prompting me to inquire about the timeline of their takeover from the previous sandwich shop. She responded with an exasperated eye roll before glancing downward and curtly stating the transition had occurred two months prior, then immediately demanded my order without pleasantries. After I placed my sandwich request she required my personal name for order tracking purposes in their system. When I provided my actual name she performed another dramatic eye roll accompanied by a defeated shrug that communicated complete apathy about her responsibilities. Her confession of spelling inability came unprompted, revealing a troubling lack of basic literacy skills for someone in customer service. Because I typically don't invest emotional energy in whether strangers butcher my name's spelling or mispronounce its syllables during casual transactions, and because I had already enunciated each sound clearly using phonetic pronunciation to assist her, I initially dismissed the incident as inconsequential. However, the cash register's customer-facing display revealed her creative interpretation: she had written "corney" instead of my actual name. My spontaneous laughter at this absurd misspelling triggered her defensive scoff before she challenged me with an indignant "What?" that dripped with attitude. After I explained the source of my amusement regarding her unconventional spelling choice, she responded with a dismissive smirk while declaring her version "works" before turning away and refusing further eye contact, demonstrating profound disrespect. The young male employee assembling my sandwich at the preparation station was also drenched in sweat that dripped onto surfaces, which he attempted to manage by wiping his forehead using the back of his wrist repeatedly. His coworker had clocked out for a scheduled lunch break, evidenced by how he sprinted past me at dangerous velocity while precariously balancing a beverage container, then skidded dramatically across three feet of tile flooring before collapsing into the nearest available chair. Look, I understand they're inexperienced workers, the desert climate creates brutal conditions, the rushing employee has poor coordination, her pregnancy complicates physical comfort, and workplace dissatisfaction might explain her negativity.... Yet none of these mitigating circumstances excuse the fundamental failure to maintain basic courtesy and professional standards that the food service industry absolutely requires from its staff members.... Where are the responsible managers who should be training these employees properly? The sandwich itself tasted absolutely delicious despite everything! Kudos, perspiring sandwich artist.

Section 51(xxxi) is a subclause of section 51 of the Constitution of Australia.

It empowers the Commonwealth to make laws regarding the acquisition of property, but stipulates that such acquisitions must be on just terms.

The provision is sometimes referred to in shorthand as the 'just terms' clause.

Aside from its importance to Australian Constitutional Law, and Property Law; the section is notable for its role as a plot device in The Castle, an iconic Australian film.

Text 
Section 51(xxxi) reads:

Jurisprudence 
While s51(xxxi) was adapted from the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment, it has many differences.

The 'just terms' requirement has been held not to affect the State Parliaments.

In Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon stated that the inclusion of the condition was to "prevent arbitrary exercises of the power at the expense of a State or a subject."

The interpretation of the terms "acquisition" and "just terms" by the High Court of Australia have had the effect, however, of limiting its protection of property rights. Moreover, it operates at any time the Commonwealth makes a compulsory acquisition of property. As such, it is a contingent guarantee rather than a general constitutional right or freedom to enjoy property rights.

The Commonwealth may only acquire property on just terms for a "purpose in respect of which the Parliament has power to make laws". This means that every law supported by s 51(xxxi) must not be supported by any other additional legislative power.

Property
The High Court of Australia has taken a wide view of the concept of "property". Several members of the court took the opportunity to consider the meaning of the term property in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944). Justice Starke said the term includes: "every species of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and choses in action." Justice McTiernan confirmed the term property extends to tangible and intangible property.

An example of the breadth of the concept of property in section 51(xxxi) is provided by Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth (the Bank Nationalisation Case). In that case, Federal legislation contemplated the acquisition of private banks through vesting of shares in private banks in the Commonwealth. Later provisions enabled the appointment of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon characterised the provisions as removing effective control over the property of the private banks. He concluded that this was, in the essential sense, an acquisition of a proprietary right.

While statutory licences have sometimes been equated with proprietary interests, the removal of rights enjoyed under a statutory licence does not typically constitute an acquisition of property within section 51(xxxi). This is because licence conditions are inherently susceptible to change by legislative amendment.

Acquisition
For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been acquired by somebody. Furthermore, the acquisition must be for a Commonwealth purpose rather than merely destructive. This is in contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, where the destination does not matter. Under American law, it is enough that the holder of property has been deprived of it. Thus in JT International SA v Commonwealth the High Court held that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which restricted the plaintiff's use of its trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth acquiring any property. The packaging restrictions merely prevented certain commercial uses without transferring rights to government. Similarly in Cunningham v Commonwealth the High Court held that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold Pass for retired members of Parliament were not an acquisition of property. The case involved modifications to parliamentary entitlements rather than transfers of proprietary interests.

In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Court held that a grant to NSW which was tied to NSW compulsorily acquiring property was invalid as an acquisition of property upon terms which were not just. The Commonwealth cannot indirectly accomplish through state action what it cannot directly achieve. The validity of a grant in the absence of a requirement to acquire property was upheld in the later case of Pye v Renshaw. That decision confirmed that conditional grants without compulsory acquisition components remain constitutionally permissible.

Just terms
Typically, a determination of just terms based on the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will be sufficient to satisfy the requirement of just terms. Unlike the "just compensation" requirement in the American Fifth Amendment, however, "just terms" imports no equivalence of market value. The arrangements offered must be "fair", or such that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair". However, this judgment of "fairness" must take account of all the interests affected, not just those of the dispossessed owner. Community interests and broader policy considerations may influence what constitutes fairness.

The requirement of "just terms" does not necessarily require that a compensation package be presented as part of the acquisition scheme. It is sufficient that the scheme provides adequate procedures for determining fair compensation. However, the Court may scrutinise such procedures closely to ensure their adequacy. Procedural safeguards must genuinely protect the rights of affected property owners.

There may be some acquisitions of property to which section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws supported exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution. Section 122 governs territories and may operate independently of just terms requirements.

Section 51(xxxi) is an exception to the norm for interpretation of the subsections of section 51, that one grant of power cannot be used to "read down" another. In this case, however, the Court will not allow another grant of power to be read so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation to the power granted by section 51(xxxi). This interpretive principle prevents legislative evasion of constitutional protections.

Related legislation
The Deakin government's Lands Acquisition Act 1906, largely drafted by Littleton Groom, was the first to deal with the compulsory acquisition of land by the federal government. Its most contentious provision was a clause authorising the federal government to grant mining leases and regulate mining on Commonwealth land. Responsibility for compulsory acquisition was initially placed with the Department of Home Affairs.

The Chifley government's Darwin Lands Acquisition Act 1945 compulsorily acquired substantial areas of land owned by Chinese-Australians in Darwin. This acquisition led to the end of the local Chinatown permanently. The legislation was suggested in 1943 by the Northern Territory's administrator Aubrey Abbott. He proposed a combination of compulsory acquisition and conversion of the land to leasehold in order to effect "the elimination of undesirable elements which Darwin has suffered from far too much in the past." Abbott stated that he hoped to "entirely prevent the Chinese quarter forming again" through these measures. He further observed that "if land is acquired from the former Chinese residents there is really no need for them to return as they have no other assets" in the territory. The territory's civilian population had mostly been evacuated during the war following Japanese bombing raids. The former Chinatown residents returned to find their homes and businesses reduced to rubble by wartime destruction.

See also

References

Australian constitutional law
ideas_up_hard.coling::46555368-c6ff-46dc-88fc-bf38c422: Canada's performance relative to the United States falls within a narrow band of similarity. Online forums like rworldnews and rpolitics often present America as a failed state. Most Americans experience reasonable quality of life despite these portrayals. Abandoning established social networks requires extraordinary motivation that most people lack. The psychological toll of cultural displacement deters even those considering relocation. Immigration bureaucracies in developed nations impose substantial financial barriers on applicants. Visa processing times can extend for years before approval. Housing costs in Canadian cities exceed those in most American metropolitan areas. Winter temperatures across much of Canada drop below levels comfortable for people from temperate US regions. Labor market saturation would follow any sudden population increase. Unemployment would spike among newcomers regardless of protective employment legislation. Armed conflicts do not occur within either nation's borders. Citizens of both countries enjoy physical security unknown in war-torn regions. The two populations share cultural traditions that minimize friction. Political systems differ in structure but produce comparable governance outcomes. Currency exchange rates favor Americans traveling north, with Canadian dollars trading at significant discounts. Climate alone discourages many potential migrants from attempting the move. Narratives of American collapse originate primarily from privileged youth lacking perspective on genuine hardship. European commentators sometimes amplify these distortions for entertainment value. Lifestyle differences between the three regions remain marginal for most inhabitants. Canadian cities offer fewer entertainment options than comparably sized American urban centers. Skilled workers typically command higher salaries south of the border. Family ties anchor individuals to their current locations more powerfully than abstract policy preferences. Incremental improvements in social services rarely justify severing all existing relationships. Northern provinces affordable to new arrivals experience the harshest weather conditions. Social media amplifies complaints from a vocal minority of dissatisfied Americans. Every nation struggles with distinct challenges that frustrate portions of its population. Statistical measures show American living standards remain high by global comparison. Healthcare access issues affect specific demographics rather than the entire population. Educational opportunities exist widely despite uneven distribution of resources. Economic mobility, while imperfect, still functions for many families. Infrastructure quality varies regionally but meets basic needs in most areas. Political polarization creates stress without destroying daily functionality. Crime rates have declined over recent decades in most categories. Environmental regulations protect public health despite ongoing policy debates. The gap between online rhetoric and lived experience remains substantial for typical residents.

Palermo defender Roberto Vitiello hopes the Sicilian outfit can improve its dismal form on the road starting on Sunday at Udinese. The Islanders have not tasted victory away from home since November 2 when they defeated AC Milan by a 2-0 scoreline at the San Siro. Following last weekend's 2-1 home defeat against Milan, Palermo find themselves mired in a three-game losing streak that has left them languishing in 11th position in the Serie A table. Roberto Vitiello (left) believes his teammates must start collecting points on their travels to reverse their disappointing away record this campaign.

'We need to keep working hard in order to defend our Serie A status as soon as possible,' Vitiello told reporters from the Italian media. 'We are disappointed not to have collected anything from our last three league fixtures across all competitions. But we must bounce back immediately. Sunday's encounter at Udinese carries great significance for our season, and the squad will give maximum effort to secure our second away victory in the Friuli region this term.'

Palermo, managed by Giuseppe Iachini since his appointment earlier this season, have accumulated merely two points from their previous six Serie A matches. Udinese currently occupy 13th position in the league standings, trailing Palermo by a single point in the table. Mattia Destro (right) challenges Vitiello for possession during their recent Serie A encounter at the Stadio Renzo Barbera.

After suffering defeat to bottom-placed Parma in their midweek fixture, the Friuli-based club appear vulnerable when playing at their home venue. Udinese have failed to register a victory in their last four matches across all domestic competitions, leaving coach Andrea Stramaccioni desperate to elicit a positive response from his struggling squad.

'Against Parma, we had the wrong approach from the opening whistle,' Stramaccioni admitted in his post-match press conference. 'My players underestimated our opponents despite their position at the foot of the table, and we suffered the consequences of our complacency. We lacked determination throughout the ninety minutes and failed to register even a single attempt on their goalkeeper. Now we must turn the page on that embarrassment and demonstrate against Palermo the quality that represents the real identity of this club.'

Udinese have struggled to deliver convincing performances in front of their home supporters, managing only one victory in their previous nine fixtures at the Stadio Friuli. The hosts will be forced to cope without defender Ivan Piris, who received his fifth yellow card of the season. Midfielder Giampiero Pinzi must also serve a one-match suspension for disciplinary reasons.

Palermo travel north without midfielder Edgar Barreto, ruled out for three weeks after sustaining a muscular injury in training. Argentinian forward Paulo Dybala, who has netted 13 goals to lead the Rossaneri's scoring charts, will spearhead the visitors' attacking formation. Franco Vazquez has been assigned the role of playing behind Dybala in an advanced playmaking position.

Internet connections appear free but involve costs somewhere in the system. WiFi providers offer complimentary access as a marketing strategy to attract customers. Businesses absorb connectivity expenses as part of their operational budgets. The borderless nature of internet infrastructure creates an illusion of zero-cost communication. Traditional telephony requires carriers to compensate foreign networks for completing international transmissions. Interconnection fees between telecommunications companies often exceed reasonable operational costs by substantial margins. Consumers ultimately bear expenses through different payment structures rather than avoiding them entirely.

Telephone networks originated during an era when cross-border communication demanded significant financial resources. Historical pricing models established expectations that persist in contemporary markets. Most nations granted single companies exclusive rights to operate telecommunication services within their borders. Legal frameworks prevented competitors from entering established telephone markets. Dominant carriers imposed substantial charges on foreign operators routing calls into their territories. Alternative routing methods did not exist for international voice traffic. Average subscribers rarely made calls beyond national boundaries during this period. High international rates functioned as premium revenue streams for monopoly operators. These profits subsidized the construction of affordable domestic calling networks. Internet technology emerged as a disruptive force in the telecommunications landscape.

Early internet service providers launched as entrepreneurial ventures challenging established players. Dial-up services utilized existing copper telephone infrastructure for data transmission. Competitive pressures motivated ISPs to establish unrestricted peering relationships with content hosts. Geographic separation between network operators posed minimal obstacles to connectivity agreements. Telecom hotels concentrated numerous carriers in shared facilities enabling economical interconnection. Multiple companies competed aggressively to provide links between metropolitan areas. This competitive environment drove internet access prices downward dramatically. Legacy telephone carriers failed to adapt their pricing strategies accordingly.

Net neutrality debates connect directly to these infrastructure ownership patterns. American dial-up users could select from numerous competing access providers. Contemporary broadband subscribers typically face duopolistic markets in cable internet service. ISPs operating without competition attempt to resurrect monopoly-era pricing power. They seek leverage over both consumer charges and content provider fees. Nations maintaining open-access infrastructure models avoid these market distortions. New Zealand regulations permit consumers to choose among many fiber providers. Local exchanges typically offer subscribers dozens of competing service options.

Established phone companies pursue additional revenue from their existing subscriber base. Skype operates on a customer acquisition model seeking initial conversions. Incumbent carriers extract incremental profits while alternative platforms chase market entry. Different business motivations drive contrasting pricing approaches between legacy and internet-based communication services.

If there is an available syllabus for the Biology class, read it carefully to know the rules, materials needed, and any other important information before going to the first Biology class. Reviewing it daily ensures preparedness for each session. Highlighting key passages creates visual markers for quick reference later. Underlining critical requirements draws attention to essential details during subsequent readings. Taking marginal notes captures personal reminders about specific syllabus points.

Use different note-taking methods such as underlining, highlighting, drawing a symbol such as a star next to something important, drawing a box around important sentences/paragraphs, and taking notes either on a separate sheet of paper or the back of the syllabus. These strategies create a personalized study system tailored to individual learning preferences. Visual learners benefit particularly from color-coded marking schemes. Kinesthetic learners retain information better through the physical act of writing annotations.

Make sure it is okay with the teacher before marking up the syllabus. Some instructors prefer students keep original documents pristine for official records. If needed, make a copy with a scanner so there are multiple copies. Keeping one unmarked preserves a clean reference version for future semesters. The annotated copy serves as your working document throughout the current term. If anything changes, new notes can be made on the second copy without obscuring previous information.

Students without scanners at home have a few different options of scanning the syllabus. One is to go to the nearest library that has a scanner and bring the syllabus along. Public libraries typically charge between ten and twenty cents per scanned page. Another option is for students with smartphones or tablets with a camera built into the device. Install an app made for scanning documents, such as Adobe Scan or CamScanner. These type of apps allow users to take a picture of a document and it will convert it to PDF, DOC, and other various document formats. Cloud storage integration enables access from multiple devices simultaneously. If these options are not available, do not hesitate to ask the school if they have a scanner of if the Biology teacher can scan the syllabus. Administrative offices usually provide free scanning services to enrolled students. Teachers appreciate proactive students who seek resources independently.

Most science classes including Biology will require students to pay a lab fee. This fee goes towards supplying the students with lab materials needed for experiments, such as chemicals, glassware, and preserved specimens. Usually the teacher will give students at least the first week of class to pay this fee. Payment plans may be available for students experiencing financial hardship. Most of the time it is refundable, meaning when students have completed the course the money is refunded by to them. Refunds typically process within two to four weeks after the semester concludes. If anything has been damaged by a student, most likely this fee will not be refunded to them. Documentation of equipment condition at course start protects students from unfair damage claims. Be careful of lab materials, both dangerous and safe ones, as replacement costs can exceed the original fee amount.

Usually pencils/pens and paper to take notes are required in most classes. Digital note-taking devices may be prohibited during laboratory sessions for safety reasons. Even if it is not required by the teacher, it is an excellent idea to bring them and take notes anyways. This will help retain information and allow students to review what they learned in class.

After the discussion below, I examined earlier publications by these researchers concerning MUS-ROVER. This prior system formed the foundation upon which the current submission builds its contributions. The earlier work clarified several concepts that remained opaque in the present manuscript. Without consulting that previous research, I would have struggled to grasp the core methodology.

Overall, I appreciate the technical merit of this research. My background includes familiarity with the JSB chorales dataset. I have experience with probabilistic modeling frameworks. I regularly work with n-gram language models in my own research. Despite these advantages, substantial portions of the manuscript proved difficult to parse. The authors employ mathematical notation extensively throughout every section. This heavy symbolic apparatus obscured rather than illuminated the underlying concepts.

The core ideas demonstrate genuine novelty and theoretical soundness. The proposed approaches deserve dissemination to the research community. Future investigations building on this foundation would advance the field meaningfully. However, ICLR may not provide the optimal publication venue given the manuscript's current presentation. Music generation applications align perfectly with the conference's scope, so domain choice poses no concern. The fundamental methodology contains no disqualifying flaws that would prevent acceptance elsewhere.

My intuition suggests a journal format would serve these contributions far better. Such venues permit the extended exposition these complex ideas require. The authors could furnish detailed worked examples walking readers through each algorithmic step. Background material on relevant musical theory could receive proper treatment. The predecessor system MUS-ROVER warrants thorough description for readers unfamiliar with that work. Additional experimental validation using a second musical corpus would demonstrate the approach generalizes beyond Bach chorales. Conference page limits force a density that undermines comprehension here. Focusing narrowly on a single system component might make a conference paper viable. Unfortunately, I cannot identify which specific aspect would stand alone effectively while remaining compelling.

Substantial revision addressing these presentation issues could prompt me to increase my evaluation. The authors' time would yield greater returns through developing an extended journal manuscript with enhanced clarity throughout.

[Addendum: subsequent discussion and author revisions have led me to adjust my assessment upward]
ideas_up_hard.coling::79eb7194-07a0-4dd2-a0b2-7911976f: Judith Scott (May 1, 1943 – March 15, 2005) was an American fiber sculptor, born with Down Syndrome and deaf. She achieved international fame through her innovative textile-based works. In 1987, Judith enrolled at the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, California, an organization that provides artistic opportunities for individuals with developmental disabilities. At this facility, Judith discovered her passion for creating abstract fiber sculptures, which allowed her to express herself through visual means rather than verbal communication. Her twin sister authored Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott (2016), a biographical account documenting their shared experiences. Judith entered the world in Cincinnati, Ohio on May 1, 1943, arriving alongside her fraternal twin sister Joyce. Joyce developed typically, while Judith was born with Down Syndrome, a chromosomal condition. During her infancy, Judith contracted Scarlet Fever, a bacterial infection that damaged her auditory system. Her hearing loss went undetected for many years, complicating her early development. Judith Scott resided with her parents, twin sister and older brothers for the first seven and a half years of her existence. The developmental differences between the twin girls became increasingly evident as they matured. Their parents made deliberate efforts to provide equal treatment to both daughters despite these disparities. When the girls reached school age, educational authorities assessed Judith's readiness for formal instruction. The local school system operated only one classroom specifically designed for students with disabilities. Judith failed the entrance examinations, which relied heavily on verbal responses that she could not provide. Her undiagnosed deafness prevented her from understanding or answering the spoken questions. Medical professionals recommended institutional placement as the solution. Her parents admitted Judith to the Columbus State Institution (formerly the Columbus State School) on October 18, 1950, a facility housing individuals classified as mentally disabled. The separation traumatized both twins deeply. Early institutional records documented that Judith possessed an IQ of 30, a measurement derived from oral testing methods. The CII 158 microns line represents the most important coolant of interstellar
medium within galaxies but substantial variations appear from object to object.
The main source of this emission at galactic scale remains poorly understood.
Previous studies of CII radiation in galaxies have a resolution of several
kpc or more so observed emissions are an average of different ISM components.
The aim of this work involves studying, for the first time, CII radiation at the
scale of a spiral arm. We want to investigate the origin of this spectral feature and its
use as a tracer of star formation. We present CII and OI observations of a
segment of M~31's spiral limb using the Infrared Space Observatory. The CII
radiation is compared with tracers of neutral gas (CO, HI) and stellar birth
(H\alpha, Spitzer 24 mu.) The similarity between CII output and Ha plus 24
mu images proves striking when smoothed to identical resolution, whereas the
correlation with neutral material is much weaker. Cooling rate per hydrogen
atom increases dramatically from approximately 2.7e-26 ergs/s/atom in the border zone
to roughly 1.4e-25 ergs/s/atom in stellar formation zones. The CII/FIR(42-122)
ratio remains almost constant at 2%, a factor three higher than typically quoted.
However, we do not believe that M~31 is unusual. Rather, whole-galaxy
fluxes used for comparisons include central zones where CII/FIR
proportion is known to be lower and resolved measurements neither isolate a
spiral limb nor include data as far out in the galactic disk as measurements
presented here. A fit to published PDR models yields a plausible average
solution of G_0~100 and n~3000 for PDR output in stellar birth areas
within M31's arm. This analysis demonstrates how localized examination reveals properties
distinct from integrated galactic values, emphasizing the importance of spatially-resolved
spectroscopy for understanding physical conditions governing interstellar cooling processes
and their relationship to ongoing stellar genesis activity.
lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::1a16d27a-89fc-4df9-8b4f-cf2532a8: We investigate a planar tight-binding framework of a topological crystalline insulator (TCI) safeguarded by rotational symmetry. This construction emerges from layering two Chern insulators possessing opposite invariants that transform under conjugate representations of the rotational group, e.g. $p_\pm$ orbitals. Despite its apparent similarity to the Kane-Mele framework, it does not host stable gapless boundary modes. Nevertheless this system exhibits topological responses including the appearance of quantized fractional charge bound to rotational defects (disclinations) and the pumping of angular momentum in response to threading an elementary magnetic flux, which are described by a mutual Chern-Simons coupling between the electromagnetic gauge field and an effective gauge field corresponding to the rotational invariance. In addition, we demonstrate that although the filled bands of this construction do not admit a symmetric Wannier representation, such obstruction is removed upon adding appropriate atomic orbitals, implying 'fragile' topology. As a consequence, the physical response can be derived by representing the system as a superposition of atomic orbitals with positive and negative integer coefficients. Following our analysis of the tight-binding framework, serving as a prototypical example of planar TCIs safeguarded by rotation, we establish that all topological crystalline insulators protected by point group symmetries without protected boundary modes are either atomic insulators or fragile phases. Remarkably, such result implies that gapless surface states exist in free electron systems if and only if there is a stable Wannier obstruction. We then use dimensional reduction to map the problem of classifying planar TCIs protected by rotation to a zero-dimensional (0D) problem which is then used to obtain the complete non-interacting classification of such topological crystalline insulators as well as the reduction of this classification in the presence of interactions.
lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243: We introduce a novel artificial intelligence (AI) methodology called the 'Digital Synaptic Neural Substrate' (DSNS). This system employs selected characteristics from entities in various fields (e.g., chess puzzles, classical compositions, renowned artworks) and recombines these features in such a manner as to generate fresh properties that can then, in principle, be utilized to create original items of creative value to humans relating to any one of the source disciplines. Such capability allows some burden of innovative content generation to be passed from people to machines. The methodology was tested in the field of chess puzzle composition. We employed it to automatically compose numerous sets of chess challenges based on characteristics extracted and recombined from chess puzzles and tournament matches by humans, renowned paintings, computer-evolved abstract art, photographs of individuals, and classical music tracks. The quality of these generated chess challenges was then assessed automatically using an existing and experimentally-validated computational chess aesthetics model. They were also evaluated by human specialists in the discipline. The findings suggest that characteristics collected and recombined from chess and other disciplines using the DSNS methodology can indeed be utilized to automatically generate chess challenges of reasonably high aesthetic caliber. In particular, a low-caliber chess source (i.e., tournament match sequences between weak players) used in combination with actual photographs of individuals was able to produce three-move chess challenges of comparable caliber or superior to those generated employing a high-caliber chess source (i.e., published compositions by human specialists), and more efficiently as well. Why information from a foreign discipline can be integrated and functional in such a manner remains an open question for now. lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad: The baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) feature, observed in cosmic matter distribution at redshifts reaching approximately 3.5, reflects continued expansion of the sonic horizon initially identified in temperature anisotropies of the microwave background radiation. This BAO feature's location can now be determined to better than roughly 1% accuracy employing galaxies, and approximately 1.4-1.6% precision utilizing Ly-alpha forests plus quasar clustering. Combined with the Alcock-Paczyński (AP) effect, which arises from changing ratios of angular to spatial/redshift dimensions of (presumed) spherically-symmetric source distributions across distance, such BAO determination is viewed as among the most powerful tools for assessing Universe geometry. In our paper, we employ five BAO feature measurements from the final release of Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV, at average redshifts <z>=0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48 and 2.33, to carry out direct head-to-head comparison of the standard model, Lambda-CDM, alongside one principal competitor, known as the R_h=ct cosmology. For completeness, we complement the AP diagnostic with volume-averaged distance probes that assume constant comoving scale r_d. Both diagnostics are free of uncertain parameters, such as Hubble's constant, and therefore ideally suited for this kind of model selection. We find that R_h=ct is favored by these observations over the standard cosmology based solely on AP effects, with likelihood approximately 75% versus roughly 25%, while Planck-Lambda-CDM is preferred over R_h=ct based solely on volume-averaged distance diagnostics, with likelihood around 80% versus about 20%. Joint analysis employing both probes produces inconclusive outcomes, yielding comparable likelihoods to both cosmologies. We are therefore not able to confirm through this work that BAO observations, on their own, support an accelerating Universe. The evidence remains ambiguous when considering all available diagnostics together for distinguishing between competing theoretical frameworks.
lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c: Accurately forecasting temporal evolution of intricate phenomena is crucial across multiple scientific domains. This widespread enthusiasm is nevertheless hampered by formulation challenges: frequently, governing equations describing underlying mechanics remain inaccessible or, when available, solving them demands computational resources incompatible with forecasting deadlines. Unsurprisingly, approximating elaborate arrangements through generic functional representations and informing these ex-nihilo from empirical observations has emerged as standard procedure during the machine-learning era, exemplified by countless successful implementations utilizing deep neural architectures. Nevertheless, model transferability, assurance boundaries, and observational influence are frequently neglected or explored primarily through reliance on prior physical understanding. We address these challenges from an alternative perspective, adopting a curriculum-based training strategy. Within curriculum-oriented instruction, datasets are organized so initial phases employ simple examples progressing toward increasingly difficult instances to promote convergence and transferability. Such methodology has been developed and fruitfully deployed in robotics and control applications. Herein, we implement this approach for learning intricate dynamical arrangements systematically. Initially, leveraging insights from ergodic theory, we determine observational quantities sufficient for guaranteeing a-priori faithful representations of physical phenomena and comprehensively examine how training collections and their organization affect long-horizon forecast quality. Building upon that foundation, we regard entropy as a complexity measure for datasets; we demonstrate how deliberate construction of training collections grounded in entropic analysis substantially enhances resulting representations regarding transferability, and offer guidance concerning observational volume and selection necessary for effective empirically-driven formulation. Our investigation reveals that strategic dataset curation informed by complexity metrics produces superior predictive capabilities compared to arbitrary sampling approaches. The curriculum paradigm enables gradual exposure to increasingly challenging scenarios, facilitating robust pattern recognition while avoiding premature overfitting to difficult cases. Through systematic entropy-guided organization, practitioners can optimize limited observational budgets, ensuring adequate coverage of relevant behavioral regimes without excessive redundancy in simpler regions while maintaining sufficient representation of complex dynamics.

Context. Filaments are ubiquitous in the Galaxy, and they host star formation. Detecting them in a reliable way is therefore key towards our understanding of the stellar birth process and how young suns emerge from molecular clouds.

Aims. We explore whether supervised machine learning can identify filamentary structures on the whole Galactic plane, examining automated recognition capabilities across vast celestial regions.

Methods. We used two versions of UNet-based networks for image segmentation, employing convolutional neural architectures designed specifically for pixel-level classification tasks. We utilized H2 column density images of the Galactic plane obtained with Herschel Hi-GAL data as input material, providing observational foundation for our analysis. We trained the UNet-based networks with skeletons (spine plus branches) of filaments that were extracted from these images, together with background and missing information masks that we produced through careful manual annotation. We tested eight training scenarios to determine the best approach for our astrophysical purpose of classifying pixels as belonging to elongated molecular concentrations.

Results. The training of the UNets allows us to create a new representation of the Galactic plane by segmentation in which pixels belonging to filamentary structures are identified successfully. With this novel method, we classify more pixels (more by a factor of 2 to 7, depending on the classification threshold employed) as part of thread-like formations than the spine plus branches structures we used as initial labels. Previously unseen formations are revealed, which are mainly low-contrast elongated features that were not detected before using traditional algorithms. We use standard metrics to evaluate the performances of the different training scenarios, applying quantitative assessment tools. This allows us to demonstrate the robustness of the technique and to determine an optimal threshold value that maximizes the recovery of the initial labelled pixel assignments.

Conclusions. This proof-of-concept study shows that supervised machine learning can reveal filamentary structures present throughout the Galactic plane, uncovering faint morphologies never observed previously.

However, there are so many problems with it that I cannot in good faith call it a "masterpiece" or proclaim it to be one of the best of the medium as anything other than a gateway series. I'll start off with the characters, which is where many of my issues lie. I'll admit, Spike and Jet are wonderful personas, but they are only two-fifths of the entire Bebop Crew. Ein's introduction as a "data dog" or otherwise hyperintelligent canine goes nowhere and he spends the rest of the program just being the crew's pet. Faye exhibits many of the worst characteristics that can be written about a female personality; she's bossy, greedy, obsessed with her own beauty, needs to either be rescued or is a hinderance to the group more often than an asset, she often wears revealing clothing for the sole purpose of fanservice. Ed is hit or miss, and walks the line between endearing and annoying, but hardly receives much development beyond her introductory episode. The main villain Vicious is especially bad. He has very little depth and motivation aside from a desire for more power, and even though the production goes a bit into his backstory it never establishes proper reasoning. At the end of the narrative, Vicious is little more than an evil guy in a black coat with enough fighting skill that it makes Spike struggle to land a bullet in him, aside from the obvious fact that Vicious becomes a representation of the syndicate Spike ran away from. Various factors explain why software might fail. Below are several typical causes:

Mathematical impossibility: Perhaps you recall from early elementary education that dividing any quantity by nothing produces an undefined outcome. When software instructs computing machinery to perform this invalid operation, the system signals an error. Should the application lack proper handling for such circumstances, termination occurs.

Memory boundary violation: Applications receive permission to utilize specific regions of storage. Additional areas remain forbidden. Should software attempt accessing prohibited storage zones, the computing system flags this transgression. Without appropriate error management, termination follows.

Resource stalemate: Imagine you and your companion Billy playing with toys. You possess the crimson cube while Billy holds the azure piece. Wanting to exchange items, you inform Billy you'll surrender the scarlet object once he relinquishes the navy piece. Billy responds he'll transfer the sapphire block once you deliver the vermillion one. Both children remain frozen indefinitely, awaiting the other's surrender, accomplishing nothing. This represents a stalemate scenario; when occurring within software, the application freezes completely, requiring forced termination and restart.

Uncaptured anomaly: Occasionally applications incorporate specialized validation mechanisms. Upon detecting problems, one section raises an anomaly signal while another section should intercept and address it. When such signals go unintercepted by any component, typically a warning window appears indicating improper issue resolution, followed by application shutdown.

These scenarios result from "defects" within the codebase. "Defects" simply represent incorrectly written segments or portions failing to anticipate every potential circumstance. Certain applications contain more "flaws" than others. What explains this variation? Perhaps developers faced tighter deadlines or conducted insufficient testing, or perhaps the complexity makes addressing every conceivable situation extremely challenging.

Consider software as "methodology for accomplishing tasks" - a familiar illustration involves preparing a peanut spread and fruit preserve sandwich. Your initial methodology might state:

obtain bread loaves
obtain legume paste
obtain fruit preserves
obtain cutting utensil
spread legume mixture on first slice
spread berry conserve on second piece
combine slices together
PRESENT MEAL

Should legume spread supplies become exhausted midway, you're stranded partway through directions without continuation options - that's failure.

A more elaborate methodology would outline pizzeria operations - greater ingredient variety, additional combination possibilities, numerous employees arriving and departing simultaneously, substantially increased error opportunities. Certain problems permit correction; others resist resolution - issues resisting correction (or where personnel prove insufficiently motivated toward remediation) constitute failures.

The fundamental principle remains consistent: whether simple sandwich assembly or complex restaurant coordination, insufficient preparation for unexpected conditions causes breakdown. Well-designed methodologies incorporate contingency plans: alternative ingredient substitutions, backup staff availability, emergency procedures. Poorly designed approaches assume perfect conditions, guaranteeing eventual malfunction when reality deviates from expectations. Robust systems anticipate complications; fragile ones ignore possibilities until disaster strikes. Understanding these distinctions helps explain why some tools prove reliable while others disappoint repeatedly.
