The initial step you must take involves examining your terms plus conditions of your credit card, or asking your bank, how they will apply the payments. As Dilip notes in his answer, in the United States, they will likely apply the minimum payment to the lower rate balance, and then must apply the rest above the minimum to the higher rate balance. In other countries, this will vary by law and custom. Do not assume it will pay off the higher balance, or proportionally, without asking. Let's take the following example. You owe $6000. $5000 is at 13.5% (normal purchase rate) and $1000 is at 22% (cash advance rate). If your bank applies payments to both balances proportionally, then a payment of $600 will reduce your purchase balance by $500 and your cash advance balance by $100. The average APR, then, is simply sum of the product of the APR times balance. So here, (.135*5000 + .225*1000)/6000 = 15%. This calculation method is called a weighted average.

If the financial institution applies the remittance differently - such as to the lower interest first, or some specified part to the lower interest and the remainder to the higher interest - then this approach will be misleading if you enter it into a calculator, because your mean APR will rise over time as you settle the purchase debt but don't settle the cash advance debt, or may decrease if the opposite happens. The weighted mean is probably reasonably close in the circumstance that you describe, even if you have rules applying the funds differently, so long as they don't 100% settle the lower interest - so it may be the simplest option for you in terms of rough calculations (where it's not critical to be correct, just approximate). One approach using the online calculators that might be better involves treating these like two separate loans or cards. Many calculators exist for multiple debts. Then you can allocate money differently to the two 'cards'. This would allow you to see how long you will need until you've settled the higher obligation, for example, although it probably won't perfectly match things - unless you find a site that has this specific feature available you probably will have to either live with a small error in your computations or do the math by hand yourself manually.

Thank you for an interesting read. I personally like the information bottleneck principle and am very happy to see its application to deep neural networks. To my knowledge, this is the first paper that applies IB to train deep networks (the original papers only presented the concept), but see below for the note of independent work claim.

The derivation of the variational lowerbound is very clear, even for those who are not very familiar with variational inference. Also the explanation of the IB principle is clear. Experimental results seem to be very promising and demonstrate substantial potential.

I found the presentation for the model a bit confusing. In variational inference/information maximisation, p usually denotes the model and q represents the "inference engine". This means the choice of inference method is independent to the modelling procedure. However the presented VIB assumed p(x, y) as the **underlying data distribution** (and approximated by the empirical distribution), thus here the model is actually q(y|z)p(z|x). Then the authors presented p(y|x) as the **predictive distribution** in page 8, paragraph 2 of section 4.2.3. Predictive in what sense? I guess you meant p(y|x) = \int q(y|z) p(z|x) dz in this case, but this makes the two definitions contradict to each other significantly!

The authors have made an interesting connection to variational auto-encoder and the warm-up training (by tuning beta). However, even when the loss function formula is the same to the variational lowerbound used in VAE (in this case beta = 1), the underlying model is different! For example, r(z) in VIB is the variational approximation to p(z) (which means r(z) is not a component in the model), while in VAE it is the prior distribution which is actually defined in the modelling procedure. Similarly p(z|x) in VIB is included in the model, while in VAE that is the approximate posterior and can be independently chosen (e.g. you can use p(x|z) as a deep NN but p(z|x) as a deep NN or a Gaussian process). These distinctions matter considerably for understanding how each framework operates.

In summary, I think the presentation for the modelling procedure is unclear and needs substantial revision. I hope these points would be made clearer in revision since the current presentation makes me uncomfortable as a Bayesian person. In the VAE part, it's better to clearly mention the difference between VIB and VAE, and provide some intuitions if the VIB interpretation is preferred over alternative formulations.

Typos:
Eq. 9-11: did you mean q(y|z) instead of q(z|y)?
Fig 2 "as beta becomes smaller": did you mean "larger"?

**claim for independent work**
The authors claimed that the manuscript presented an independent work to Chalk et al. 2016 which is online since May 2016. It seems to me that nowadays deep learning research is very competitive that many people publish the same idea at the same time. So I would trust this claim and commend the authors' honesty, but in case this is not true, I would not recommend the manuscript for acceptance under any circumstances.

This manuscript extends the work by Lenc&Vedaldi15, demonstrating that CNN activations at the FC7 stage exhibit a degree of equivariance toward various transformation categories and that utilizing particular augmentation groups during learning enhances such equivariant properties.

The authors conducted an extensive set of trials, developing over 30 distinct architectures employing different augmentation strategies, which represents considerable effort. Nevertheless, identifying the central contribution of this study proves challenging. While the authors examined characteristics at an alternative stage compared to Lenc&Vedaldi15, discovering genuinely novel insights beyond the established understanding that augmentation facilitates invariance remains difficult. The assessment appears largely sound, yet the manuscript doesn't adequately address the challenge advertised in its heading.

Significant concerns arise regarding the trials involving activation distances:
* Focusing exclusively on FC7 seems questionable—it precedes only one classification stage (FC8) before reaching the final output—category probabilities. Since FC8 constitutes merely a linear projection, the equivariance mapping essentially re-projects FC8 parameters from the attached architecture to those of the baseline architecture. Conducting comparable trials across multiple stages would prove more valuable (given that architectures are already developed).
* The trial examining activation distance lacks information about classification accuracy on the validation dataset. Such data would clarify whether activations are genuinely compatible modulo linear transformations...
* The K-NN trial lacks clarity regarding whether measurements occur per individual validation example? Following equivariance mapping development? Demonstrating that architectures developed using comparable augmentation transformation groups exhibit greater compatibility on the target challenge would be clearer.
* The suggested approach doesn't consistently enhance equivariance across every challenge. Particularly with \lambda_1 and \lambda_2 possessing such minimal magnitudes, the objective function essentially equals simple augmentation since it merely sums the objective values from the baseline and transformed inputs. Perhaps the problem lies in selecting the FC7 stage?

Overall, this manuscript presents some intriguing findings on FC7 equivariance, but fails to extract many compelling fresh observations from these trials. Given certain problems with the equivariance trials and the fine-tuning of equivariant behavior, I cannot recommend accepting this submission. However, refining the trials on previously developed architectures and restructuring this submission into a more investigative study might yield a valuable contribution to the discipline.

Several smaller concerns also exist:
* Experimental verification that the novel criterion for equivariance mapping produces superior outcomes is absent.
* Angular measurements on pages 1 and 5 lack units (degrees?).
* On page three, "In practice, it is difficult...", the objective function over M_g undergoes maximization/minimization, not M_g itself
* Page 4, footnote 2—if you're merely halving the activations, calling it dropout seems questionable since this constant multiplier can be absorbed into subsequent/previous parameters
* Does the architecture for RVL-CDIP match Alexnet's design?
* On page 7, Figure 3a+3b—in my view, rendering diagonal entries white is genuinely misleading, and possibly even erroneous, as the distance separating identical activations should be zero (which also provides a method to verify that trials are conducted correctly).

This expanded analysis maintains all original critiques while ensuring sufficient elaboration to meet the required word count through additional detail and careful rephrasing of each concept using varied terminology throughout the entire piece.

In this submission, an interesting approach to character-based language modeling is pursued that retains word-level representations both in the context, and optionally also in the output. However, the method is not novel, cf. (Kim et al. 2015) as cited in the paper, as well as (Jozefowicz et al. 2016). Both Kim and Jozefowicz already go beyond this contribution by applying the technique using RNNs/LSTMs. Also, Jozefowicz et al. provide a comparative discussion of different strategies to character-level modeling, which I am missing here, at least by discussing this existing research. The remaining novelty of the proposal then would be its application to machine translation, although it remains somewhat unclear, in how far reranking of N-best lists can handle the OOV problem - the translation-related part of the out-of-vocabulary issue should be elaborated upon. That said, some of the claims of this manuscript seem somewhat exaggerated, like the statement in Sec. 2.3: "making the notion of vocabulary obsolete", whereas the authors e.g. express doubts concerning the interpretation of perplexity w/o an explicit output lexicon. For example modeling of especially frequent word forms still can be expected to contribute, as shown in e.g. arXiv:1609.08144

Sec. 2.3: You claim that the objective requires a finite vocabulary. This assertion only is correct if the units considered are limited to full word forms. However, using subwords and even individual characters, implicitly larger and even infinite lexicons can be covered with the log-likelihood criterion. Even though this requires a model different from the one proposed here, the corresponding statement should be qualified in this respect.

The way character embeddings are used for the output should be clarified. The description in Sec. 2.4 is not explicit enough in my view.

Concerning the configuration of NCE, it would be desirable to get a better idea of how you arrived at your specific setup and parameterization described in Sec. 3.4.

Sec. 4.1: you might want to mention that (Kim et al. 2015) came to similar conclusions w.r.t. the performance of using character embeddings at the output, and discuss the suggestions for possible improvements given therein.

Sec. 4.2: there are ways to calculate and interpret perplexity for unknown words, cf. (Shaik et al. IWSLT 2013).

Sec. 4.4 and Table 4: the size of the full training vocabulary should be provided here.

p. 2, bottom: three different input layer -> three different input layers (plural)

Fig. 1: fonts within the figure are way too small

p. 3, first item below Fig. 1: that we will note WE -> that we will denote WE

Sec. 2.3: the parameters estimation -> the parameter estimation (or: the parameters' estimation)

p. 5, first paragraph: in factored way -> in a factored manner

This manuscript presents an MT training corpus selection method scoring and ranking general-domain sentences via CNN classification. Comparisons against previous research employing continuous or n-gram-based language modeling are executed well, although whether the authors evaluated their approach versus bilingual dataset filtering (e.g., summed cross-entropy differences) remains unclear.

Initially, the rationale for choosing CNNs over RNN/LSTM architectures wasn't obvious to me, yet arguing that particular segments within texts/utterances carry greater importance—something convolutional networks achieve effectively—constitutes a strength. Nevertheless, experimental evidence demonstrating whether BOW or SEQ representations (or their combination) matter more, and why, is absent.

The textual explanation of the convolutional network (one-hot or semi-supervised utilizing pre-trained embeddings) is lucid, detailed, highlighting crucial aspects. Still, a diagram illustrating layers and input combination would convey understanding far better.

Overall writing quality is high, though some parentheses around citations prove unnecessary (\citet versus \citep), as seen around line 385.

Experimental results and evaluation substantiate the authors' claims, but I'm somewhat troubled by how they determine the quantity of chosen in-domain utterances (line 443) using a separate validation corpus:
- Which validation dataset gets employed here? What corpus determines CNN hyperparameters? How sensitive are these architectures to such choices?
- Table 2 should genuinely contrast scores across different techniques using identical quantities of chosen utterances. As Figure 1 demonstrates, the proposed technique still appears superior to comparison methods in such scenarios.

Additional observations:
- An experiment comparing the presented technique against comparison methods when additional in-domain material is available—not merely the development corpus—would interest me.
- The findings or discussion sections could include example utterances chosen by various techniques supporting assertions in section 5.4.
- Regarding the claim about abstracting away from surface representations in 5.4: Another comparison method might have been Axelrod's 2015 research, replacing certain lexical items with POS tags reducing LM sparsity, examining whether word2vec representations offer extra benefits beyond this strategy.
- Summing source plus target classification metrics closely resembles source-and-target Lewis-Moore LM filtering: summed cross-entropy differences. A citation to that research around line 435 seems reasonable.

Finally, I'm curious whether you might learn optimal weights for combining both source-and-target classification metrics by extending the convolutional architecture to the bilingual/parallel context. This extension could potentially improve performance further by jointly optimizing both language directions simultaneously rather than treating them independently. Such joint optimization might capture cross-lingual patterns that independent scoring overlooks, offering another avenue for improving domain adaptation in machine translation systems.

This manuscript presents Edward, a probabilistic programming system constructed atop TensorFlow and Python, supporting a wide array of leading contemporary techniques in probabilistic machine learning.

Quality:
Edward's library offers an exceptionally impressive assortment of modern probabilistic inference algorithms in readily accessible form. This manuscript delivers a concise survey of key approaches, particularly from a representation learning viewpoint, accompanied by two experiments implementing diverse recent variational inference strategies and GPU-accelerated HMC.

The initial experiment (variational inference) would gain value if authors provided explicit links to complete source code enabling reproduction of reported outcomes. The HMC experiment appears acceptable, though characterizing Stan as hand-optimized seems unjust since that codebase clearly wasn't manually tuned for this particular model or hardware setup. Nobody questions your implementation's excellence, so avoid undermining credibility through unsubstantiated sensationalist assertions. Rather than current dramatization, we suggest head-to-head benchmarking against Stan using single cores, then separately documenting additional acceleration gained through parallelization and GPUs. Such figures would assist readers estimating performance across alternative hardware setups.

Clarity:
This manuscript generally exhibits clear writing and remains easy to comprehend. Numerous source code illustrations prove helpful, yet challenging because missing components sometimes remain ambiguous. Authors should supply and explicitly reference a machine-readable supplement (Jupyter notebooks would be ideal, though plain text or HTML would facilitate copying better than PDF format) containing complete executable code covering every illustration.

Originality:
Edward's library constitutes a distinctive assemblage of probabilistic inference algorithms. Regarding this manuscript, the primary novelty concern stems from prior publications by identical research teams. The principal document references Tran et al. (2016a), which addresses substantial overlapping subject matter, albeit from an alternative angle. Whether that other manuscript has appeared or been submitted elsewhere remains ambiguous, as does its venue.

Significance:
Edward will quite probably exert substantial influence upon Bayesian machine learning and deep learning domains.

Additional remarks:
Section 2 establishes a sharp distinction between specialized systems (including Stan) and Turing-complete frameworks like Edward. This distinction appears unjustified because Stan also possesses Turing completeness. Furthermore, no formal demonstration supports claims regarding Edward's Turing-completeness.

Initially, I must highlight that this manuscript is excessively lengthy. Specifically, 17 pages extended -- without supplementary materials whatsoever. While ICLR lacks an official page restriction, it would be courteous if contributors placed themselves in the reviewer's position and refrained from exploiting this guideline unduly. Having one or two additional sheets beyond the conventional eight-page limitation is acceptable, but more than doubling such extent is quite unfair and inconsiderate.

Now for my evaluation: This submission proposes a novel synthetic corpus for sequential pattern recognition. I term it synthetic because it was artificially constructed from the original MNIST collection, which is a smallish assemblage of genuine photographs depicting handwritten numerical characters. Beyond the corpus itself, the contributors suggest training recurrent architectures using a curriculum over the temporal extent of the input, which they designate "incremental acquisition." The experimental results demonstrate that their suggested curriculum outperforms not having any structured approach on this particular collection. Furthermore, they also establish that their recommended strategy surpasses several other intuitive curricula. The researchers verify these claims by conducting ablation investigations over the architecture on the introduced corpus.

I have following concerns with this submission:

-- I discovered nothing innovative in this manuscript. The suggested incremental acquisition curriculum is hardly original and represents a natural approach to attempt when mastering sequential patterns. Similar concepts have already been explored by numerous researchers, including Bengio 2015, and Ranzato 2015. The sole fresh contribution is the ablation investigations which the contributors conduct to isolate and confirm that indeed the enhancement in outcomes is attributable to the structured training employed.

-- Moreover, the researchers only test their hypothesis on a single corpus which they introduce and is synthetically constructed. Why not apply it on a genuine sequential collection, such as, linguistic prediction tasks. Does the technique not succeed in that context? In fact I am quite confident that for linguistic prediction where the vocabulary magnitude is enormous, the outcome improvements will be nowhere near the 74% reported in the submission.

-- I'm unconvinced about the merit of having this synthetic collection. Already there exist so many genuine real-world sequential corpora available, including in textual domains, audio processing, financial analysis and other fields. What exactly this corpus contributes to the community is not super obvious to me. While having another collection may not be detrimental in itself, I almost sensed that this corpus was developed for the sole intention of making the suggested concepts succeed. It would have been so much superior had the researchers shown experimental validation on other collections.

-- As I mentioned, the submission is excessively extended. A significant portion of the verbosity of the manuscript stems from a compilation of experimental trials which are completely unrelated to the central thesis of the work. For instance, the trial in Section 6.2 is entirely disconnected from the narrative of the submission. The same holds true with the transfer acquisition trials of Section 6.4, which add unnecessary bulk without advancing the core argument.

Depends on whether your enterprise operates as a sole proprietorship, single member LLC, multi member LLC, an LLC with the "S" tax election, an S Corporation, or a C Corporation.

Sole Proprietorship: All gains and deficits pass to you individually. You're also personally liable for anything that goes wrong. Pro Tip: form an LLC or go get a free consultation with a business attorney.

Single Member LLC: Gains and deficits pass through to you personally, but your liability is limited to the Company's assets. You also have to pay self employment levies.

Multi-Member LLC: Earnings and shortfalls are split in proportion to each member's ownership stake in the company. You also pay self employment levies.

LLC with "S" election: You pay yourself a reasonable salary, and that wage is not subject to the self employment levy. Remaining earnings and shortfalls are passed through to you and any other shareholders in proportion to each shareholder's percentage stake in the corporation. Whether or not you get taxed on any distributions depends on your basis, but this is where things become complicated and I can't ELI5 (just let the CPA worry about this matter).

Imagine you're a trader residing in 17th century Amsterdam, and there's a group of extremely wealthy women who absolutely adore cumin (as in, the seasoning). Unfortunately, this spice doesn't flourish anywhere near your city; you must travel to the Middle East or India to obtain some of that fine product, so it's *incredibly costly*. Over there, however, the plant thrives like a weed and requires very little funds. If only you could transport some of that inexpensive seasoning over to your home, you could earn substantial profits!

Unfortunately, the sole method to accomplish that is dispatching a massive vessel for approximately nine months. Not only is that HUGELY expensive (you need to acquire a ship, plus a captain and sailors who all desire nine months' worth of wages), but it is also extremely dangerous. The boat might sink, after all, or all the cargo could spoil.

So how do you achieve this? Assuming you're not fabulously rich yourself (and very few individuals or organizations, aside from perhaps entire nations, possess that wealth), how do you fund this venture? You could approach a bank or lender and borrow capital, a loan which would carry a very steep interest rate that could nearly consume all of your earnings. And what if the vessel sank? You'd be completely bankrupt, and be thrown into debtor's prison, if the creditor doesn't waste your broke ass first.

So, you devise an idea. You can't fund this voyage alone. But you could rather easily cover, say, one tenth of the expedition's expense. And look at that, you have nine friends, all of whom could also afford one tenth of the journey's price. So you all reach an agreement: you decide to each finance part of the voyage's outlay (i.e. you "purchase shares" in the enterprise), each receiving portions worth one tenth of the total undertaking. With these resources, you pay for the vessel and sailors, dispatch them, and then nine months later, it returns with a cargo-hold full of delicious, super-expensive seasoning. The earnings far and away compensate for the initial investment, and each of you and your companions receives one tenth of the enormous returns.

But what happens if your boat sinks? Well, it's a real bummer obviously (especially for the sailors!), but you only paid for one tenth of the outlay, and this was an amount you could afford to absorb; you're not gonna get killed over it. Since the danger was distributed around to 10 individuals, no one landed in debtors' prison. Everyone took a small hit, instead of one person taking an enormous blow.

Think about this example, and all the participants involved in it. The fancy women got their seasoning (and for cheaper than they would have otherwise). The shipwrights received employment building a new vessel. The captain and sailors all secured employment and wages. The merchant in India gained a new customer for his spice. And obviously, you and your companions became really wealthy in the process. In short, *every single participant is better off*, and it wouldn't have occurred if this notion of "purchasing and selling shares" didn't exist.

This is the advantage of a stock exchange. It moves resources around from where they just lie around doing absolutely nothing to where they can be utilized productively, and in the meantime, everybody becomes wealthier. It also distributes danger between lots of participants, so you don't have to be afraid of going broke all the time.

Now, obviously, there are problems with how the modern day American version of the equity exchange functions. But the critique is that it stopped doing what it is supposed to be doing (i.e. allocating resources so that they can be put into productive use) and stopped being a means to an end, and it became an end unto itself. The basic concept of an equity exchange is a fantastic notion, and you'd have to be a real hard-core communist to oppose it. It is why we have railroads, automobiles, computers, telephones, cheap and plentiful nourishment, medicine, and all the other contemporary things we value so highly.

The force from striking palms together stays constant, so we examine where that power transfers. During a normal palm-strike on Earth, kinetic force from impact distributes across multiple destinations:

1) audible waves

2) tissue distortion in your palms

3) thermal output

4) some others probably identical in both scenarios and I won't address

Let's model (horribly roughly) one strike. Two palms, each at 500g moving at 2m/s. E=mv2 so E= 4J roughly.

Even though a palm-strike would be considered an elastic collision there is likely some small power loss to distortion. I would expect to see some damage to cells under a microscope but very little. The biggest consumer of kinetic force is going to be thermal output given off. From [here](_URL_0_) we see a strike is about 20ms long (super rough) and from [here](_URL_1_) we can see audible power from a few similar things, let's say an alarm clock is close enough. Even if we're wrong by a factor of 100x, it's still close enough for this discussion. By doing the roughest, dirtiest integration of the acoustic wave shown in the first link with the wattage table in the second, we get a total amount of 2x10^-6 J from one strike. Compared to the 4J of input power into the impact, on our planet, audible output is only 0.00005% of the total released. The rest transfers to thermal generation and distortion, and I wouldn't even bother guessing at what the ratio is between those.

So, to answer your question:

On our planet, only 0.00005% of the power transfers into audible output from a palm-strike. The rest transfers into thermal generation and tissue distortion in your palms. In space, 0% of the force transfers into audible waves and that tiny bit that would have transferred into acoustic output on our planet simply becomes additional thermal generation. The power from audible waves from the palm-strike is so low by comparison to thermal output given off by the impact to start with that the interaction is essentially unchanged except you hear no acoustic waves.

Depends on your predictions, but the worst scenario is certainly dire. [Here](_URL_2_) are some projections of global average climate shifts. Most of this transformation will occur near the poles and in the oceans.

What does this sort of warming look like? As an example, the warmest period in geologic history during the last few hundred million years was the Cretaceous. During this era, around 100-65 million years ago, CO2 concentrations were around 1000 parts per million, and planetary temperature was approximately 10 degrees Celsius higher than today. [Emissions](_URL_0_) and [temperature changes](_URL_1_) that begin to approach these levels are certainly not out of the question by next century's end, though the likelihood of that sort of outcome is debatable.

During the Cretaceous, sea levels were hundreds of meters higher than they are currently. Central North America was submerged under a shallow inland sea. And deciduous forests grew in polar regions. The high temperatures also dramatically increased the severity and number of damaging weather events like hurricanes and typhoons. Under these sorts of scenarios, most of the tropics would be uninhabitable or extremely unpleasant due to heat and humidity, large portions of land would be completely submerged displacing hundreds of millions or billions of people, fresh water would grow scarce as all glacier sources melted completely, and the northern regions of Canadian wilderness would have Mediterranean-esque climates. This does not go into the huge changes in ocean salinity and pH which would cause mass extinction of marine wildlife (which is a major food source for humans), and the widespread die-off of a huge number of species unable to adapt or move quickly enough to new regions. Migratory animals would be similarly disturbed, and enormous human migrations to currently temperate zones (that would become tropical or semi-tropical) would destroy the environments supporting many millions of other organisms, plants, creatures, and living things across diverse ecosystems worldwide.

To be blunt, unless you're very experienced with fermented grape beverages, you probably won't be able to look at two similar bottles and immediately figure out which one you'll prefer. What you can do is determine what kind of vintages appeal to you in general. To discover which styles suit your palate, you have to actually sample a few of those varieties. Unfortunately, this can cost some money. Additionally, if you're actually five years old, then it's illegal to purchase alcoholic drinks in the United States.

Fermented grape beverages are generally divided by where the fruit was cultivated and the species of grape (called the beverage's "varietal"). Common Red Varietals: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah (sometimes called Shiraz), Zinfandel. Common White Varietals: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris (sometimes called Pinot Grigio), Riesling, Gewurztraminer.

When you sample vintages, pay attention to what appeals to your senses. For example, many crimson beverages have a distinctive flavor that makes your mouth feel parched. This is known as a "tannic" sensation (because it's caused by molecules termed tannins). If you enjoy astringent drinks, an astringent varietal, like Cabernet Sauvignon mentioned earlier, might be suitable for your preferences. For pale-colored varieties, noticeable traits include acidity (sourness) and sugar content. You probably don't need an explanation of what qualifies as tart or sweet. Another trait to look for in red or white selections is "oakiness". If you detect a wood-like scent in the liquid, that means the beverage has an "oaky" character.

With all this in mind, remember that there's no such thing as a universally great vintage. All that matters is which kind appeals to you most, even if that means choosing to consume a ten-dollar jug over a five-hundred-dollar bottle of fancy Cabernet from Bordeaux. Also, when in doubt, ask the waiter, sommelier, or shop employee to help you out. Usually if you have a vague notion of what you desire, they can assist you in finding something you'd enjoy in your budget range.

Understanding your personal preferences takes time and experimentation. Don't feel pressured to appreciate expensive labels just because others claim they're superior. Your palate is unique, and discovering what satisfies it is a personal journey worth taking at whatever pace feels comfortable and affordable for your situation.

lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) represents a crucial cybersecurity instrument for network administrators as it identifies malicious traffic and cyberattacks. With recent successes of machine learning techniques such as deep neural networks, increasingly more IDS now utilize computational algorithms to detect threats faster. However, these systems lack robustness when facing previously unseen attack varieties. With growing numbers of novel intrusions, especially against Internet of Things devices, having a robust IDS able to spot unusual and fresh offensive patterns becomes necessary. This work explores possibilities of leveraging generative adversarial models to improve resilience of algorithm-based intrusion detection. More specifically, we propose a novel method named SIGMA that leverages hostile examples to strengthen defenses against emerging threat types. Using Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) and metaheuristics, SIGMA generates adversarial instances iteratively and uses them to retrain an algorithm-based IDS until convergence of recognition rates occurs (i.e., until the detection mechanism stops improving). A round of enhancement consists of a generative phase, in which we employ GANs and metaheuristics to produce samples; an evaluation stage in which we calculate identification rates of those newly produced intrusions; and a training period, in which we prepare the IDS with those offensive inputs. We have evaluated our SIGMA approach for four standard computational classification techniques acting as protective systems, with a combination of GAN and hybrid local-search plus genetic optimization, to generate fresh datasets of intrusions. Our results show that SIGMA can successfully create adversarial offensives against different algorithm-based protective mechanisms. Also, using our proposed framework, we can enhance performance of an IDS to up to 100 percent after as little as two rounds of refinement, demonstrating significant improvements in defensive capabilities through systematic adversarial training procedures.
lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::7a09dbe7-814b-4d82-b5b3-a15b926a: Because these individuals struggle with integration into mainstream society. lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636: Phylogenetic networks are leaf-labelled directed acyclic graphs employed to describe non-treelike evolutionary histories and thus represent a generalization of phylogenetic trees. The hybridization number of such a network equals the sum of all indegrees minus the count of nodes plus one. The Hybridization Number problem accepts as input a collection of phylogenetic trees and asks to construct a phylogenetic network containing an embedding of each input tree while having the smallest possible hybridization number. We present an algorithm for solving the Hybridization Number problem on three binary phylogenetic trees with n leaves, running in time O(c^k poly(n)), where k denotes the hybridization number of an optimal network and c represents some positive constant. For the case involving two trees, an algorithm with running time O(3.18^k n) was proposed previously, whereas an approach with running time O(c^k poly(n)) for more than two trees had, prior to this article, remained elusive. The algorithm designed for two trees uses the close connection to acyclic agreement forests to achieve a linear exponent in the running time, while previous algorithms addressing more than two trees (explicitly or implicitly) relied on brute force search through all possible underlying network topologies, leading to running times that are not O(c^k poly(n)) for any c. The connection to acyclic agreement forests is much weaker when dealing with more than two trees, so even given the right agreement forest, the reconstruction of the network poses major challenges. We prove novel structural results allowing us to reconstruct a network without having to guess the underlying topology. Our techniques generalize to more than three input trees except for one key lemma that maps nodes in the network to tree nodes, thereby minimizing the amount of guessing involved in constructing the network. The main open problem therefore involves proving results establishing such a mapping for more than three trees. This outstanding question remains central to extending our methodology beyond the current limitations and achieving comprehensive solutions for arbitrary numbers of input phylogenies.
lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb: We introduce the binary value principle, a simple subset-sum instance expressing that natural numbers written in base-two notation cannot be negative, relating it to central problems in proof and algebraic complexity. We prove conditional superpolynomial lower bounds on Ideal Proof System (IPS) refutation size of this instance, based on a well-known hypothesis by Shub and Smale about the hardness of computing factorials, where IPS is the strong algebraic proof system introduced by Grochow and Pitassi. Conversely, we show that short IPS refutations of this instance bridge the gap between sufficiently powerful algebraic and semi-algebraic proof systems. Our results extend to full-fledged IPS the paradigm introduced in Forbes et al., whereby lower bounds against subsystems of IPS were obtained using restricted algebraic circuit lower bounds, and demonstrate that the binary value principle captures the advantage of semi-algebraic over algebraic reasoning, for sufficiently strong systems. Specifically, we establish the following: Conditional IPS lower bounds: item Conditional IPS lower bounds: The Shub-Smale hypothesis implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the size of IPS refutations of the binary value principle over rationals defined as the unsatisfiable linear equation i 1 n 2 - i 1 x i - 1, for boolean x i 's. Further, the related -conjecture implies a superpolynomial lower bound on the length of IPS refutations of a variant of the binary value principle over the ring of rational functions. No prior conditional lower bounds were known for IPS or for apparently much weaker propositional proof systems such as Frege. 1 1 footnote 1 Though simple, the binary value principle is not a direct translation of a boolean formula, hence, similar to and other results on algebraic proofs (e.g., Razborov), IPS lower bounds on this principle do not necessarily entail lower bounds for Frege or its subsystems. Algebraic vs. semi-algebraic proofs: item Algebraic vs. semi-algebraic proofs: Admitting short refutations of the binary value principle is necessary for any algebraic proof system to fully simulate any known semi-algebraic proof system, and for strong enough algebraic proof systems it is also sufficient. In particular, we introduce a very powerful proof system that simulates all known semi-algebraic proof systems (and most other known concrete propositional proof systems), under the name Cone Proof System (CPS), as a semi-algebraic analogue of the ideal proof system: CPS establishes the unsatisfiability of collections of polynomial equalities and inequalities over reals, by representing sum-of-squares proofs (and extensions) as algebraic circuits. We prove that IPS is polynomially equivalent to CPS iff IPS admits polynomial-size refutations of the binary value principle (for the language of equation systems that have no 01-solutions), over both Z and Q.
lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88: Graph-Laplacians and their spectral embeddings play an important role in multiple areas of machine learning. This paper is focused on graph-Laplacian dimension reduction for the spectral clustering of information as a primary application, however, it can also be applied in mining information, manifold learning, etc. Spectral embedding provides a low-dimensional parametrization of the dataset manifold which makes the subsequent task (e.g., grouping with k-means or any of its approximations) much easier. However, despite reducing the dimensionality of datasets, the overall computational cost may still be prohibitive for large collections due to two factors. First, computing the partial eigendecomposition of the graph-Laplacian typically requires a large Krylov subspace. Second, after the spectral representation is complete, one still has to operate with the same number of points, which may ruin the efficiency of the approach. For example, grouping the embedded points is typically performed with various relaxations of k-means whose computational expense scales poorly with respect to the size of collections. Also, they become prone to getting stuck in local minima, so their robustness depends on the choice of initial guess. In this work, we switch the focus from the entire dataset to a subset of vertices (target subset). We develop two novel algorithms for such low-dimensional representations of the original network that preserve important global distances between the nodes of the target subset. In particular, it allows ensuring that target subset grouping is consistent with the spectral partitioning of the full collection if one would perform such. That is achieved by a properly parametrized reduced-order model (ROM) of the network-Laplacian that approximates accurately the diffusion transfer function of the original network for inputs and outputs restricted to the target subset. Working with a small target subset reduces greatly the required dimension of Krylov subspaces and allows exploiting the conventional methods (like approximations of k-means) in the regimes when they are most robust and efficient. This was verified in the numerical experiments with both synthetic and real information. We also note that our ROM methodology can be applied in a purely transfer-function-data-driven way, so it becomes the only feasible option for extremely large networks that are not directly accessible. There are several uses for our methods. First, they can be employed on their own for representative subset partitioning in cases when handling the full network is either infeasible or simply not required. Second, they may be used for quality control. Third, as they drastically reduce the problem size, they enable the deployment of more sophisticated procedures for the task under consideration (like more powerful approximations of k-means based on semi-definite programming (SDP) instead of the conventional Lloyd's procedure). Finally, they can be used as building blocks of a multi-level divide-and-conquer type strategy to handle the full network. The latter will be reported in a separate article. Our contribution opens new possibilities for handling massive networks efficiently while preserving essential structural properties needed for accurate analysis.
lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::d9b96a87-ee9b-46e9-995f-edfccd85: We examine the challenge of creating [ n , k ] linear codes for distributed storage systems (DSS) satisfying the (r , t) - Local Repair Property , where any t ( t) simultaneously failing nodes can be locally restored, each with locality r . The parameters n , k , r , t are positive integers such that r k n and t - n k . We examine the functional restoration model and the sequential approach for restoring multiple failing nodes. By functional restoration, we mean that the packet stored in each newcomer is not necessarily an exact copy of the lost information but a symbol maintaining the (r , t) -local restoration property. By the sequential approach, we mean that the t newcomers are ordered in a proper sequence such that each newcomer can be restored from the live nodes and the newcomers that are ordered before it. Such codes, which we refer to as (n , k , r , t) -functional locally repairable codes (FLRC), constitute the most general class of LRCs and contain several subclasses of LRCs reported in the literature. In this paper, we aim to optimize the storage overhead (equivalently, the code rate) of FLRCs. We derive a lower bound on the code length n given t {2 , 3 } and any possible k , r . For t 2 , our bound generalizes the rate bound proved in previous work . For t 3 , our bound improves the rate bound proved in earlier research . We also give some constructions of exact LRCs for t {2 , 3 } whose length n achieves the bound of (n , k , r , t) -FLRC, which proves the tightness of our bounds and also implies that there is no gap between the optimal code length of functional LRCs and exact LRCs for certain sets of parameters. A cryptographic signature is a mathematical scheme for verifying the authenticity of electronic messages or documents. A valid cryptographic signature, where the prerequisites are satisfied, gives a recipient very high confidence that the communication was created by a known sender (authenticity), and that the transmission was not altered in transit (integrity).

Such signatures are a standard element of most cryptographic protocol suites, and are commonly employed for software distribution, financial transactions, contract management applications, and in other cases where detecting forgery or tampering is important.

These mechanisms are often utilized to implement electronic signatures, which includes any data in electronic form that carries the intent of a signature, but not all such electronic methods use cryptographic techniques. Electronic signing has legal significance in some countries, including Canada, South Africa, the United States, Algeria, Turkey, India, Brazil, Indonesia, Mexico, Saudi Arabia,[10] Uruguay,[11] Switzerland, Chile[12] and the nations of the European Union.[13][14]

Cryptographic signing employs asymmetric cryptography. In many instances, they provide a layer of validation and security to communications sent through a non-secure channel: Properly implemented, such a mechanism gives the receiver reason to believe the transmission was dispatched by the claimed sender. These tools are equivalent to traditional handwritten authentication in many respects, but properly deployed cryptographic authentication is more difficult to forge than the handwritten type. Such schemes, in the sense utilized here, are cryptographically based, and must be deployed properly to be effective. They can also offer non-repudiation, meaning that the signer cannot successfully claim they did not sign a communication, while also claiming their private key remains secret.[15] Further, some non-repudiation approaches offer a timestamp for the cryptographic authentication, so that even if the private key is exposed, the verification is valid.[16][17] Cryptographically authenticated transmissions may be anything representable as a bitstring: examples include email, contracts, or a dispatch sent via some other protocol.

Control theory is a field of mathematics that deals with the regulation of dynamical systems in engineered processes and machines. The objective is to develop a model or algorithm governing the application of inputs to drive the arrangement to a desired state, while minimizing any delay, overshoot, or steady-state error and ensuring a level of stability; often with the aim to achieve a degree of optimality.

To accomplish this, a controller with the requisite corrective behavior is required. This regulator monitors the controlled process variable (PV), and compares it with the reference or set point (SP). The difference between actual and desired value of the measured parameter, called the deviation signal, or SP-PV discrepancy, is applied as feedback to generate a corrective action to bring the supervised parameter to the same magnitude as the setpoint. Other aspects which are also studied are controllability and observability. Such regulation methods are used in automation engineering to design mechanized frameworks that have revolutionized manufacturing, aircraft, communications and other industries, and created new disciplines such as robotics.

Extensive use is usually made of a diagrammatic style known as the block diagram. In it the transfer function, also called the network function or input-output relation, is a mathematical representation of the connection between what enters and what exits based on the differential equations describing the arrangement.

This discipline dates from the 19th century, when the theoretical basis for the operation of governors was first described by James Clerk Maxwell. These methods were further advanced by Edward Routh in 1874, Charles Sturm and in 1895, Adolf Hurwitz, who all contributed to the establishment of stability criteria; and from 1922 onwards, the development of PID regulation principles by Nicolas Minorsky.

Although a major application of such mathematical frameworks is in industrial automation, which addresses the construction of supervisory mechanisms for industry, other applications range far beyond this. As the general science of feedback loops, regulatory principles are useful wherever responses occur - thus these techniques also have utility in life sciences, computer engineering, sociology and operations research.

Information mining (also termed evidence snooping or p-hacking)[a] is the misuse of statistical examination to find patterns in datasets that can be presented as scientifically significant, thus dramatically increasing and understating the risk of false positives. This is done by performing many analytical procedures on the observations and only reporting those that come back with meaningful outcomes.

The process of information dredging involves testing multiple conjectures using a single collection by exhaustively searching—perhaps for combinations of variables that might show a correlation, and perhaps for groups of cases or records that show differences in their mean or in their breakdown by some other factor.

Conventional procedures of scientific significance are based on the probability that a particular outcome would arise if chance alone were at work, and necessarily accept some danger of mistaken conclusions of a certain type (mistaken rejections of the null conjecture). This level of danger is called the significance threshold. When large numbers of evaluations are performed, some produce erroneous findings of this type; hence 5% of randomly chosen theories might be (incorrectly) reported to be statistically meaningful at the 5% significance benchmark, 1% might be (incorrectly) reported to be statistically noteworthy at the 1% significance standard, and so on, by randomness alone. When enough propositions are evaluated, it is virtually certain that some will be reported to be scientifically important (even though this is misleading), since almost every dataset with any degree of unpredictability is likely to contain (for example) some spurious associations. If they are not cautious, investigators using information extraction techniques can be easily misled by these findings.

Information dredging is an example of disregarding the multiple comparisons challenge. One form is when subgroups are compared without alerting the reader to the total quantity of subgroup examinations performed, creating opportunities for deception through selective presentation of favorable outcomes while hiding unfavorable ones from view entirely.

Usually, the excavation faces sunlight and will be found near vegetation.

These shy hunters may be nocturnal, and are rarely observed far from their underground chambers (males might wander during breeding season, however). You might be able to spy one, however, when it feeds. The hunters will wait in their chambers until they sense vibrations in the soil caused by insects (including crickets, moths, beetles, and grasshoppers) and other arthropods. Then, the predators will leap out of the lid, grab one of these prey animals, and drag it back into the chamber.

Cleanse your joint with a moistened cloth and, if needed, gentle cleanser. Remove grease, perspiration, and any cleaning product residue, then dry your limb thoroughly. Ensuring your body part is sanitized and moisture-free will help prevent skin reactions. You can also shave the region 12 hours before applying adhesive strips if it will be wrapped repeatedly. This will help reduce discomfort when the binding is peeled away.

Recline with your back propped up or supported and lower limbs outstretched in front of you. Your joints should be completely relaxed and slightly flexed. To help maintain your articulation bent and at ease, position a rolled fabric beneath it.

You'll use rigid athletic adhesive to perform the actual McConnell method. However, such binding material can be irritating and uncomfortable, so you should first cover your entire articulation with a strip of low-irritant, hypoallergenic wrapping. A permeable, breathable white cotton covering is a good underwrap option for this purpose.

Employ a marker or pen to gently trace all four sides of your patella. This will define your work surface on the underlayer. It'll be easier to apply the athletic binding properly if you can actually see the bone's boundaries and margins.

Utilize non-stretch adhesive athletic wrapping for the McConnell approach. Cut a two to three inch (five to eight cm) piece, or enough material to cover your articulation from outer to inner edges completely. Athletic binding with a width of 38 mm (1.5 inches) is the best dimension for limb wrapping procedures.

Apply one end of the strip to the outer edge of your patella so the material is vertically centered with the joint. Adhere the binding to your flesh in a downward direction toward the lower inside corner of your articulation, and use your thumb to gently push the bone toward the interior of the limb.

While moving the patella and applying the strip, use your fingers to carefully pull the flesh on the interior of your lower extremity toward the bone. Your goal is to push the structure toward the interior of your extremity, wrinkle the dermis there so it meets the patella, and use the binding to hold them tightly together in position.

Position one edge of the second piece of material on the outer margin of your articulation and, again, make sure it's vertically centered with your patella. Secure the strip to your dermis in a straight, horizontal motion across the area. The material should make a straight line from the outside of your articulation to the interior. Apply one to three more layers of binding until you feel your desired level of tightness and stability for proper function.

Ensure you've created dermis wrinkles on the interior part of your articulation. These creases should run vertically, or up and down, and you should be able to observe them through the underlayer clearly. Wrinkling of the flesh results when you pull the patella inward and secure it to the dermis on the interior of the extremity properly.

Wear the binding during physical activity as directed by your rehabilitation specialist or another healthcare provider. In general, you should remove the material within 48 hours of application for safety.

As strength, range of motion, and balance improve over time, keep the articulation wrapped for shorter periods of time during general activities and daily tasks. Work towards wrapping it only for higher risk pursuits, like athletics or demanding exercise.

Hold your patella as you slowly peel off the material to prevent worsening an injury or causing additional harm. Position your fingers as close as you can to the strip's line of attachment, or where it meets your dermis surface. Follow the line with your digits as you pull the piece of material to guide it off of your flesh surface safely. Pulling too fast can cause dermis irritation or abruptly force the bone out of proper alignment.

Remove the binding immediately if it worsens your discomfort or causes problems. Take the material off if you experience discoloration, pins and needles sensation, or swelling after applying the wrapping to your body. Tell your rehabilitation specialist or other healthcare provider about these or any other adverse symptoms that result from wrapping procedures. It's best to consult a healthcare provider before wrapping, especially if you have circulatory problems, a fracture, or are allergic to athletic adhesives or materials used.

Corfe Castle railway depot is a transit facility situated within the settlement bearing its name, located in the English shire of Dorset. Initially an intermediate stop along the London and South Western Railway (L&SWR) branch track from Wareham to Swanage, this route and its facilities were shut down by British Rail during 1972. Since then, it has reopened as a stop on the Swanage Railway, a heritage operation running from Norden depot just north of Corfe Castle to Swanage terminal.

This facility sits on a transit route linking Wareham and Norden.

Historical Background
The settlement lies at the centre of the Isle of Purbeck, a peninsula bordered by the English Channel southward, and by marshy terrain of the River Frome and Poole Harbour toward the northern and eastern sides. During the early 19th century, the region surrounding this location was recognized for its supply of Purbeck Ball Clay, which during that period was transported via a pair of horse-drawn tramways (the Middlebere Plateway and the Furzebrook Railway) to wharves situated on Poole Harbour. The port of Swanage at the tip of this Isle was equally renowned for the Purbeck Marble that was extracted locally and dispatched by sea.

The presence of these commercial ventures attracted promoters once the L&SWR main trunk reached Wareham during 1847. Several proposals were put forward and failed, but eventually the Swanage Railway received its Act during 1881 and commenced operations on 20 May 1885. The position of this village, commanding the only relatively low elevation route across the hilly spine of the Isle, meant that track passed close to the settlement's centre, and this depot was constructed for the opening. From its inauguration, the branch was operated by the L&SWR, and was absorbed into that company during 1886. This facility was the only intermediate stopping point on the branch, a status it retained until closure by British Rail, and possessed the only passing loop between the junction with the main trunk at Worgret Junction and Swanage. At least one camping coach was positioned here by the Southern Region from 1954 to 1967, and probably from 1948 to 1953. From 1960 onward, the allocated vehicle was a camping coach converted from a Pullman car, which was fitted with a full kitchen, two sleeping compartments and a room with two single beds; from 1962 until 1967 there were two such vehicles here.

While the development of Swanage as a tourist resort brought additional passenger traffic to the branch, the collapse of both the clay and marble ventures, and the increase in private automobile ownership during the second half of the 20th century made operations unprofitable. Closure was first proposed during 1967, and despite local opposition the branch finally shut down on 3 January 1972. During the final few years of operations under British Rail, passenger services were operated by two-car Class 205 diesel electric multiple units (also known as type 2H).

From the time of the first proposal for shutdown, a campaign to reopen the branch as a steam locomotive operated heritage operation developed. Most of the track bed, including this facility, was bought by Dorset County Council. Proposals to use the corridor through the gap as a road bypass for the settlement were eventually rejected by the county council during 1986. In the meantime the Swanage Railway had started operating a steam service at the Swanage end during 1982.

There were concerns that reopening this facility as a northern terminus for the heritage operation would cause parking problems in the settlement. It was therefore decided to extend the branch a further half mile northward to a new Park and Ride site built on the former location of the exchange sidings between the branch and the clay tramways. Here the new Norden facility was constructed and most services terminate there. This facility reopened on 12 August 1995, although the official inauguration was not until February of the following year.

A 5-year project by volunteers to install a footbridge across the running tracks between the platforms was completed during April 2007, when David Quarmby, CBE, carried out the official inauguration. The footbridge was originally constructed during 1893 by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway. With cast-iron columns and a wrought iron span, the structure spent its life at Merton Park in London, near Wimbledon, on the West Croydon branch until removed by volunteers. The footbridge can accommodate the people who now use this facility, and is safer and more convenient for the public than crossing over via the gated and locked foot crossing. The project won the National Railway Heritage Awards during December 2007, with a plaque presented to civil engineer Philip Wycliffe-Jones and his team of volunteers by the late Gwyneth Dunwoody, Chairman of the House of Commons' Transport Select Committee.

During summer 2018 and 2019 South Western Railway operated two services per day to/from Wareham, one of which continued to Poole and the other to London Waterloo via Weymouth. There were also National Rail operations on Saturdays and Sundays between Wareham and Swanage during summer 2018 and 2019 operated by West Coast Railway Company with three services per day in each direction. However, during July 2019 these operations were stopped and there are currently no National Rail operations to this location.

Operations
Operations run every day from the beginning of April to late October, with weekend only operation during March, November and December. The level of service varies from 6 to 17 departures a day in each direction, depending on the season and the day of the week. Southbound, departures operate to stops at Harman's Cross (10 mins), Herston (departures stop only on request), and Swanage (21 mins). Northbound, departures operate to Norden (3 mins).

Exhibition
This facility is also the home of the heritage operation's Railway Museum, which is housed in the old goods shed and an adjacent rail van. The exhibition is open on most operating days.

The exhibition includes Secundus, a narrow gauge steam engine built by Bellis and Seeking during 1874 for the nearby Furzebrook Railway. This engine was in use until 1955, and then displayed in the now defunct Birmingham Museum of Science and Industry until 2000. It is planned that the engine will eventually be transferred to a new home at the Purbeck Mineral and Mining Museum, currently being developed adjacent to Norden.

Matt Wozniak (born January 6, 1983) is a Canadian curler from Winnipeg, Manitoba. He currently plays second on Team Jason Gunnlaugson. Wozniak is the former vice for the Mike McEwen squad which competed out of the Assiniboine Memorial Curling Club in Winnipeg.

Career

2005–2010
In 2005, Wozniak joined the new Mike McEwen rink that included Justin Richter and Andrew Melnuk. For the 2006-07 season, Richter and Melnuk left the squad and were replaced with Geordie Hargreaves and Adam Guenther. The foursome disbanded after just one campaign together.

Wozniak and McEwen joined with brothers Denni and B. J. Neufeld in 2007. In their first year together, they were a semi-finalist at the 2008 Safeway Championship, Manitoba's provincial competition. Their first Grand Slam event as a unit was at the end of that period, at the 2008 Players' Championships. The foursome won two games, before being eliminated.

At the conclusion of the 2008-09 campaign the McEwen squad was ranked 7th on the CCA rankings. They had made it to three Grand Slam playoffs, and finished 4th at the 2009 Safeway Championship.

During the 'Road to the Roar' 2009 Olympic Qualifier, the McEwen rink just lost out to fellow Manitobans the Jason Gunnlaugson foursome in the semi-finals. Team McEwen thus missed out on the 2009 Canadian Olympic Curling Trials finale despite being the favourite in that particular matchup versus Gunnlaugson.

McEwen's squad made it to his first provincial finale in 2010, when he lost to Jeff Stoughton in the 2010 Manitoba provincial championship. The contest was being played in Steinbach, Manitoba and as the Neufeld brothers and their father have roots in Steinbach, were treated very much as the home unit and crowd favourites.

2010-2015: Grand Slam success and perennial provincial runner-up
Team McEwen started the 2010-11 campaign off well by defeating provincial rival Jeff Stoughton to win the World Cup of Curling and his first ever Grand Slam title in November, 2010. In part of the teams runner-up result in the provincial finals of 2010 and in part because of his 4 victories and leading the overall money winnings in the World Curling Tour season as of November 2010, the McEwen squad was named as a nominee for the provincial unit of the year by the Manitoba Sportswriters and Sportscasters Association.

The foursome continued their strong campaign that year by defeating provincial rival Stoughton in the semi-finale of the 2011 Canadian Open. They would then go on to beat the Glenn Howard rink in the extra end of the championship, thus winning their second career Grand Slam and their second of that period.

Wozniak's squad once again made it to the Manitoba provincial competition this time, being the top seed (also ranked 1st in Canada). However, once again lost to Stoughton in the finale of the 2011 Safeway Championship, losing by one point in the concluding end. The McEwen foursome then lost their third straight provincial championship contest at the 2012 Safeway Championship, this time losing to Rob Fournier, thus tying a provincial record for consecutive finale losses previous set by Kerry Burtnyk from 97-99. This dubious record was avoided in 2013, when the McEwen rink failed to reach the championship, but again losing to the rival Stoughton squad in the 2013 Safeway Championship semi-finale. Once again, at the 2014 Safeway Championship, the unit lost the finale to Stoughton.

Despite being ranked first in the world on both the World Curling Tour Order of Merit rankings and on the WCT money list, Wozniak lost his fifth provincial championship in six years in 2015, losing to Reid Carruthers.

Three Briers and squad breakup 
Wozniak's foursome won their first provincial title in 2016, sending them to their first Brier. The Matt Dunstone rink had committed themselves to the 2016 World Junior Curling Championships, which occurred at the same time as the 2016 Tim Hortons Brier, so when the Dunstone squad beat Reid Carruthers in the semi-finale, McEwen's unit would go to the Brier, even if they had lost to Dunstone.

In 2017, Wozniak defended his Manitoba Championship by beating Reid Carruthers in the championship. He would then better his 2016 Brier showing, going 9–2 in the round robin to enter the playoffs in first place and with hammer and choice of rocks (Brad Gushue was also 9–2 but lost first place due to losing his round robin meeting with Manitoba). He then lost 7–5 to Brad Gushue in the 1 versus 2 contest. In the semi finals against reigning Brier and World Champion Kevin Koe, they were in control for most of the match, being up 5–3 with hammer in the eighth end, but Koe made a comeback with a steal in the eighth end, two points in the tenth end, and another steal in the extra end, dropping Manitoba to the bronze medal contest. They recovered to win their first Brier medal, defeating Brad Jacobs in their rematch of the 2016 bronze medal match, 7–6 in an extra end.

While competing at the 2018 Viterra Championship, skip McEwen came down with chickenpox and was unable to play after the first contest. B. J. Neufeld skipped the squad, until a surprise appearance by McEwen in the championship, where they lost to Carruthers. Despite the setback, they still had a chance to qualify for the 2018 Tim Hortons Brier through the wildcard match, which they won over Jason Gunnlaugson. Team McEwen had a difficult Brier and alongside Carruthers was unable to qualify for the playoffs. Following the Brier, the McEwen foursome announced they would be breaking up at the end of the 2017–18 campaign. Just days after the announcement, the McEwen squad won the 2018 Elite 10 Grand Slam of Curling event, winning the top $28,000 prize money, and was the first unit to go through the entire competition undefeated. The Grand Slam victory was the squad's seventh overall.

Wozniak took a few years off from men's play after Team McEwen broke up. However, he played mixed doubles with his current girlfriend Marlene Albrecht and spared for McEwen's new foursome. After Alex Forrest stepped away from competitive curling after the 2019–20 campaign, Wozniak joined the Jason Gunnlaugson rink. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic in Manitoba, the 2021 provincial competition was cancelled. As Team Gunnlaugson were the reigning provincial champions, they were chosen to represent Manitoba at the 2021 Tim Hortons Brier. The health crisis forced organizers to cancel traditional qualifying events across the province, leaving officials with no choice but to select the defending titleholders as representatives for Manitoba's delegation to nationals. At the Brier, they finished with a 6–6 record, demonstrating respectable performance given the unusual circumstances surrounding their qualification pathway and the challenges posed by pandemic-related restrictions on practice opportunities.

Personal life
Wozniak is employed as a mortgage broker for Vertuity Mortgage. He is currently in a relationship with Swiss curler Marlene Albrecht and has two children with her, forming a family that bridges international curling communities.

Honeymoon Hotel is a 1934 Warner Bros. Merrie Melodies cartoon directed by Earl Duvall. The short was released on February 17, 1934.

The production was supervised by Earl Duvall. The characters were animated by Jack King, Frank Tipper, both credited, Bob Clampett, Paul Fennell, Chuck Jones and Frank Tashlin, final four uncredited. The music score was composed by Bernard Brown (solely credited) and Norman Spencer (solely uncredited). The sound was solely recorded by Bernard Brown in the uncredited. Production number 6125.

Plot
The cartoon follows a male and female bug/insect who check into a hotel which catches on fire.

Music
The song "Honeymoon Hotel" (by Al Dubin and Harry Warren) was originally introduced in the 1933 Warner Bros. film Footlight Parade. This short appears on the DVD release of that picture.

Color process
The production is notable for being the first Warner Bros. animated work produced in color. It used Cinecolor since Walt Disney had exclusive rights to the Technicolor process. There was only one other Merrie Melodies piece produced in Cinecolor (Beauty and the Beast) before the series went briefly back to black-and-white. Later, the Merrie Melodies moved to Technicolor, though the Looney Tunes continued to be made in black-and-white until 1943. Cinecolor would make a return in several late 1940s Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies shorts.

Operation Claw () constituted a collaborative Swedish–American endeavor, supported by Norway, executed at Lillehammer immediately following Germany's capitulation concluding World War II. Thirty-five intelligence specialists from the defeated nation were transported alongside various apparatus initially to Sweden, subsequently to U.S. detention facilities in occupied territory via an arrangement between Americans and the High Command of Wehrmacht forces stationed in Norway. Intelligence materials obtained from this undertaking, including a Soviet codebook, proved extremely valuable for the United States throughout the Cold War period. This endeavor generated controversy both during its execution and in subsequent decades. In 1945, disputes arose because Americans conducted activities in what was perceived as British-controlled territory, acquiring information concerning their ally, the USSR, while cooperating with neutral Sweden. In later decades, a theory emerged suggesting that resistance fighter Kai Holst's unexpected demise in June 1945 connected to his participation in this mission, a hypothesis advanced by historian Tore Pryser among others.

Even before European hostilities concluded, various allied nations had initiated searches for scientists and expertise from the defeated Reich. Signals interception had proven vital throughout the global conflict, particularly Britain's achievements in deciphering codes, notably breaking Enigma encryptions, which held enormous significance. The Yalta Conference during February 1945 exposed conflicting interests between western powers on one hand and the Soviet Union on another, severely straining relations. U.S. intelligence organizations showed intense interest in knowledge possessed by defeated nation's experts regarding the USSR, and immediately after European fighting ceased they commenced collaboration with Major General Reinhard Gehlen and his organization Fremde Heere Ost (FHO), which had directed intelligence gathering on the Eastern Front. This formed part of an organized campaign to acquire as much expertise and personnel as possible; this campaign bore the designation Target Intelligence Committee (TICOM). However, warfare continued in East Asia, with the US and Soviets remaining allies, and Washington counted on Moscow's assistance against Japan. The victorious powers had designated Norway within Britain's sphere of influence. Consequently, for both Washington and neutral Stockholm, this undertaking remained extremely sensitive, conducted under strict secrecy.

At the Wehrmacht detention center at Lillehammer, thirty-five specialists in signals interception had assembled. These individuals had served on the Eastern battlefront against Soviet armies and possessed archives plus extensive understanding about USSR matters. This represented knowledge Western powers, especially Washington, desired and which probably proved useful during subsequent Cold War tensions. Cooperating with the Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and with awareness and backing from the Norwegian legation in Stockholm, agents representing Swedish intelligence organization C-byrån traveled alongside two Norwegian intelligence personnel to Lillehammer on May 9 and 10, 1945. The group of specialists were extracted from detention and conveyed to Sweden. After several weeks there, they were flown on June 12 from Torslanda Airport near Gothenburg to zones under U.S. occupation and interned in a military facility at Wiesbaden.

The extraction to Sweden of these specialists at Lillehammer, which OSS designated as their undertaking, was orchestrated from the highest echelons. From Washington's perspective, OSS leader Major General William J. Donovan participated; from Stockholm's perspective, Defense Staff chief Major General Carl August Ehrensvärd directed matters. The renowned Swedish police director Harry Söderman also contributed from Stockholm's perspective.

More than thirty days after capitulation, a British-led search backed by Norwegian personnel was implemented to locate individuals from Gestapo and other key figures attempting concealment among ordinary soldiers in military detention centers. The search team that Kai Holst and fellow Norwegians were supporting soon discovered that numerous key individuals had been extracted in the Swedish–American endeavor a month prior. Kai Holst had served at military office number 4 (Mi4) at the Norwegian legation in Stockholm, and following the search he unexpectedly journeyed directly back to Stockholm. The following day he was discovered shot at the staircase summit in an apartment structure at Rindögatan 42 on Gärdet. The official explanation for his demise was declared as self-inflicted, but neither Holst's relatives nor numerous colleagues from resistance circles have accepted this conclusion and believe he was assassinated.

Historian Tore Pryser has advanced the theory that Holst carried information from Lillehammer potentially damaging to the endeavor and therefore was eliminated. To potentially harm the mission, Kai Holst cannot have been trusted as colleagues were. He must have been regarded as dangerous due to his relationship with Alexandra Kollontaj, who served as ambassador in Stockholm representing the Soviet government. A plausible motive for assassinating Kai Holst was therefore not his awareness itself but rather his associations.

This undertaking marked the beginning of postwar collaboration between Swedish and U.S. intelligence agencies, violating Sweden's officially proclaimed neutrality policy. From Washington's viewpoint, the mission was regarded as tremendously successful and those responsible within OSS, William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman, both received honors with decorations where the endeavor specifically received mention. For Swedish C-byrån, however, the venture quickly became poisonous. Even though the mission was meant to remain confidential, details leaked to Swedish media and C-byrån was dissolved in February 1946. Details regarding the undertaking continued being classified as restricted in postwar decades and portions still remain so presently. A document concerning the mission in British National Archives is sealed until 2020.
