"No Wedding Bells for Him" is a short story by British author P. G. Wodehouse, which first appeared in the United States in the October 1923 issue of Cosmopolitan, and in the United Kingdom in the November 1923 Strand. It features the irrepressible Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, and was included in the collection Ukridge, published in 1924.

Plot

Stanley and Corky run into a friend of Stanley's, a chauffeur driving a shiny new Daimler, and he offers to take them for a ride. Along the way they are seen by a creditor of Stanley's, whom they shake off, and almost hit a young girl, whom Stanley insists they drive to her home near Clapham Common. He befriends her family, who are impressed by the car and Stanley's famous Aunt Julia.

When Corky meets Stanley a week later in the British Museum, he is accompanied by two children. He reveals he has been visiting the house, mainly for the free food, and promising to take the family out on trips in his friend's car, which they believe to be his, and to introduce them to his aunt, who, he reveals, has disowned him, in a letter which states "from now on, I have no nephew".

Returning from short holiday, Corky hears from George Tupper that Stanley is engaged. Visiting his companion, he finds him with a black eye, and hears the tale of how Stanley found himself inadvertently engaged to the girl from Clapham Common, and got punched by a rival suitor named Finch. As they talk on Stanley's doorstep, the creditor from the car ride arrives, and Stanley hides. A friendly passer-by soothes the enraged creditor, arguing that he knows where Stanley lives; Stanley moves out of his house, remarking on the good fortune that led him to use the pseudonym "Mr. Smallweed" when dealing with the man.

Stanley and Corky form a plot to get Stanley out of the engagement by feigning ill-health, but as Corky is delivering his speech to the family, the passer-by arrives. He is George Finch, Stanley's rival for the girl; he reveals that Stanley is an impoverished imposter, in fact called Smallweed, and produces the creditor to prove it. He also bears a letter from Stanley's aunt, claiming that she has no nephew. Once Corky has paid off the debt to the creditor, the two are chased from the house.

Main characters

Stanley Featherstonehaugh Ukridge, the irrepressible entrepreneur
Julia Ukridge, his haughty writer aunt
Jimmy Corcoran, Stanley's writer companion
George Tupper, an old schoolfriend of Stanley and Jimmy
Frederick, a chauffeur, a companion of Stanley
Mabel Price, a girl Stanley meets on the road
Mr Price, her doting father
Ernie Finch, her admirer, a resourceful man
Mr Grindlay, a man Stanley owes money to, who knows him only as "Mr Smallweed"

Publication history

The narrative was illustrated by T. D. Skidmore in Cosmopolitan. It was illustrated by Reginald Cleaver in the Strand.

"No Wedding Bells for Him" was included in the 1932 collection Nothing But Wodehouse, edited by Ogden Nash and published by Doubleday, Doran & Company. It was included in Week-End Wodehouse (UK edition), first published by Herbert Jenkins Limited in 1939. It was also collected in The World of Ukridge, published in October 1975 by Barrie & Jenkins.

Adaptations

"No Wedding Bells for Him" was adapted for radio in 1956, with Michael Shepley as Stanley, Hubert Gregg as Jimmy, Olaf Pooley as Frederick, Jeffrey Segal as Mr Grindley, Mairhi Russell as Mabel Price, and Brewster Mason as George.

It was adapted for the television series The World of Wodehouse. The episode, titled "The Wedding Bells", aired in 1968, and incorporated the character Looney Coote (from "The Long Arm of Looney Coote").

Contemporary Hellenic visual expression encompasses creations from the era spanning the establishment of the newly autonomous Hellenic nation until the twentieth century.

Since continental Hellas remained under Ottoman dominion throughout four complete centuries, it did not participate in the Renaissance nor subsequent cultural movements sweeping through Western Europe. Nevertheless, Hellenic islands including Crete, plus the Ionian archipelago specifically, experienced extended intervals under Venetian or alternative European powers' governance, thereby gaining capacity to more effectively absorb the revolutionary aesthetic transformations occurring across Europe throughout the fourteenth through eighteenth centuries.

The Cretan School alongside notably the Heptanese School represent two significant cultural movements within Hellas that pursued parallel trajectories to Western Europe.

Contemporary Hellenic visual expression can be understood as having been chiefly molded by the distinctive socioeconomic circumstances of Hellas, the substantial Hellenic diaspora scattered throughout Europe, plus the emerging Hellenic social elite, along with external aesthetic influences, chiefly from Germany and France.

Three-dimensional works and pictorial creations

Nineteenth century

The Munich Academy

Contemporary Hellenic visual expression commenced development around the era of Romanticism. Hellenic creators absorbed numerous elements from their European counterparts, culminating in the emergence of the distinctive manner of Hellenic Romantic expression, motivated by revolutionary ideals alongside the nation's geography and heritage. Following centuries of Ottoman dominion, scarce opportunities for education in visual disciplines existed within the recently autonomous Hellas, so pursuing studies abroad proved imperative for creators. Munich, functioning as a crucial international hub for visual disciplines during that period, became the destination where the majority of Hellenic creators throughout the nineteenth century elected to pursue training. Within the academy of Munich, directed by Karl von Piloty, authentic fresco technique was instructed for mural creations on fresh wet lime plaster. Throughout this interval much visual expression proved emotional and theatrical in character. The most prominent subjects of the Munich academy included urban existence, rural existence, stationary objects, plus landscape scenery.

Subsequently, they would return to Hellas and transmit their expertise. Some remained in Munich, the so-called Athens on the Isar. Both institutional and personal connections developed between early Hellenic painters and Munich artistry giving birth to the Hellenic "Munich School" of pictorial creation. Nikolaos Gysis served as a crucial instructor and creator at the Munich Academy, soon becoming a leading figure among Hellenic creators. Academism, realism, genre depiction, upper middle class portraiture, stationary object representation and landscape depiction, frequently displaying impressionist characteristics, would be superseded at the conclusion of the nineteenth century by Symbolism, Jugendstil, Art Nouveau, which are predominantly traced in the output of Nikolaos Gysis, Aristeas and others. Early-twentieth-century modernism is similarly represented by significant Hellenic creators in Munich. Numerous these Munich School creators selected subjects including everyday Hellenic existence, local customs, plus living circumstances. Several prominent painters emerged during this interval. Theodoros Vryzakis specialized in historical depiction, especially motivated by the 1821 Hellenic War of Independence. Nikiphoros Lytras concentrated on realistic portrayals of Hellenic existence. Georgios Jakobides devoted his attention to infants and youngsters, later becoming the inaugural Director of the new National Gallery of Athens. Georgios Roilos was another leading painter of the interval closely associated with the Munich School, especially in his early career. Konstantinos Volanakis was motivated mostly by the Hellenic sea.

Additional creators associated with the Munich School included Symeon Sabbides, Yannoulis Chalepas, Leonidas Drosis, along with quite several modernist creators who pursued training in Munich, which encompassed Theofrastos Triantafyllidis, Jorgos Busianis, and additionally Giorgio de Chirico.

Notable sculptors of the new Hellenic Kingdom included Leonidas Drosis (his major output was the extensive neo-classical architectural ornament at the Academy of Athens), Lazaros Sochos, Georgios Vitalis, Dimitrios Filippotis, Ioannis Kossos, Yannoulis Chalepas, Georgios Bonanos plus Lazaros Fytalis.

The Parisian Academy

A few Hellenic painters pursued studies in Paris. Despite residing in the French capital and adhering to guidelines of the French Art Academy, they invariably possessed their own interpretations. Jacob Rizos was involved with the rendering of female grace, Theodoros Rallis with scenes from the Orthodox East and Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos with portraiture, stationary object representation plus genre depiction. Throughout this interval in Paris the avant-garde Impressionist movement developed, but most Hellenic painters remained faithful to the precepts of their instructors with only some nebulous thrusts in the direction of this movement. The initial Hellenic impressionist was Périclès Pantazis who, after Paris, settled in Belgium and became a component of the avant-garde group Circle de la pâte.

Subject matter and visual portrayals

Numerous Hellenic creators of this interval also drew upon El Greco's manner for motivation, particularly when producing expression based on religious subjects. This connected with the concept of contemporary secular Hellenic expression of the interval referencing more classical manners, while religious expression referenced Byzantine, or Byzantine motivated expression. Moreover, a crucial and frequently pioneering role was performed by creators from Ionian islands in the eighteenth century and the commencement of the nineteenth century, who exploited conquests of the Italian Renaissance and baroque workshops. As efforts persisted with new directions and objectives, Hellenic creators emerging in the world throughout the initial decades of the nineteenth century reconnected Hellenic expression with its ancient tradition, along with the quests of the European workshops, especially those of the Munich School, with defining examples of the Hellenic contemporary expression of the interval including the outputs of Theodoros Vryzakis and Nikiphoros Lytras.

Twentieth century

At the commencement of the twentieth century landscape depiction held sway and the interest of painters turned toward the examination of illumination and pigmentation. The dependence on Munich slackened and Paris became the pole of attraction for the creators of the interval. In the early twentieth century Demetrios Galanis, a contemporary and friend of Picasso, achieved wide recognition in France and lifelong membership of the Académie française following his acclaim by the critic Andre Malreaux as a creator capable "of stirring emotions as powerful as those of Giotto". Subsequently in the century Nikos Engonopoulos achieved international recognition with his surrealist conceptions both of pictorial creation and poetry, while in the late 1960s Dimitris Mytaras and Yiannis Psychopedis became associated with European critical realism. Impressionism was the original influence on the leading figures of the expression of the initial half of the twentieth century, Konstantinos Parthenis and Konstantinos Maleas, while Nikiphoros Lytras associated himself with the avant-garde groups of Munich constituting the final known connection with the series of painters in the great tradition of Munich in Hellenic expression. The further development of these painters led to alternative roads, but always within the framework of the avantgarde movement albeit with a Hellenic dimension.

Gradually the impressionists and alternative contemporary schools increased their influence. In the early twentieth century Hellenic creators turned from Munich to Paris. The interest of Hellenic painters, creators shifts from historical representations to Hellenic landscapes with an emphasis on illumination and pigments so abundant in Hellas. Representatives of this aesthetic transformation are Konstantinos Parthenis, Konstantinos Maleas, Nikiphoros Lytras and Georgios Bouzianis. Konstantinos Parthenis, specifically, introduces historical, religious and mythological elements that allow the classification of Hellenic pictorial creation into contemporary expression. The same is accurate with the landscapes of Konstantinos Maleas and the expressionism of Georgios Bouzianis. The interval of the 1930s was a landmark for the Hellenic painters, with Yiannis Tsarouchis, Yiannis Moralis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Kontopoulos (introduced abstraction in Hellenic depictions) and Spyros Papaloukas coming into the limelight of Hellenic Expression. These painters attempted mainly to connect leading European trends with Hellenic tradition.

Notable twentieth- and twenty-first-century creators

The second half of the twentieth century has witnessed a range of acclaimed Hellenic creators, including Constantine Andreou, recipient of the French Légion d'honneur, and Thodoros Papadimitriou, an internationally acclaimed sculptor. Giorgio de Chirico was an influential pre-Surrealist Hellenic-Italian painter who founded Metaphysical expression. Jannis Kounellis ranks among the pioneers of the Arte Povera aesthetic movement. Electros Vekris, Kinetic creator and Sculptor, is the most well-known creator to be working in the field of illumination, Sound and Motion. Theodoros Stamos was a renowned abstract expressionist painter. Takis, Chryssa and Constantin Xenakis are internationally acclaimed creators of Kinetic sculpture. Additional notable Hellenic creators are Hermon di Giovanno, Varotsos, Dimitris Mytaras, Spyros Vassiliou, Alekos Fassianos, Theocharis Mores, Dimitris Koukos (1948-), Nikos Stratakis, Steven Antonakos, Kostas Tsoklis, Nikos Hadjikyriakos-Ghikas, Thanassis Stephopoulos, Aggelika Korovessi, and Yiannis Melanitis.

He took another drag from the cigarette, pondering how self-destructive behavior was truly our most human trait. Peering back at the alien creature, more focused on contrasts between our species than similarities. "So are you guys finally ready to let us in the Intergalactic Council? Have we proven ourselves?" His inquiry had a flippant and sarcastic edge, which he knew, after many encounters with this foreign being, wouldn't be lost on Zor't.

"Well, you've demonstrated yourselves in several capacities, none of which are sought after in the assembly." He thumbed through some electronic documents, scrutinizing each thoroughly, although briefly. "Innovation from your kind seems like it is only driven through conflict and destruction. Your warmongers, that you call 'politicians' and 'monarchs,' instigate mass murder and genocide, then the destitute members of those societies carry them out. Why do the indigent and poor from your world hate each other so?"

It was almost more infuriating that he asked in earnest rather than to taunt me. I had always thought of warfare being Darwinian in nature: the strong deserve to live, the weak do not. If Darwin is right, how did these peace freaks ever evolve from primordial ooze?

"I cannot answer for the past. Our ancestors were violent, greedy creatures." That seemed agreeable enough. Zor't appeared to ponder on it a moment, before he followed up with an unexpected response.

"Since we established contact, our sensors lead us to believe that an abundant amount of your resources have been redirected to weapon-manufacturing sites. Why is this so?"

"I know nothing of what you speak. It would go against the decree set forth by the assembly. Perhaps you've misread your sensor data."

Zor't seemed acutely indignant from the implication that they'd misinterpreted information. "Mr. Hartigan, we do not misinterpret facts. This is not hubris, it is truth. You have diverted an alarming quantity of your materials towards armament production, at great peril to the poorer among you, who now starve and riot outside this very building. We at the governing body not only abhor brutality, but are incapable altogether of inflicting it. This is gross misconduct and will be grounds for your denial from membership, and I will see to it personally."

Boy, Zor't can get fiery about his peace-loving. Too bad the hippies couldn't get elected, or maybe Zor't would have it his way. I almost feel sorry for him. Incapable of aggression.....

"That's all I needed to hear. Thank you Councillor."

As the bullet entered the chamber, the barrel rose to meet Zor't's face. As the firing pin struck the charge, he closed his eyes and seemed at peace, prepared for the end. Was it acceptance? Was it bravery? Or was it something else..... Can fear exist without brutality?..... hmm. That's a question for philosophers and scientists, not diplomats like myself.

Now, let's show the governing assembly how aggressive humans can be to get what we want. Let's demonstrate the capacity for mayhem that defines our race. Let's prove that ruthlessness drives us forward when obstacles block our path to power and recognition among the stars.

Its employees, like me, all share one little gift from the Chief Executive: Immortality. So long as we continue to do our jobs, we're given all the time we could ever want or need. A large chunk, usually a bit less than three quarters of it, is spent working. Mostly because there are so many people running around the world dying at any given moment. Even with the advantage of existing outside of Time and Space, we Reapers still have a bit of trouble processing all the folks who are expiring. Of course, we can all still take off a quarter of our infinity to chill out on Earth or around the Department's Campus, and that leads to another fun thing that being immortal causes: you get individuals from everywhere and everywhen you can think of. One of the older reapers was around when the Aztec Empire was basically a handful of guys with an insane idea involving a cactus, a snake, and an eagle. Another of us was on the Senate Floor when Gaius Julius Caesar was killed. You get a lot of weird interactions when you mix in so many individuals. For example, you get Roman sitting in front of a big screen TV watching a Chariot Race from back when the Empire was at its height. The Aztec is chatting with a Norseman about the merits of hanging as opposed to cutting the heart out as a method of ritual sacrifice. Some of the Americans, such as myself, are chatting about college sports around a water cooler, and the younger members of our staff are setup in the region we call "The Arcade." After all those folks... there's the guy at the bar. He's the oldest of the Reapers. We don't even know the guy's name, since he hasn't bothered telling anyone and his records are covered up. He doesn't get out much, but we've all seen him milling around the Department. Never seen him in the Break Room though, much less at the bar. We've got every drink imagined, at least up until the present day out on Earth. I took a seat next to him. "Evening," I said without thinking too much about the guy understanding me since Language barriers don't exist for Reapers, we hear everything in our native language. Everyone hears us in their native tongue as well, which leads to all kinds of insanity in the modern world... or when we talk to individuals in Ancient Greece or Rome. "Evening," the Eldest said. His voice sounded deep, and ancient. "What are you drinking to," I asked. "Death," the Eldest said. I didn't laugh, and neither did he. "Whose?" I asked. "Millions," he said. I nodded in reply. Reapers may be immortal, and we may have a lot of not-quite-natural abilities, but we're all still human at our core. Our minds are just like the minds of the individuals we reap, and doing our job is rough. I'd honestly call it the hardest job in the world... having to be there when someone's dying. Seeing the grieving families of those who slip away to cancer, or other diseases, and having to deliver a bitter mercy to spare someone the pain. That's not even thinking about the horrors you get when you walk into a combat zone to retrieve the deceased, or have to retrieve someone who succumbed to despair... Anyway, there isn't a Reaper on staff who hasn't gotten depressed over that, over not being able to help the expiring beyond giving them the bitter mercy that is death. We're all human, and we all still have our empathy. I figured that the Eldest had managed to experience that. "You talked to the Counselors about it?" I asked. The Counselors aren't Reapers for the most part. They're among the Dead, the individuals who live in whatever comes next. They're also volunteers who come into the Department to help us out with our mental hang-ups. I know I spend a lot of time talking to 'em. "No..." the guy said, "at least... not this century." "Which deaths have you down?" I asked. "Fratricide..." the Reaper said, "It... it reminds me of myself a bit too much." I nodded. Reapers come in all forms. Some of us are like me, and we took the job offer to get someone else a better afterlife than they would have had otherwise. Some are here serving to get themselves into something halfway decent. The Eldest was apparently among the latter. "So," I said, "You thought about requesting that those assignments be diverted to other Reapers?" "Can't..." he said, "It's part of my... my sentence." "Ouch," I said, and I genuinely meant it. When it comes to Reapers like the Eldest, they have something called a Sentence which is designed to reform them to a state where they would be acceptable in the Afterlife they're due to be sent to. It's a set of obligations they must fulfill, or be sent on ahead of schedule to one of the... less desirable final rests. If they're lucky, they just get reincarnated. If they're unlucky, they're supposed to get thrown into Torment. "It's just..." He said, "I've seen so many of them. Every time I go out... I don't see the person I'm sent for. I see someone... someone I knew back before I was a Reaper... and I see myself standing over them." I saw a tear roll down the Eldest's cheek at those words, and I remained silent. The weight of his confession hung heavily between us, filling the space with unspoken understanding. His burden seemed almost unbearable, a constant reminder of past transgressions that haunted every assignment. "Damn it..." the Eldest said, "I need to get back to work... need to get out of here..." "Luck," I said, "and consider scheduling an appointment. We don't need you going renegade. That generally results in a lot of paperwork for the rest of us." The Eldest scoffed at that, and nodded in my direction as he got up to leave. It was only once he'd left the room that I realized that I still didn't have his name. The mystery remained unsolved, another enigma in our strange existence within these walls.

She speaks of a radical transformation in audience profile, of a lack of representation of people from BAME background among the staff and in the sector more generally. But when discussing the organization she now leads, which is to be the agent for the reform she desires, she remarks, "it's not that we need to alter anything particularly." There exists no doubt she is sincere in her ambitions, and probably more capable than most in the museum and exhibition world when broadening the demographic. But if she is to be successful in her aims she will need to take a leaf out of Sir Nicholas's job application for the director's position back in the nineteen-eighties - in which he wrote that for the institution to evolve he would need to grasp the nettle. Typically the inexpensive advertised rates apply to term coverage. Such protection has an expiration date, and is generally used during periods of higher expenses.... for instance, one might purchase temporary protection that lapses when children graduate university or a home loan is repaid, to ensure that an untimely demise doesn't prevent offspring from attending school or forcing a surviving partner to sell property. But if you survive until that point in time, the contract lapses without payout. So say the average purchaser is in their 30's and maintains coverage into their 50's or 60's.... most will survive, so only a small fraction pay out and those that don't help fund those that do.

The chances of a disbursement are so minimal and the number of individuals paying is so large. For example let's say 100 customers buy a 100 dollar plan for 10 dollars and 1 individual dies. The insurer gets 100 times 10 equals 1000 dollars. The carrier pays 100 to the deceased person's estate leaving them with 900 dollars. The firm can also invest the 900 and earn returns from investing. Now raise the quantity of customers purchasing policies and lower the percentage making claims and potential profits for companies are huge. Insurers are also very careful to screen out individuals who are more likely to file a claim. Coverage is difficult or impossible to obtain if you have a threatening condition, vehicle protection gets harder the worse your driving record is, etc.

It isn't cheap by accident. The payouts are calculated based on probability and odds. Also the length of the contract and a myriad of other factors come into play. Make no mistake; the industry is in it for profit. Just like a casino, if you put a quarter in a slot machine, you may win thousands. Actuaries carefully analyze mortality tables, risk pools, and demographic data to price premiums accordingly. Statistical models predict expected losses with remarkable accuracy, ensuring sustainable business operations while providing valuable financial security to policyholders and their beneficiaries.

The truth is that Canada isn't far superior to the United States. They aren't far inferior either. If you listen to rworldnews or rpolitics you could come to believe that America is some third-world police state. The truth is the USA is a fairly good place to live.

Uprooting your existence, leaving everything you've ever known, and starting over in a new nation is incredibly difficult. It's not something you want to do unless your current situation really is hopeless. People in the States don't feel that their lives would improve all that much to justify the effort. Plus, developed nations like Canada don't just let anyone in, there's likely a long and expensive immigration process.

Canada is in general more expensive to reside than America. It's also generally a lot colder. If a sudden influx of individuals appeared in the northern country, chances are the vast majority wouldn't be able to get jobs anyway so what good are labor laws then?

Why would there be mass immigration? There are no ground wars in the United States or its northern neighbor. The majority of Americans and Canadians have comfortable existences and raise their families in peace. We're both HUGE nations, but we are allies, and we don't persecute one another. Our governments might be a little different, but basically we're pretty homogeneous. Also, the Canadian dollar is worth approximately seventy-six cents in US currency. And the northern territory is frigid.

Because the idea of the USA being a dystopia that is falling apart at the seams is a bunch of bullshit spouted by idiotic teenagers from the States who think they endure a hard existence because they can't afford a brand-new iPhone every year and European trolls. There really isn't much difference between residing in the northern neighbor, the United States or Europe except that the first option is really boring.

Individuals mobile enough to immigrate often can make more money in America. Not everyone wants to uproot their existence for what would be a slight increase in standard of living. It is cold in the northern territory, especially in the places that would be affordable to immigrants.

Existence in the USA isn't as bad as angry teenagers on Reddit would have you believe. It has its downsides, sure, but every location has its problems. Overall it's not too terrible for most individuals. The reality remains that both neighboring countries offer reasonable quality of existence for their residents despite political rhetoric suggesting otherwise.

Section 51(xxxi) is a subclause of section 51 of the Constitution of Australia.

It empowers the Commonwealth to make laws regarding the acquisition of property, but stipulates that such acquisitions must be on just terms.

The provision is sometimes referred to in shorthand as the 'just terms' clause.

Aside from its importance to Australian Constitutional Law, and Property Law; this subsection is notable for its role as a plot device in The Castle, an iconic Australian film.

Text 
Section 51(xxxi) reads:

Jurisprudence 
While s51(xxxi) was adapted from the US Constitution's Fifth Amendment, it has many differences.

The 'just terms' requirement has been held not to affect the State Parliaments.

In Grace Bros Pty Ltd v The Commonwealth (1946), Justice Dixon stated that the inclusion of the condition was to "prevent arbitrary exercises of the power at the expense of a State or a subject."

The interpretation of the concepts "acquisition" and "just terms" by the High Court of Australia have had the effect, however, of limiting its protection of property rights. Moreover, it operates at any time the Commonwealth makes a compulsory acquisition of property. As such, it is a contingent guarantee rather than a general constitutional right or freedom to enjoy proprietary entitlements.

The Commonwealth may only acquire property on just terms for a "purpose in respect of which the Parliament has power to make laws". This means that every law supported by s 51(xxxi) must not be supported by any other additional legislative power.

Property
The High Court of Australia has taken a wide view of the concept of "property". Several members of the court took the opportunity to consider the meaning of the term property in Minister of State for the Army v Dalziel (1944). Justice Starke said the word includes: "every species of valuable right and interest including real and personal property, incorporeal hereditaments such as rents and services, rights-of-way, rights of profit or use in land of another, and choses in action. Justice McTiernan confirmed the expression extends to tangible and intangible assets.

An example of the breadth of the notion of ownership in section 51(xxxi) is provided by Bank of New South Wales v Commonwealth (the Bank Nationalisation Case). In that case, Federal legislation contemplated the taking of private banks through vesting of shares in private banks in the Commonwealth, and later the appointment of directors by the Governor of the Commonwealth Bank. Justice Dixon characterised the provisions as removing effective control over the holdings of the private banks. He concluded that this was, in the essential sense, an appropriation of a proprietary entitlement.

While statutory licences have sometimes been equated with proprietary interests, the removal of privileges enjoyed under a statutory licence does not typically constitute an acquisition of property within section 51(xxxi), as licence conditions are inherently susceptible to change.

Acquisition
For the purposes of section 51(xxxi), property must have been acquired by somebody, and the appropriation must be for a Commonwealth purpose. This is in contrast to the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution, where the destination does not matter – it is enough that the holder of possessions has been deprived of them. Thus in JT International SA v Commonwealth the High Court held that the Commonwealth's plain tobacco packaging laws, which restricted the plaintiff's use of its trademark, did not involve the Commonwealth acquiring any assets. Similarly in Cunningham v Commonwealth the High Court held that changes to the retiring allowances and life Gold Pass for retired members of Parliament were not an acquisition of property.

In P J Magennis Pty Ltd v Commonwealth the High Court held that a grant to NSW which was tied to NSW compulsorily acquiring property was invalid as an acquisition of property upon terms which were not just. The validity of a grant in the absence of a requirement to acquire property was upheld in the later case of Pye v Renshaw.

Just terms
Typically, a determination of just terms based on the market value of the property at the time of acquisition will be sufficient to satisfy the requirement of just terms. Unlike the "just compensation" requirement in the American Fifth Amendment, however, "just terms" imports no equivalence of market value. The arrangements offered must be "fair", or such that a legislature could reasonably regard them as "fair". However, this judgment of "fairness" must take account of all the interests affected, not just those of the dispossessed owner.

The requirement of "just terms" does not necessarily require that a compensation package be presented as part of the acquisition scheme. It is sufficient that the scheme provides adequate procedures for determining fair recompense. However, the Court may scrutinise such procedures closely to ensure their adequacy.

There may be some acquisitions of property to which section 51(xxxi) does not apply, such as those made under laws supported exclusively by section 122 of the Constitution.

Section 51(xxxi) is an exception to the norm for interpretation of the subsections of section 51, that one grant of power cannot be used to "read down" another. In this instance, however, the Court will not allow another authorization of authority to be read so broadly as to circumvent the specific limitation to the power granted by section 51(xxxi).

Related legislation
The Deakin government's Lands Acquisition Act 1906, largely drafted by Littleton Groom, was the first to deal with the compulsory acquisition of land by the federal government. Its most contentious provision was a clause authorising the federal government to grant mining leases and regulate mining on Commonwealth land. Responsibility for compulsory appropriation was initially placed with the Department of Home Affairs.

The Chifley government's Darwin Lands Acquisition Act 1945 compulsorily acquired parcels of land owned by Chinese-Australians in Darwin, leading to the end of the local Chinatown. The legislation was suggested in 1943 by the Northern Territory's administrator Aubrey Abbott, who proposed a combination of compulsory seizure and conversion of the territory to leasehold in order to effect "the elimination of undesirable elements which Darwin has suffered from far too much in the past" and stated that he hoped to "entirely prevent the Chinese quarter forming again". He further observed that "if parcels are seized from the former Chinese residents there is really no need for them to return as they have no other assets". The territory's civilian population had mostly been evacuated during the war and the former Chinatown residents returned to find their homes and businesses reduced to rubble. This historical episode demonstrates how constitutional powers concerning appropriation could be deployed toward discriminatory ends, illustrating tensions between formal legal frameworks and substantive justice outcomes in practice.

They're not costless though, are they. Both participants regardless of location require an internet connection. Even if you both used complimentary wifi, the wireless service is gratis to entice business and is still being paid for. The fact that it appears without charge is down to it utilizing the web which is borderless. For traditional voice and messaging it requires your provider paying the carrier in the other nation for their service to deliver the call or message. Although usually the fees are massively inflated. Bottom line you pay either way just in a different manner.

Telephone systems were built a long time ago, when international communication was really expensive - that set a precedent. Generally telecommunications companies were national monopolies, often with legal protection from competition. So they would impose high charges to other telecoms trying to hand conversations into their territory. They could do this because there was no other option and cross-border calling rates weren't worried about by most individuals (in effect these levies were like the cream that the teleco was allowed in payment for providing an affordable domestic dialing infrastructure). Then the digital network came along. Many ISPs started as small competitive startups offering connectivity over telephone lines (dial up). That meant they were keen to freely interconnect with content suppliers as it made them more competitive (by providing better access to their customers), even when they were far apart they could get cheap links as they'd have access to a "telecom hotel" with lots of enterprises competing to offer connections between cities, towns, etc. So online entry has become very inexpensive, while landline operators haven't kept up.

NB: this should also provide you with a good background on net neutrality. As the US shifts to a monopolised infrastructure (you could dial into any dial-up supplier but most Americans only have one or two high-speed cable options) ISPs are trying to shift back to the old model where they had much more power over what they charged consumers. In countries with more open infrastructure (eg in NZ you can choose any fibre provider in your local exchange, normally a few dozen alternatives) this isn't such an issue.

You're already a mobile operator customer (trying to earn more). Skype is still hoping to make you a patron (earn anything).

Master effective notation skills to become even more successful. Consult "Part 2 of 3: Recording Observations" for additional guidance.

This preparation readies pupils for instruction faster so they aren't rummaging through their school bags when it's actually time to utilize supplies. lexical_diversity_up_hard.coling::79eb7194-07a0-4dd2-a0b2-7911976f: Judith Scott (May 1, 1943 – March 15, 2005) was an American fiber sculptor, born with Down Syndrome and deaf. She was internationally renowned for her artwork. In 1987, Judith enrolled at the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, California which supports people with developmental disabilities. There, Judith discovered her passion and talent for abstract textile creations and she was able to communicate in a novel form. An account of Scott's existence, Entwined: Sisters and Secrets in the Silent World of Artist Judith Scott (2016) has been written by her twin sibling. Judith was born into a middle-class family in Cincinnati, Ohio in May 1, 1943 along with her fraternal twin Joyce. Unlike Joyce, Judith arrived with Down Syndrome. During infancy, Judith suffered from Scarlet Fever, which caused her to lose hearing, a fact that remained unknown until much later on in existence. Judith Scott spent her first seven and a half years at home with parents, twin and older brothers. Although the developmental gap between the two girls was apparent, "the parents consciously sought to treat these youngest members of the household alike." However, when it was time for the girls to start attending school, Judith was found to be "ineducable." There existed only one classroom for children with disabilities, and Judith could not pass the verbally-based entrance tests, due to her still undiagnosed deafness. Consequently, on medical advice, parental figures placed Judith in the Columbus State Institution (formerly the Columbus State School), an establishment for the mentally disabled, on October 18, 1950. This separation had a profound effect on both twins. The records from Judith Scott's first few years at the Institution indicate that she possessed an IQ of 30 (based upon oral testing before deafness was recognized). For this reason she was denied any training opportunities. Deprived of her twin, Judith became severely alienated, and behavioral problems soon surfaced. Her Clinical Record states that "She does not seem to be in good contact with environment. She does not get along well with other youngsters, is restless, eats messily, tears clothing, and beats other youngsters. Her presence on the ward is a disturbing influence." Soon after, she was moved to a smaller state establishment at Gallipolis, Ohio. In 1985, after 35 years of complete separation and lengthy and difficult negotiations, Joyce became her sister's legal guardian, and brought Judith to live with her in California, a state where all mentally disabled citizens are entitled to an ongoing education. Judith died of natural causes at her sister's residence in Dutch Flat, California, a few weeks short of her 62nd birthday. She outlived life expectancy at birth by almost fifty years. On April 1, 1987, Judith began attending the Creative Growth Art Center in Oakland, one of the first organizations in the world to provide studio space for artists with disabilities. For almost two years, Judith showed little interest in any artistic activity. She was unexceptional with paint. She scribbled loops and circles, but work contained no representational imagery, and she was so uninterested in creating that the staff considered ending involvement with the program. It wasn't until Judith casually observed a fiber class conducted by visiting practitioner Sylvia Seventy, that she had her artistic breakthrough. Using the materials at hand, Judith spontaneously invented her own unique and radically different mode of artistic expression. While other students were stitching, she was sculpting with an unprecedented zeal and concentration. Her creative gifts and absolute focus were quickly recognized, and she received complete freedom to choose her own materials. Taking whatever objects she found, regardless of ownership, she would wrap them in carefully selected colored yarns to construct diverse sculptures of many different shapes. Some resemble cocoons or body parts, while others are elongated totemic poles. Many of works also feature pairs, reflecting Scott's experience as a twin. Judith worked on creations five days a week for eighteen years, producing over 200 pieces in total. Judith had her first exhibition in 1999, which coincided with the publication of John MacGregor's book Metamorphosis: The Fiber Art of Judith Scott. Together, these events helped propel her to worldwide recognition. Scott's output has become immensely popular in the realm of outsider creativity, and pieces sell for substantial sums. Scott is now hailed as a contemporary practitioner, no longer just an outsider. Her creations are held in the permanent collections of many museums, including: Museum of Modern Art (Manhattan, New York), the American Visionary Art Museum (Baltimore, Maryland), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Museum of American Folk Art (Manhattan, New York), Intuit: The Center for Intuitive and Outsider Art (Chicago, Illinois), Irish Museum of Modern Art, Dublin, The Oakland Museum, Oakland, CA. L'Aracine Musee D'Art Brut (Paris, France), Art Brut Connaissance & Diffusion Collection (Paris and Prague), Collection de l'art brut (Lausanne, Switzerland). Below is a list of select notable exhibitions for Judith Scott. 2018 – Judith Scott: Touchdown, Creative Growth Art Center, Oakland, California 2014-15 – Bound and Unbound, Brooklyn Museum, Brooklyn, New York 2009 – Judith Scott: Retrospective, Ricco Maresca Gallery, New York City, New York 2002 – Cocoon: Judith Scott, Ricco-Maresca Gallery, New York City, New York 2019 – Memory Palaces: Inside the Collection of Audrey B. Heckler, American Folk Art Museum, New York City, New York 2019 – The Doors of Perception, Curated by Javier Téllez in collaboration with the Outsider Art Fair, Frieze Art Fair, New York City, New York 2019 – Flying High: Women Artists of Art Brut, Bank Austria Kunstforum, Vienna 2018 – Outliers and American Vanguard Art, National Gallery of Art, Washington DC 2017 – Forget Me Not: Judith Scott, Zuckerman Museum of Art, Kennesaw, Georgia 2017 – Viva Arte Viva, the 57th Venice Biennale, Venice, Italy 2015 – Collection ABCD, La Maison Rouge, Paris, France 2013 – Create, Creative Growth Art Center, Oakland, California 2013 – Create, Boca Raton Museum of Art, Boca Raton, Florida 2013 – Extreme Art, The Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum, Ridgefield, Connecticut 2012 – Rosemarie Trockel: A Cosmos, New Museum of Contemporary Art, New York City, New York 2011 – World Transformers, Schirn Kunsthalle Frankfurt, Frankfurt, Germany 2000 – Visions, American Visionary Art Museum, Baltimore, Maryland 2005 – Creative Growth, The Ricky Jay Broadside Collection, Yerba Buena Center for the Arts, San Francisco, California

After the discussion below, I examined previous work by these authors (MUS-ROVER) on which this manuscript was based. On one hand, such examination proved very helpful for me to better understand the current submission. On the other hand, this investigation was very needed for me to better comprehend the present manuscript.

Overall, while I believe that I appreciate this research, and while I am familiar with the JSB chorales, with probabilistic approaches, with n-grams, etc, I did find the document quite hard to follow at various parts. The extensive use of notation did not help the clarity.

I believe the concepts and methodologies are good, and certainly worth publishing and worth pursuing. I am not sure that, in the submission's current form, ICLR is an appropriate venue. (Incidentally, the issue is not the application as I consider that music applications can be very appropriate, nor is the problem necessarily with the methodology... see my next suggestion..). I get the sense that a long-form journal publication would actually give the researchers the space necessary to fully explain these ideas, provide clearer running examples where needed, supply the necessary background for the appropriate readership, offer the requisite context on the previous system, perhaps demonstrating results on a second dataset to show generality of the technique, etc. A short conference submission just seems to me to be too dense a format for giving this project the description it merits. If it were possible to focus on just one aspect of this framework, then that might succeed, but I do not have good suggestions for exactly how to accomplish that.

If the document were revised substantially (though I cannot suggest details for how to accomplish this within the appropriate page count), I would consider raising my score. I do believe that the effort would be better invested in turning this into a long (and clearer) journal article.

Two Pennsylvania financial institution thieves are believed to possess military experience and are being described by federal investigators as 'armed and extremely dangerous'. A pair of masked criminals carrying handguns have stolen from three lending establishments in the Pittsburgh region so far this year, most recently on April 10. The unknown perpetrators, who are seen on surveillance footage pointing their firearms at teller heads, have threatened to abduct those at their targets and shoot law enforcement officers. However, the manner that the duo handle their weapons has led federal agents to suspect that the bandits are actually former police themselves.

Authorities believe that the two financial institution thieves suspected in a string of recent heists may possess law enforcement or military experience because of the way they grip a firearm. Officials say that the robberies, most recently on April 10, have become increasingly violent, with the criminals threatening kidnappings and saying they will fire upon officers if engaged.
